items.title: filer: keep generated inodes in signed 64-bit range
items.body:
## What changed

- Keep path-based and hard-link inode values within the positive signed 64-bit range.
- Reserve zero by converting the rare zero result to one.
- Add regression coverage for both inode generation paths.

## Why

SeaweedFS exposes inodes as `uint64`, but generated values are persisted by metadata stores whose integer fields commonly use signed 64-bit values. A generated inode with the high bit set cannot be encoded into an Elasticsearch `long`, causing metadata writes to fail for affected paths or hard links.

Masking generated values to `math.MaxInt64` keeps them compatible with signed 64-bit stores while preserving deterministic inode generation and hard-link identity.

## Validation

```text
go test ./weed/filer -run 'TestEnsureEntryInode(SharesAcrossHardLinks|FitsSignedLong)$' -count=1
```

Fixes #10806

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved inode generation for files and hard links to keep values within signed 64-bit limits.
  * Prevented invalid zero inode values by assigning a safe fallback.
  * Added coverage for edge-case identifiers, paths, and hard-linked entries.

items.title: filer: skip UpdateEntry when inline content is unchanged
items.body: ## Summary Fixes #11571 On an otherwise idle cluster, every `UpdateEntry` produces a metadata event that the local meta log persists to `/topics/.system/log`, appending a chunk to a volume on each flush. `filer.SaveInsideFiler` — used for all the `/etc` config files (IAM identities, `filer.conf`, remote mappings, policies) — rewrote the file unconditionally, so a client that periodically rewrites identical config kept `.dat`/`.idx` growing forever and prevented HDD spindown. The reporter's reproducer is the seaweedfs-operator: its 5-minute `Bucket`/`S3Identity` resync calls `SetBucketAccess` → `UpdateUser` → `saveIdentity` → `SaveInsideFiler` → `UpdateEntry` even when nothing changed. This change makes `SaveInsideFiler` compare the stored inline `Content` and skip `UpdateEntry` when the bytes are identical, so unchanged config writes emit no metadata event and no volume writes. Real changes are unaffected. #### Reproduction (local, `weed mini`) - Before: 3 identical `s3.bucket.access -name debug -user user1 -access Read,Write,List` calls → `1.dat` 1368 → 2352 B, `1.idx` 16 → 32 B. - After: same calls → zero new `.dat`/`.idx` writes; a real change (`-access Read`) still appends normally. #### Notes - All identical-write callers are covered at this single point (`saveIdentity`/`saveServiceAccount`/`saveGroup`/`savePolicy`, `PutConfiguration` full sync, `fs.configure`, remote storage conf, lifecycle dispatcher persister). Only the mtime/etag refresh of a byte-identical file is skipped; the compare reuses the `LookupEntry` `SaveInsideFiler` already issues, so no extra RPC. - Go/Rust parity: not applicable — the change is in the filer layer, which the Rust volume server does not implement; the volume write path is untouched. - Enterprise: `SaveInsideFiler`'s signature and create/update contract are unchanged; skipping a byte-identical update is transparent to callers. #### Test plan - [x] `go test ./weed/filer/ ./weed/credential/...` - [x] New unit test `TestSaveInsideFilerSkipsIdenticalContent` asserts identical writes issue no `UpdateEntry` - [x] Manual `weed mini` verification above --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Saving content that is unchanged now avoids an unnecessary update. * Changed content continues to be saved, and existing content without a checksum is updated so later identical saves can be skipped.

items.title: filer: honor is_moved only from ring member connections
items.body: ## Summary - `is_moved` is a caller-controlled proto field, so a direct `UpdateEntry`/`CreateEntry`/`ObjectTransaction`/lock RPC caller could set it to skip owner routing and run a conditional check under a non-owner's lock (raised in #11435 review). - Adds `FilerServer.movedFromPeer`: the marker is only honored when the request arrives on a connection whose source IP belongs to a lock-ring member. An unverified marker is ignored and the request is routed like a fresh one, so a forged flag gets the owner-routed behavior instead of a local evaluation. - Applied uniformly to the `is_moved` gates in `CreateEntry`, `UpdateEntry`, `ObjectTransaction`, `DistributedLock`, `DistributedUnlock`, `FindLockOwner`, and `PosixLock`. - Graceful degradation: if peer verification fails on a genuine forward (e.g. NAT), the receiver routes to the owner again — at most one extra hop; a self-owner applies locally regardless. Stacked on #11435 (`remote-sync-if-chunks-equal`), which introduced the conditional `UpdateEntry` routing gate. #### Test plan - [x] `TestCreateEntryMovedAppliesLocally` — verified peer marker applies locally (updated to inject peer ctx) - [x] `TestCreateEntryMovedFromClientIsNotTrusted` — new: forged `is_moved` does not bypass owner routing - [x] `TestObjectTransactionIsMovedSkipsForward`, `TestObjectTransactionForwardsToOwner` (real gRPC forward hop), `TestPosixLockForwardsToOwner` Generated with [Devin](https://devin.ai) --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Improved routing for conditional and exclusive writes, updates, transactions, and distributed locks so requests reach the appropriate filer. * Forwarded requests are verified before processing; requests that cannot be verified are rejected instead of being applied by the wrong filer. * POSIX lock requests now validate ownership before forwarding, including requests marked as forwarded. * Distributed unlock forwarding failures are reported in the response.

items.title: IAM identity.json migration race condition causes permanent identity loss when legacy clients write concurrently
items.body:
## Summary

When upgrading SeaweedFS server to v4.17+ while still using legacy clients (or custom clients) that directly read/write `/etc/iam/identity.json` via Filer gRPC, a race condition between the client's read-modify-write cycle and the server's automatic migration causes **permanently lost identities**.

## Environment

- SeaweedFS server version: v4.17+
- Client behavior: legacy `weed shell s3.configure` (≤v3.85) or custom clients that replicate its logic of directly reading/writing `/etc/iam/identity.json` via Filer gRPC

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start SeaweedFS server v4.17+ with filer + S3 API enabled
2. Use a legacy/custom client that follows the v3.85 `s3.configure` pattern:
   - Read `/etc/iam/identity.json` via Filer gRPC
   - Deserialize as `S3ApiConfiguration`
   - Append new identity in memory
   - Write back to `/etc/iam/identity.json` via `SaveInsideFiler`
3. Create user **alice** (first call — file does not exist yet, `CreateEntry` is used)
4. Create user **bob** (second call — file exists, `UpdateEntry` is used)
5. Wait a few seconds
6. Observe: **bob is permanently gone**

## Root Cause

The bug is a race condition between the legacy client's second write and the server's `migrateToMultiFile` triggered by a Filer metadata subscription event.

items.title: filer: stop isSameChunks from sorting caller-owned chunk slices
items.body: ## Summary - `slices.SortFunc` in `isSameChunks` reorders its input slices in place. `IsSameData` is used by `filer.remote.sync` on a metadata event's entries — the event's `NewEntry.Chunks` ends up ETag-sorted, and the subsequent conditional `UpdateEntry` stamp (`IF_ENTRY_EQUAL`) carrying that entry never matches the stored one, so remote-sync stamps fail for every multi-chunk object. - Sort clones of the slices instead, leaving caller-owned chunk order untouched. #### Test plan - [x] Verified the fix downstream in seaweed-mono: `TestKvcacheRemoteLifecycle` passes (19s; previously timed out at ~105s) --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Comparing chunk lists no longer changes the order of the original lists.

items.title: Fix filer GET error caused by incorrect database connection management
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?
This resolves filer errors like "Internal /buckets/XXX: find /buckets/XXX: context canceled" when using SQL filer store. The *sql.DB uses ctx from http.Request to create new connection, and then put it back to the connection pool. That means connections inside the pool are mostly unhealthy because the request context are cancelled just after http request finished.

# How are we solving the problem?
By uses sql.Conn instead of directly sql.DB. The sql.Conn are retrieved with context.Background(), while the later query still executes on request context, ensuring correct release logic.

# How is the PR tested?
Tested by manually stress testing, as that's a lifecycle problem making it hard to build unit tests.


# Checks
- [x] I have added unit tests if possible.

items.title: filer.remote.sync: stamp entries with IF_CHUNKS_EQUAL so a stale write-back cannot delete live chunks
items.body: Fixes #11434 # What problem are we solving? `filer.remote.sync` records the `RemoteEntry` stamp after an upload by writing the event's entry back to the filer with `UpdateEntry` (`updateLocalEntry`). The filer deletes every stored chunk that is absent from an updated entry (`cleanupChunks`). When the file was rewritten while its upload was still in flight, or when the event is a `-timeAgo` replay, that write-back is a stale snapshot and it deletes the rewrite's chunks: 1. the daemon starts uploading `f` at version A and reads A's chunks; 2. a client rewrites `f` (version B); the filer stores B's chunk and drops A's; 3. the upload of A completes and `updateLocalEntry` writes snapshot A back; the filer deletes B's chunk; 4. the event for B arrives; its chunk is gone, the upload fails, `isSuperseded` (#11149) sees the entry no longer references B's chunk and skips it. The entry now points at B's fid with no needle behind it and the remote holds A. The last write is lost on both sides once a vacuum runs. #11149 consults the filer only after a failed upload, so a successful upload of a stale event still writes back. # How are we solving the problem? The stamp write carries `WriteCondition IF_CHUNKS_EQUAL` over the event's chunk fids, which the filer already evaluates under the path lock (`chunkFidsEqual`, fid multiset). A `FailedPrecondition` answer means the filer moved past this event; the superseding event follows in the log and stamps the current entry, so the refusal is logged and skipped the same way a superseded upload is. Two functions added: `ifChunksEqual(entry)` builds the condition, `isFailedPrecondition(err)` recognises the refusal through `WithFilerClient`'s wrapping. An entry with inline `Content` and no chunks yields an empty fid list; the filer satisfies it only while the stored entry has no chunks either. `cleanupChunks` deletes nothing in that case, so no needle can be lost there. # How is the PR tested? - Unit tests in `filer_remote_sync_dir_test.go`: the condition carries the event's chunk fids (both `FileId` and `Fid` forms, empty for inline content); the refusal is detected as a gRPC status, wrapped, and by message. - Integration: `weed server -filer` plus a second `weed server -s3` as the remote, `remote.mount`, `filer.remote.sync -dir=`. `docker pause` the remote so one upload stays in flight, rewrite the file through the filer, `docker unpause`. - master before this change: after the daemon settles, the entry's chunk is 404 on every volume server and the read fails after `volume.vacuum -garbageThreshold=0`; - with this change: the daemon logs `skipping stale stamp of : ... precondition failed`, the B event stamps the entry, the chunk stays live and the content reads back after the vacuum. # Checks - [x] I have added unit tests if possible. - [ ] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging. - [ ] All AI code review comments have been addressed. No more comments to fix if reviewed again. Reviewer may request additional gemini and copilot reviews. # Checks for AI generated PRs - [ ] I have reviewed every line of code. - [x] The PR is kept as minimum as possible. Large PRs would not be accepted. --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Remote directory synchronization now skips updates when a file’s content or metadata has changed since the sync event. * Conditional file updates are routed to the filer responsible for the file, helping ensure they’re applied consistently. * Errors are treated as refused preconditions only when they have the matching gRPC status, allowing other errors to remain available for retry. * Remote sync applies the configured storage class to remote-bound copies without changing the filer’s original entry; an empty setting removes the class from the copy.

items.title: filer: compare IF_ENTRY_EQUAL chunks by fid, not file_id
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes #11512. `filer.remote.sync` stamps each uploaded entry with an `UpdateEntry` carrying `IF_ENTRY_EQUAL` over the metadata-log event's entry — but the filer refused every stamp with `FailedPrecondition`, so `RemoteEntry` never landed and every subsequent event re-uploaded.

The two sides of the `proto.Equal` spelled chunk ids differently: `BeforeEntrySerialization` (in `filerstore_wrapper`) moves each chunk's `file_id` string into `fid` and blanks it — that is the form the metadata-log event carries — while `FindEntry` runs `AfterEntryDeserialization` on the stored copy, restoring `file_id`. So the condition compared `file_id: ""` against `file_id: "7,019609a9eb"` and failed for every entry with chunks.

The clause now clones both sides and runs `BeforeEntrySerialization` on each before comparing, so chunks are matched by their `fid` and the `file_id` spelling is ignored; the stored entry and the request's `ExpectedEntry` are left untouched.

#### Test plan

- [x] `TestIfEntryEqualSerializedExpected` — reproduces the issue (serialized expected vs deserialized stored); failed before the fix, passes after
- [x] `TestIfEntryEqualNormalizesExpected` and all `weed/server` tests pass
- [x] `gofmt`, `go vet` clean

Generated with [Devin](https://devin.ai)

* **Bug Fixes**
  * `IF_ENTRY_EQUAL` conditions now correctly match entries when chunk data has been transformed during storage and serialization. This improves the reliability of equality checks for entries that are read back and compared with their serialized form.

items.title: filer: guard FoundationDB 100KB value limit and pack earlier
items.body: Fixes #11158 The filer stores an entry's chunk list as one FoundationDB value. FDB caps values at 100,000 bytes, but `UpdateEntry` checked the 10 MB transaction limit, and `MaybeManifestize` only folded at `ManifestBatch = 10000`. With default `-maxMB=4`, a few-GiB PutObject hit error 2103 before packing ran. ## Changes - FoundationDB store implements `ManifestBatcher` and returns 500. Other stores keep 10000. - Process-wide batch (`GetManifestBatch` / `SetManifestBatch`) is set from the default store in `SetStore` and advertised as `GetFilerConfiguration.manifest_batch`. - S3, mount, WebDAV, and `filer.copy` apply that field on handshake (`ApplyRemoteManifestBatch` ignores 0 so old filers keep 10000). - `MaybeManifestize` uses the process-wide batch. SSE chunks still skip packing. - `UpdateEntry` and `KvPut` reject `len(value) > 100000` *after* gzip and *before* `Transact`, with an error that names the value limit. `FDB_TRANSACTION_SIZE_LIMIT` is removed; directory delete still batches by entry count. - `cleanupChunks` (CreateEntry / UpdateEntry gRPC only) uses `ManifestizeOrKeepFlat`: on packing failure it deletes partial manifest blobs and continues with the flat list. `ObjectTransaction` PUT is unchanged (callers send a prepared list; current-tree S3 falls back to CreateEntry if the named guard fires). Single-pass packing at batch 500 and `-maxMB=4` still has a ~2 TiB ceiling; nested packing is out of scope. ## Tests - Unit tests for the batch API, wrapper/`SetStore`, fold-at-500, SSE skip, packing rollback, FDB value-size helper, and `GetFilerConfiguration`. - Existing `weed/filer` and `weed/s3api` manifest tests (still on `ManifestBatch = 10000`). - `cargo check --manifest-path seaweed-volume/Cargo.toml -p weed-volume` for the proto field. The FDB helper tests live in untagged files so they run without `libfdb_c`. Tagged store tests still need FoundationDB headers. --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **Bug Fixes** - Improved manifest processing reliability by preserving existing file chunks when folding fails. - Added cleanup for partially created manifest data, reducing the risk of orphaned storage. - Oversized metadata values are now rejected consistently before storage writes, with clearer size-limit errors. - Failed manifest operations continue to preserve a correct flat object representation. - **Performance** - Reduced manifest batch sizes to accommodate storage value limits and improve compatibility. - **Tests** - Added coverage for size validation, rollback, failure recovery, and manifest preservation.

items.title: Filer access-time (atime) tracking for LRU eviction — design & PR roadmap
items.body:
## Summary

This issue tracks adding optional POSIX-style **access-time (`atime`)** tracking to
filer entries, so operators can evict cache entries by *least-recently-accessed* rather
than least-recently-modified/synced. It records the design and the sequence of small PRs
implementing it, so each PR can be reviewed as one step of an agreed plan.

The feature is **opt-in and defaults to `off`** — no behaviour changes unless an
operator enables it.

## Motivation

Filers fronting remote/cloud storage (the `remote.mount` + cache-eviction flow) need to
keep a local cache within a size budget by evicting the "oldest" entries. Today the only
available signal is `RemoteEntry.LastLocalSyncTsNs` (when the entry was cached), which is
a poor proxy for "oldest": a file cached once and then read thousands of times still
looks old and gets evicted, causing avoidable re-fetches. True LRU needs an access-time
signal, which the filer does not currently track.

## Design

- **`atime` field** on `FuseAttributes` (proto field tags 22/23 for seconds/nanos),
  serialized with the existing entry codec — entries are opaque protobuf blobs, so no
  per-backend migration is required.
- **Legacy fallback:** when an entry has no stored atime, reads fall back to `Mtime`
  (or `Crtime` if mtime is zero), so existing data is immediately sortable.
- **Update policy** (`off` | `relatime` | `strict`), modeled on POSIX mount options:
  - `off` (default) — never track.
  - `relatime` — only persist when the new atime is older than a threshold (default 24h)
    or older than mtime/ctime. Debounces writes.
  - `strict` — persist every forward-moving access.
  - Optional **path-prefix allow-list** to scope tracking to specific subtrees, matched
    at path-component boundaries (`/buckets/cache` matches `/buckets/cache/x` but not
    `/buckets/cache_backup/x`).
- **Persistence** goes through the canonical `Filer.UpdateEntry` path to keep
  inode/crtime invariants and metadata events consistent. Updates are explicitly
  best-effort (a concurrent write can clobber a bump); relatime debouncing keeps the
  race window small, and bumps only occur on read paths.
- **Read paths** bump atime via a fire-and-forget helper that coalesces duplicate
  `(dir, name)` requests within a flush window and short-circuits for background reads
  (replication, EC, prefetch, lifecycle) so those never affect atime.

## PR roadmap

| Step | Scope | PR | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Proto + codec foundation (`FuseAttributes.Atime`, `TouchAccessTime` RPC, init-from-mtime) | #9556 | ✅ Merged |
| 2a | `AtimePolicy` core (off/relatime/strict, path-prefix scoping) — pure logic + tests | #9898 | Open |
| 2b | `TouchAccessTime` server handler + `-atime*` flags (built on 2a) | #9583 | Draft until 2a merges |
| 3 | `weed/util/atime` client helper (coalescing Toucher, system-read bypass) — no wiring | _(planned)_ | — |
| 4 | Wire atime bumps into S3 / FUSE / WebDAV / Filer HTTP read paths | _(planned)_ | — |
| 5 | Surface atime in `weed shell fs.meta.cat` | _(planned)_ | — |

Each PR is intentionally kept small and self-contained. Feedback on the split
granularity or ordering is very welcome before I open the remaining ones.

items.title: filer.remote.sync 4.48: every stamp is refused with FailedPrecondition (IF_ENTRY_EQUAL compares an event chunk with empty file_id against the stored chunk with file_id filled)
items.body:
**Version:** chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.48 (filer, volume, daemon all 4.48). Regression from PR #11435.

**What happens.** `filer.remote.sync` uploads the object, then its stamp `UpdateEntry` (condition `IF_ENTRY_EQUAL` over the event's `NewEntry`, `filer_remote_sync_dir.go` `updateLocalEntry`) is refused for every entry, including a freshly created file with no concurrent writer:

```
I0928 22:06:36.417511 filer_remote_sync_dir.go:174 create r/archive/f.txt
I0928 22:06:36.418474 filer_remote_sync_dir.go:326 create r/archive/f.txt
E0928 22:06:36.623612 filer_remote_sync_dir.go:453 skipping stale stamp of /buckets/mount/f.txt: rpc error: code = FailedPrecondition desc = precondition failed: /buckets/mount/f.txt
```

The entry never gets a `RemoteEntry`; every subsequent event re-uploads, and the inline remote delete (which keys off `Remote`) never fires.

**Why.** `writeConditionSatisfied` (`weed/server/filer_grpc_server_condition.go`, `IF_ENTRY_EQUAL`) does `proto.Equal(current.ToProtoEntry(), filer.FromPbEntry("", c.ExpectedEntry).ToProtoEntry())`. The two sides spell chunk ids differently:

- `weed/filer/filerstore_wrapper.go` calls `filer_pb.BeforeEntrySerialization` on every insert/update (lines 142, 171, 197 at 4.48): each chunk's `file_id` string is moved into the `fid` message and blanked. The metadata-log event is emitted from that entry, so the daemon's copy has `file_id: ""`.
- `FindEntry` (line 241) calls `filer_pb.AfterEntryDeserialization`, which fills `file_id` back from `fid`. `UpdateEntry` compares against that copy.
- Nothing on the `ExpectedEntry` side calls `AfterEntryDeserialization`, so `proto.Equal` sees `file_id: ""` against `file_id: "7,019609a9eb"` and the condition fails for every entry with chunks. Entries with inline content and no chunks compare equal, which is probably why the change looked fine in a unit test.

Observed on one 4.48 filer (`weed filer.meta.tail` vs `fs.meta.cat` for the same fresh file), chunk 0, every other field identical:
```
event:  "fileId": "",             "fid": { "volumeId": 7, "fileKey": "1", "cookie": 2517215723 }
stored: "fileId": "7,019609a9eb", "fid": { "volumeId": 7, "fileKey": "1", "cookie": 2517215723 }
```

**Repro** (single node):
```
docker network create sw
docker run -d --name remote --network sw chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.48 server -s3 -dir=/data -master.volumeSizeLimitMB=64
docker run -d --name srv --network sw -p 8888:8888 chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.48 server -filer -dir=/data -master.volumeSizeLimitMB=64
docker exec remote sh -c 'echo "s3.bucket.create -name=archive" | weed shell -master=localhost:9333'
docker exec srv sh -c 'printf "remote.configure -name=r -type=s3 -s3.endpoint=http://remote:8333 -s3.access_key=any -s3.secret_key=any -s3.region=us-east-1\nremote.mount -dir=/buckets/mount -remote=r/archive/\n" | weed shell -master=localhost:9333'
docker restart srv
echo hello > f.txt; curl -F file=@f.txt http://127.0.0.1:8888/buckets/mount/f.txt
docker run -d --name sync --network sw chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.48 filer.remote.sync -filer=srv:8888 -dir=/buckets/mount
sleep 10; docker logs sync            # "skipping stale stamp ... FailedPrecondition"
docker exec srv sh -c 'echo "fs.meta.cat /buckets/mount/f.txt" | weed shell -master=localhost:9333' | grep -i remote   # no RemoteEntry
```

**Expected.** The stamp lands on an unchanged entry. Suggested fix: run `filer_pb.AfterEntryDeserialization` over `ExpectedEntry`'s chunks (or `BeforeEntrySerialization` over both) before `proto.Equal`, or compare chunks by fid the way `IF_CHUNKS_EQUAL` does. A daemon built from tag 4.47 plus the `IF_CHUNKS_EQUAL` form of #11435, run against stock 4.48 filers, stamps correctly and still refuses a stale write-back, which isolates the regression to the `IF_ENTRY_EQUAL` comparison.

items.title: shell: refuse s3.bucket.create on an existing bucket
items.body: ## Summary Fixes #11450 — `s3.bucket.create -name ` on an existing bucket replaced its filer entry, silently dropping every extended attribute: lifecycle configuration, owner, versioning, and Object Lock (which is documented as irreversible). - Send `o_excl` on the `CreateEntry` request so `Filer.CreateEntry` returns `ErrEntryAlreadyExists` instead of routing to `UpdateEntry`, which only preserves `Crtime`/`Inode` and discards `Extended`. - Report `bucket already exists`, matching the S3 `CreateBucket` semantics of `BucketAlreadyOwnedByYou`/`BucketAlreadyExists` that `PutBucketHandler` already implements. - Use `filer_pb.CreateEntry` so the `ENTRY_ALREADY_EXISTS` error code maps back to the sentinel (the raw `client.CreateEntry` leaves it in `resp.Error` unchecked). #### Test plan - [x] `TestCreateEntryOExclPreservesExistingEntry`: `CreateEntry` with `o_excl` on an existing path returns `ErrEntryAlreadyExists` and leaves the stored entry's `Extended` attributes intact - [x] `go build ./weed/shell ./weed/filer` Generated with [Devin](https://devin.ai) --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * S3 bucket creation now reports a bucket-specific error when the bucket already exists, while preserving the existing bucket and its metadata. * Exclusive creation now returns lookup errors instead of treating them as evidence that the requested path is absent. Non-exclusive creation behavior is unchanged. * Errors encountered while checking for an existing path no longer result in an exclusive create proceeding as though the path were available.

items.title: filer: evict remote-cached objects under storage pressure
items.body: ## Summary Remote-mounted objects cache to ordinary local volumes on read, but nothing evicts them when the disk fills: failed fills leave tombstoned garbage, the mount collection loses writable volumes, and every later read streams from remote forever (reproduced locally with 2 nodes and 5 x 16MB objects against 64MB of volume capacity). This adds pressure-driven eviction at the filer level, where the metadata knows which chunks are safely re-fetchable. - `filer.IsEvictableRemoteEntry` / `ListEvictableRemoteEntries`: entry is a candidate only when remote-backed, synced (`LastLocalSyncTsNs >= remote mtime`), and holding local chunks - never dirty or pending-upload content. Ordered by `LastLocalSyncTsNs`, oldest cached first. - `FilerServer.uncacheRemoteEntry` applies the same state transition as `remote.uncache` (clear chunks, reset sync ts) through the normal entry lock + `CreateEntry` mutation path. - Reactive: a cache fill that fails with a capacity error launches a reclaim pass (evict oldest until the object fits) before the read falls back to remote streaming. Passes coalesce via TryLock, so a write-failure storm does not queue mount traversals. - Proactive: a filer janitor runs the same pass when any volume-server disk crosses `-filer.remoteCacheEvictThreshold` (default 0.9, 0 disables), evicting down to ~85% of that threshold for hysteresis. - Reclaim: the pass flushes the deletion queue synchronously and triggers a master vacuum, so evicted chunks and orphaned partial-fill garbage return to the filesystem promptly instead of waiting for the next auto-vacuum. - Metric: `seaweedfs_remote_cache_evicted_total`. Enterprise cache volumes are unaffected: this only drops chunks of entries with remote-mount metadata in ordinary volumes, and never touches remote-tiered volume needle data. #### Test plan - [x] `weed/filer` unit tests: eligibility matrix, oldest-first ordering, min-age cutoff, dirty/remote-only skips, subdirectory recursion - [x] `TestRemoteCacheEvictUnderPressure` (test/s3/remote_cache): self- contained two-mini cluster, 2 x 32MB volumes vs 5 x 16MB objects; asserts the oldest entry is evicted, garbage is vacuumed, and a re-read re-caches - [x] Live two-node repro validated: wedged cache (272MB garbage, zero live data) self-heals on the next read - [ ] CI Generated with [Devin](https://devin.ai) --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added automatic reclamation of locally cached remote files when volume disk usage reaches a configurable threshold. Eligible files are evicted oldest-first; the default threshold is 90%, and setting it to 0 disables eviction. * Evicted files remain available remotely and can be fetched locally again when needed. * When remote-cache capacity is exhausted, the system can reclaim local cache space to make room for new cached files. * **Bug Fixes** * Improved cache tracking so locally modified files are not mistaken for unchanged remote copies during eviction.

items.title: filer: opt-in inode->path index with shell nfs.enable / nfs.disable
items.body:
Groundwork for bringing back the `weed nfs` gateway. The gateway resolves NFS filehandles by reversing an inode to its path, which the deterministic hash inode cannot do, so the filer needs a reverse index — but nobody should pay for it unless they export something.

- filer.conf `PathConf` gains an `inode_index` option. The store wrapper writes inode->path rows only for entries under a marked location; with no rule (the default) no index work happens at all. Every filer picks the rule up through the normal filer.conf reload, so there is no per-process flag to keep in sync across a cluster.
- `nfs.enable -path=/exports -apply` marks the path and backfills rows for the entries already under it, assigning inodes to entries that predate filer-assigned inodes, so pre-existing files resolve by filehandle immediately. Re-running is idempotent.
- `nfs.disable -path=/exports -apply` removes the mark and deletes the rows, so turning NFS off leaves no index data behind.

Verified against a live server: enable backfills exactly the in-scope entries, files created afterwards get rows through the filer-side hook, out-of-scope paths get nothing, and disable clears every row.

The gateway restore itself comes as a follow-up on top of this.

items.title: S3: PutObject refuses a valid key that is already a prefix of another key, and fails with a retryable 500
items.body:
`weed s3` + `weed filer`, version `8000GB 4.37` (`c06a2dca87`, stock upstream), leveldb2 store.
Behaviour and cause are unchanged on `4.44`, `master` and `dev`.

```bash
aws s3api put-object --bucket b --key "collision/foo/bar" --body empty.bin --endpoint-url $EP   # 200
aws s3api put-object --bucket b --key "collision/foo"     --body empty.bin --endpoint-url $EP   # 500 InternalError
```

Both keys are valid and independent: S3's namespace is flat, and `/` is a delimiter rather than a
directory ([docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-keys.html)). On AWS
both PUTs return 200 and both objects coexist, in either order — so the expected result here is
**200, not an error at all**. Writing them in the opposite order does succeed, which makes the
outcome depend on creation order.

Separately, and much more cheaply fixable: when it does fail, the failure is a **retryable 500**
for a permanently impossible condition, so the AWS SDK retried it four times. The deterministic
error the code already intends is unreachable — `filerErrorToS3Error`
(`weed/s3api/s3api_object_handlers_put.go`) maps `filer_pb.ErrExistingIsDirectory` to
`s3err.ErrExistingObjectIsDirectory` (409), but `Filer.CreateEntry` flattens the `%w`-wrapped
sentinel that `Filer.UpdateEntry` returns (`weed/filer/filer.go:303` on master, 274 on 4.37):

```diff
         if err := f.UpdateEntry(ctx, oldEntry, entry); err != nil {
             glog.ErrorfCtx(ctx, "update entry %s: %v", entry.FullPath, err)
-            return fmt.Errorf("update entry %s: %v", entry.FullPath, err)
+            return fmt.Errorf("update entry %s: %w", entry.FullPath, err)
         }
```

With the wrap gone `errors.Is` stops matching, so `resp.ErrorCode` stays `FilerError_OK`,
`FilerErrorToSentinel` is skipped, and the mapper falls through to `default: ErrInternalError`.
`ErrExistingIsFile` is unreachable the same way — both have been since #8767 added the mechanism
without touching this line. `ErrEntryNameTooLong` works only because it is returned bare rather
than through `UpdateEntry`.

That one character is worth doing regardless, but it only makes the refusal honest. Supporting the
flat key namespace is the actual fix, and I appreciate that is a far larger change.

Related: #10660 (copy/rename side of the same collision), #8731 / #8742 (delete side, fixed).

items.title: fix(s3): initialize destination ACLs for CopyObject
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

CopyObject carries the source object's owner and ACL into the destination and ignores ACLs supplied on the copy request. A public source can therefore produce a public destination even when no ACL was requested. [S3 specifies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/API/API_CopyObject.html) that a copy does not preserve the source ACL and defaults to private.

Metadata-only self-copies also need to keep the destination ACL and file mode consistent when another writer changes the entry between the gateway read and the filer commit.

# How are we solving the problem?

Reuse existing upload ACL preparation and authorization, including ownership controls and signed query policy conditions. Apply destination owner/grants to ordinary, versioned and metadata-only self-copies; explicit ACLs still require PutObjectAcl permission. Multipart part copies retain their existing behavior.

For a routed metadata-only self-copy, read the owner and submit an UpdateEntry with the existing IF_ENTRY_EQUAL condition, updating ACLs, file mode and MIME together without re-uploading content. A conflict triggers at most three fresh reads and revalidations. Preserve prefix-object directories and unmanaged metadata; keep request-condition failures as 412 and return 409 ConditionalRequestConflict when contention persists. An authoritative owner rejection stops failover without marking the owner unhealthy. No new filer protocol fields are required.

The S3 API unit-test CI job has a 20-minute budget for its nine-minute suite timeout, checkout, Go setup and the preceding focused test run.

# How is the PR tested?

- Reproduced source ACL inheritance and copy ACL authorization failures on the original upstream revision, and stale file modes across both self-copy race windows before this fix.
- 289 focused cases passed, including authenticated ACL/ownership/policy controls, both race windows, MIME/content updates, source/destination condition rechecks, deletion, bounded conflicts, prefix objects, two-node business-error handling and a replica behind the owner. Native filer tests independently exercise the whole-entry condition and commit.
- On Server-200, `go test -json ./weed/s3api ./weed/s3api/s3err ./weed/s3api/policy_engine ./weed/server -count=1` passed all four packages: 3,901 tests/subtests passed, 5 skipped, and none failed.
- `go vet` over those packages reported only five existing `IdentityAccessManagement contains sync.RWMutex` warnings in unchanged upstream test files. Applying the exclusions already used by `.github/workflows/go.yml` leaves no warnings. The unfiltered vet exit status is 1.
- `git diff --check` passed. An independent review identified possible failover of authoritative business rejections; the fix and a two-node regression test address that case.

- Parsed the workflow and confirmed that all setup steps and test commands remain unchanged; only the enclosing unit-test job budget was raised.

# Checks

- [x] I have added unit tests if possible.
- [ ] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging. (Restores documented S3 behavior without adding a configuration option.)
- [ ] All AI code review comments have been addressed. No more comments to fix if reviewed again. Reviewer may request additional gemini and copilot reviews. (Reported findings addressed; awaiting review of the latest revision.)

# Checks for AI generated PRs

- [x] I have reviewed every line of code.
- [x] The PR is kept as minimum as possible. Large PRs would not be accepted.

items.title: shell: clean up the target copy when a merge upload fails
items.body:
Reported in https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/11009#issuecomment-5508071217: "fs.mergeVolumes with volumes that are replicated creates a LOT of orphans".

That is right, for one specific reason. `topology.ReplicatedWrite` commits the needle to the local volume *before* it fans out to the other replicas, so an upload that reports failure can still have left a copy on the target. `moveChunk` returns the error, `fs.mergeVolumes` prints "failed to move" and carries on to the next chunk, and that copy stays behind forever: the filer is never re-pointed at it, so nothing will ever reference or delete it.

One sick replica orphans roughly half the chunks of a merge (two thirds with three copies): the entry node is picked at random by `LookupVolumeServerUrl`, and the replica upload uses `MaxAttempts: 1` ("fail fast on a dead replica; the client write retries") — except here there is no retrying client, so a single transient timeout per chunk is enough. A volume with a single copy has no such window: `GetWritableRemoteReplications` returns early, and the write is one local append that either succeeds or leaves nothing behind.

This deletes the needle we may have written, on every replica of the target, before continuing. The source side already did exactly this after a successful move, so `deleteMovedSourceNeedles` is renamed to `deleteOrphanedNeedles` and reused for both ends. The freshly assigned manifest needle in `uploadManifestChunk` has the same window and gets the same treatment.

## Verified on a 2-node cluster, replication 001

Merge with a healthy target: source needles deleted on both replicas, `volume.fsck` clean. Unchanged by this PR.

Merge into a target whose replica cannot accept the write (`volume.mark -node=... -readonly` on one copy):

before
```
dataNode:127.0.0.1:21002  volume:5  entries:11  orphan:3  27.27%  1572924B
Total                                entries:125  orphan:3   2.40%  1572924B
```
The target volume's replicas were left permanently divergent, 11 live needles vs 8.

after
```
Total                                entries:122  orphan:0   0.00%  0B
no orphan data
```
The stranded copies are written and then deleted (`FileCount 19 DeleteCount 10` vs `17/8`), so both replicas agree on 9 live needles and the dead bytes are reclaimable by vacuum. All 60 files read back byte-identical.

Note for anyone reproducing this: `volume.fsck`'s `-cutoffTimeAgo` defaults to 5 hours, so a run straight after a merge reports `orphan:0` either way. The runs above pass `-cutoffTimeAgo=1s`.

## Not addressed here

The same report asks for two other things. Marking the source read-only before draining it would not have fixed these orphans (they land on the *target*), and `createMergePlan` currently rejects a read-only source outright — `IsReadOnly()` is true for `readonlyCanDelete` too, so even `volume.mark -readonlyCanDelete` would not get past the plan. Having `fs.mergeVolumes` delete the drained volumes itself is a separate feature.

https://claude.ai/code/session_01XjiMGK72F4Gs3yWNJhnVjy

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved cleanup of orphaned data left behind after failed volume moves or uploads.
  * Added cleanup for partially written manifest data when uploads fail or operations are abandoned.
  * Ensured temporary data and reserved capacity are released consistently after interrupted rewrites.
  * Added validation to reject invalid source and destination volume IDs before processing.
  * Prevented source volume IDs exceeding the supported maximum from being accepted.
  * Improved cleanup logging to make volume-operation issues easier to diagnose.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## From review

- `a7afb2e3e` — target deletes now verify the cookie. `BatchDelete` matches on the needle id alone, and while ids come from one global sequence, a volume restored from another cluster or written either side of a master sequence reset can hold a colliding one; a failed move would then delete a live needle out from under its filer entry. Source deletes still match on id, as every other filer-driven delete does.
- `7379735f3` — `rewriteManifestChunk` now deletes the target copies it leaves when it is abandoned partway. It moves sub-chunks one at a time and only uploads the rewritten manifest at the end, so a nested rewrite failing, the marshal, or the manifest upload each returned leaving those copies behind, one orphan per sub-chunk moved so far. Nested rewrites hand theirs up so an outer failure clears the whole subtree.

  Verified on the same cluster shape with `ManifestBatch` temporarily lowered from 10000 to 3 in a throwaway binary, so a 5MB file manifestizes. No fault injection needed: sub-chunk moves are direct writes to the target volume server and succeed on their own, while the manifest re-upload has to `AssignVolume`, which fails once every volume is past `-volumeSizeLimitMB` and both volume servers are at `-max`. Before, three sub-chunk copies stranded on both replicas of the target (`orphan:6`, 6.3MB from two 5MB files); after, `orphan:0`. `-findMissingChunksInFiler` reports nothing missing either way and both files read back byte-identical, so only the abandoned copies go and the sources the old manifest still points at stay.

A failed `UpdateEntry` still leaks its target copies, deliberately. That error can also mean the filer applied the update and lost the response, in which case those copies are what the entry now points at, and deleting them would turn a leak into data loss.

items.title: S3 read of remote-mounted object fails with 404 when a local chunk needle is missing instead of re-pulling from remote
items.body:
## Problem

When a SeaweedFS **remote-storage mount** is used as a read-through cache over an object store (e.g. GCS/S3), an S3 `GetObject` can fail with a `404 Not Found` even though the object is fully intact in the remote store.

## Setup

We run a remote-storage mount as a read-through cache:

- Objects are dual-populated: the application writes to **both** the backing object store and SeaweedFS.
- A local eviction/uncache process later clears local chunks and stamps a remote-only `RemoteEntry` on the filer entry, so subsequent reads re-pull from the remote.

The **remote-only re-pull path works correctly**: when a filer entry has no local chunks and a `RemoteEntry` (`IsInRemoteOnly()` is true), `streamFromVolumeServers` calls the stream-through cache (`cacheRemoteObjectForStreamingWithShortTimeout` → `CacheRemoteObjectToLocalCluster`) and serves the object.

## The bug

Sometimes a filer entry **still has local chunks** (so it is *not* remote-only) but the referenced volume needle has been **reclaimed** by vacuum-compaction or deletion. The S3 GET then reads a dead needle, receives a 404, retries the same dead needle for the duration of the retry window, and finally errors the request — even though the object is intact in the remote store.

Because the entry still has (stale) chunks, `IsInRemoteOnly()` returns `false`, so the code never falls back to the remote stream-through cache.

### Observed log evidence (generalized; placeholders for internal values)

```
stream.go: read chunk <VID>,<NEEDLE> failed, invalidating cache and retrying: <VOLUME_URL>/<VID>,<NEEDLE>?readDeleted=true: 404 Not Found
reader_at.go: fetching chunk {FileId:<VID>,<NEEDLE> ... ChunkSize:4096}: 404
s3api_object_handlers.go: streamFromVolumeServers: streamFn failed after writing 0 bytes: ...404
s3api_object_handlers.go: GetObjectHandler: failed to stream <bucket>/<key> from volume servers: ...404
```

## Root cause

`streamFromVolumeServers` only re-pulls from the remote when `entry.IsInRemoteOnly()` is true (entry has zero chunks). When a remote-backed entry retains **stale** local chunks pointing at a reclaimed needle, the read fails with 404 and there is no fallback to the remote copy.

## Impact

Transient `GetObject` failures (surfaced as 404/500 to S3 clients) for objects that are fully present in the remote store, whenever a local needle backing a cached-but-not-uncached entry is lost (vacuum-compaction/deletion) before the entry has been converted to remote-only.

## Proposed fix

In the S3 GET path, when a local chunk read fails with **not-found** (needle missing), *before any response bytes have been written*, and the entry is **remote-backed** (under a remote-storage mount):

1. Drop the stale local chunks so the entry becomes remote-only again (this also makes future reads self-heal through the existing, well-tested remote-only path).
2. Re-pull the object from the remote using the existing mechanism (`CacheRemoteObjectToLocalCluster` / `cacheRemoteObjectForStreamingWithShortTimeout`).
3. Stream the requested range from the freshly cached chunks.

The fallback is guarded to only trigger for entries with a remote backing, so behavior for non-remote buckets is unchanged.

A draft PR implementing this is linked below.

items.title: filer.remote.sync: a non-transient job failure pins the sync offset for the life of the process; three such failures are routine (absent-object delete, stamp of a deleted entry, GCS 429 on replay)
items.body:
## Describe the bug
`weed filer.remote.sync` persists its subscription offset as the processor's watermark, and the watermark is never advanced to or past the oldest event whose job returned an error (`MetadataProcessor.oldestFailedTsNs`, `weed/command/filer_sync_jobs.go`). A job gets one attempt unless `util.IsTransientError` matches (`weed/util/retry.go`). So a single non-transient failure holds the offset until the process restarts, and the restart replays everything since the pin.

Three failures that are not real failures pin it in practice:

1. **Delete of an object that was never uploaded.** An app rotates `x.db.tmp -> x.db -> x.db.prev` faster than the sync uploads; the delete of `.tmp` / `.prev` reaches the remote for an object that does not exist. GCS reports `remote_storage.ErrRemoteObjectNotFound`; the rename path (`processUpdateEvent`) already ignores it, the plain delete path (`filer_pb.IsDelete`) returns it as the job error.
2. **Stamp of an entry deleted after its upload.** `updateLocalEntry` writes the `RemoteEntry` back with `UpdateEntry`; the filer answers `not found <path>: filer: no entry is found in filer store` (gRPC Unknown) when the entry was deleted meanwhile. The delete's own event follows in the log.
3. **GCS 429 on a hot object during a replay.** A replay re-uploads every intermediate version of a hot file; GCS allows one mutation per second per object and answers `googleapi: Error 429 ... rateLimitExceeded`, which matches no entry of `transientErrorMessages`, so one attempt and pin.

Observed 2026-10-02 on two clusters (4.47-based daemon against 4.48 filers; the relevant lines are identical in 4.48 and master): a restart replayed seven days of events at ~180/s, two OOM kills at a 256Mi limit, and the daemon pinned again within 20 s of each restart.

## System Setup
- `weed server -filer -s3 ...` (4.48) + `weed filer.remote.sync -filer=... -dir=/buckets/<dir>` with a GCS remote
- OS: Linux (GKE, amd64). Daemon: `weed filer.remote.sync` built from tag 4.47 with the #11435 conditional stamp; filers and s3 gateway: `chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.48`. The lines involved are unchanged on master (67034de).

## Expected behavior
A delete whose object is already absent, a stamp whose entry is already gone, and a backlog version the filer has already moved past are complete work; none of them should hold the offset. A 429 should be retried with the existing backoff.

## Proposed fix (PR to follow if wanted)
- `processDeleteEvent` / `syncDeleteMarker`: `ErrRemoteObjectNotFound` is success.
- `updateLocalEntry`: filer `not found` is skipped (logged), like the stale-stamp skip.
- `retriedWriteFile`: ask `isSuperseded` before the first attempt as well as after a failed one, so a backlog uploads only the version the filer still holds (also removes the 429 burst at its source).
- `util/retry.go`: `ratelimitexceeded`, `rate limit`, `too many requests` are transient.
Tests: unit tests for all four; the existing `TestRetriedWriteFileStopsWhenSuperseded` gains a "superseded before the first attempt" case.

items.title: filer: conditional UpdateEntry with a chunk-set write condition
items.body:
A filer entry can end up referencing a needle that a concurrent update already queued for deletion. UpdateEntry is a read-modify-write: it diffs stored-vs-incoming chunks to compute garbage, so two concurrent updates on one entry are last-write-wins on the chunk list. A chunk-preserving metadata write (tagging, setattr, copy-in-place) that commits after a concurrent chunk removal resurrects fids already queued for deletion; vacuum then strands the entry on a dead needle (#10366).

Instead of a bespoke expected-chunks field (#10368), this reuses the WriteCondition machinery:

* UpdateEntryRequest gains the same optional `condition` CreateEntry already has, evaluated under the filer's per-path lock. UpdateEntry now takes that lock, so the precondition, the garbage diff, and the write are atomic on the owner filer. A failed condition returns FailedPrecondition, matching expected_extended.
* A new clause kind IF_CHUNKS_EQUAL compares the stored chunk fid multiset against what the caller read, order-independent. Clause presence carries the meaning, so an empty fids list expresses "expect no chunks" — guarding the reverse race, where a stale writer wipes chunks a concurrent update just added. The clause composes inside CreateEntry and ObjectTransaction conditions unchanged.

Wiring call sites (S3 tagging/attrs, FUSE setattr) is left for follow-ups; metadata-only callers are better served by ObjectTransaction PATCH_EXTENDED, which merges into the stored entry server-side under the lock and needs no precondition at all.

Tests drive the handler through the stranding interleaving: an unconditional stale write resurrects the dead reference (current behavior), a conditional one is rejected and the entry stays empty, a fresh read-modify-write passes, and the empty-fids clause rejects a stale wipe.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Added `IF_CHUNKS_EQUAL` conditional writes to ensure the stored chunk FID multiset matches the caller’s expected set (used by `UpdateEntry`).
  * Extended `UpdateEntry` requests with an optional write precondition, evaluated atomically under the per-path lock.
  * Standardized exclusive per-path locking for `AppendToEntry` and `DeleteEntry` to keep conditional and non-conditional operations consistent.
* **Bug Fixes**
  * Conditional failures now reliably return gRPC `FailedPrecondition` and do not apply any state changes.
* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for chunk multiset equality, stale-write prevention, and delete lock waiting behavior (plus `IF_ETAG_MATCH` enforcement).
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

items.title: s3api: two residual paths where putToFiler deletes the chunks of an entry that already exists (follow-up to #11366)
items.body:
> **Note:** this write-up comes from an **AI-assisted static review** of `master`
> (code reading only, no runtime reproduction). The paths below look reachable to
> me from the code, and the ones I could verify against the source are quoted
> inline — happy to dig further if any of them doesn't hold.

## Context

Follow-up to **#11366** (closed by **#11376**, "s3api: don't delete chunks when
CreateEntry outcome is ambiguous"). That change treats transport errors
(`Canceled`, `DeadlineExceeded`, `Unavailable`) as ambiguous and verifies the
entry before cleanup — good. But `ambiguous` is derived from the error *class*,
whereas what we actually need is the fact "the entry definitively does not
exist". Two paths remain where the entry exists while the error is classified as
definitive, so `deleteOrphanedChunks` still runs **without any verification** and
leaves live metadata pointing at tombstoned needles (silent, delayed data loss
once the volume is vacuumed).

## 1. The filer can return an error *after* the entry has been inserted — no restart required

`weed/filer/filer.go`, `func (f *Filer) CreateEntry`, insert branch:

```go
if oldEntry == nil {
    if err := f.Store.InsertEntry(ctx, entry); err != nil {    // entry inserted
        ...
    }
    if !skipCreateParentDir {
        ...
        if err := f.ensureParentDirectoryEntry(...); err != nil {
            // The entry stays: deleting by path would destroy a concurrent create
            // that already succeeded through the update branch, ...
            glog.ErrorfCtx(ctx, "create parent directories of %s: %v", entry.FullPath, err)
            return err                                          // error returned, entry stays
        }
    }
}
```

The comment ("The entry stays") confirms this outcome is intentional on the filer
side. `ensureParentDirectoryEntry` can fail at:

- `f.FindEntry(dirPath)` returning a non-`NotFound` error. Note this lookup goes
  straight to the store — `FindEntry` calls `f.Store.FindEntry` with no cache (the
  call site even logs "find uncached directory"), so it runs for **every new
  object**, not just for missing directories; and
- the `InsertEntry` for a missing parent directory failing while the directory is
  still absent (the empty-folder-cleaner race the comment above describes).

The filer reports this as `resp.Error` with **gRPC status OK**
(`weed/server/filer_grpc_server.go`, the `createErr != nil` branch). The client
wrapper turns it into a plain error with no gRPC status:

```go
// weed/pb/filer_pb/filer_pb_helper.go, CreateEntryWithResponse
return nil, fmt.Errorf("CreateEntry: %w", errors.New(resp.Error))
```

so `status.Code(err)` is `codes.Unknown` — outside
`{Canceled, DeadlineExceeded, Unavailable}` — and `filerErrorToS3Error` falls
through to `ErrInternalError`. `ambiguous` is therefore `false` and
`deleteOrphanedChunks` runs **without any verification**, deleting the chunks of
an entry that exists.

Reachability for S3: the S3 PUT path does **not** set `SkipCheckParentDirectory`
(only `weed/mount/*` does), so `ensureParentDirectoryEntry` really does run for
S3 creates — including the `PUT` mutation of a routed `ObjectTransaction`, whose
`applyObjectMutation` also passes `false`. So this is not dead code for S3.

Not affected: the overwrite branch. `UpdateEntry` is a single `Store.UpdateEntry`
and the following `NotifyUpdateEvent` / `deleteChunksIfNotNew` are void, so a
failure there leaves the *old* entry and its chunks intact — no dangling
reference.

**What this means for frequency:** the trigger is one transient filer-store error
landing between the insert and the ancestor lookup — no restart, no ring change.
That is a lower bar than the restart-triggered case #11376 fixes, and it should
show up in bursts whenever the metadata store is degraded (timeouts, connection
pool exhaustion, IO stalls), or more readily for keys that need a new directory
prefix or sit deeper in the tree.

## 2. A routed ObjectTransaction can partially apply

`routedPut` sends `[PUT entry, ...finalize]` as one transaction
(`weed/s3api/s3api_object_routed_write.go`). The filer applies mutations in order
and returns `resp.Error` on the first failure, with the earlier ones already
applied (`weed/server/filer_grpc_server.go`, `ObjectTransaction`):

```go
for i, m := range req.Mutations {
    if err := fs.applyObjectMutation(ctx, m, ...); err != nil {
        return &filer_pb.ObjectTransactionResponse{Error: fmt.Sprintf("mutation %d: %v", i, err)}, nil
    }
}
```

`applyObjectMutation`'s `PUT` branch is `fs.filer.CreateEntry(...)` — the same
function as case 1.

In `putToFiler`, `resp.Error != ""` only logs a warning and falls back to the
lock path. If that fallback then fails with a non-transport error (e.g.
`ErrInternalError`), `ambiguous` is `false` → the chunks are deleted while the
entry written by the earlier mutation still exists.

This needs three conditions at once (routed path taken, a later mutation failing
after the PUT applied, and the fallback also failing with a non-transport error),
and the fallback usually succeeds because it takes the update branch — so it is
considerably rarer than case 1. The path is still reachable.

## How this shows up in the wild

- Gateway log (Warning/Error level, so it is captured at default verbosity):
  `putToFiler: failed to create entry for <path>: CreateEntry: create parent directories of ...` —
  with the object still readable afterwards.
- The `readDeletedNeedle` counter added in #11376 keeps growing, which is the
  direct signal that live metadata points at deleted needles.

## Suggestion

Gate the destructive cleanup on the *fact*, not the *error class*: on **any**
create failure, look the entry up (owner-preferring, no failover) and delete the
uploaded chunks **only when the entry is confirmed absent**. Everything else —
including a lookup that cannot be answered — should keep the chunks; vacuum
reclaims true orphans, whereas deleting chunks a live entry references is
unrecoverable.

Concretely: hoist the verification `confirmCreateLanded` already performs so it
becomes the precondition of `deleteOrphanedChunks` in *every* failure branch, not
only when `ambiguous` is true.

## Related

- #11366 — original report (closed by #11376)
- #11376 — "s3api: don't delete chunks when CreateEntry outcome is ambiguous"

items.title: filer: format adapters align storage chunks to file structure (HLS TS, parquet)
items.body:
This generalizes the idea in #10658. Instead of an HLS-specific virtual namespace, the filer gets a small format adapter system: an adapter reduces one container format to extent sizes, an alignment quantum, and an opaque payload. The core never learns what a TS packet or a row group is, and adapters never see chunks, file ids, or authorization. HLS TS and parquet ship as the first two adapters.

## Why align chunks to file structure

The chunk is the unit of lookup, caching, CRC, EC recovery, and tiering. When chunk boundaries coincide with the file's internal structure, a segment or row-group read maps to exactly its covering chunks: one lookup and one volume round trip instead of two, whole-needle reads that verify CRC, caches that hold exactly the hot bytes, and half the fan-out on EC and cloud-tiered volumes. Arbitrary fixed-size cuts give none of that when readers fetch sub-ranges.

## How it works

The upload loop now accepts a boundary source instead of a fixed chunk size; the fixed size stays as the default implementation. A `Layout` (extent sizes + align + adapter payload) is derived by the adapter and drives the cuts: chunks never span extents, extents larger than `maxMB` split on the align quantum. The layout persists in one compact `x-seaweedfs-` extended attribute, keyed by extent sizes rather than chunk ids so it survives chunk manifest folding — about 3 bytes per extent.

Everything runs on the entry's real path, so JWT prefix scopes, WORM, and read-only rules apply unchanged. No new namespace, no auth bypass knob, no config.

- `POST /path?format.ingest=hls-ts` ingests a multipart `index` sidecar (the FFmpeg-generated EXT-X-BYTERANGE playlist) plus the `media` bytes, cutting chunks on segment boundaries at 188-byte packet alignment.
- `GET /path?format.view=hls-ts` serves a rewritten playlist with plain numbered segment URLs for clients that do not speak byte-range HLS; `&seq=N` streams one segment through the normal prefetch path with entry ETag, preconditions, and HEAD.
- `POST /path?format.repack=parquet` derives the layout from the stored bytes (parquet keeps its index in the footer, so ingest-time cutting is impossible) and rewrites the chunks cut at row-group starts, swapping the entry and queueing the old chunks for deletion. Parquet needs no view; readers already fetch row groups by offset, alignment alone delivers the benefit.

```
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 ... -f hls -hls_playlist_type vod -hls_flags single_file \
  -hls_segment_filename video.ts index.m3u8

curl -F 'index=@index.m3u8' -F 'media=@video.ts;type=video/mp2t' \
  'http://filer:8888/videos/movie.ts?format.ingest=hls-ts'
curl 'http://filer:8888/videos/movie.ts?format.view=hls-ts'          # playlist
curl 'http://filer:8888/videos/movie.ts?format.view=hls-ts&seq=0'    # segment

curl -X POST 'http://filer:8888/data/part-0001.parquet?format.repack=parquet'
```

## Boundaries that keep it maintainable

Adapters implement identity plus whatever capabilities fit (`Sniffer`, `Indexer`, `SidecarIndexer`, `Viewer`) and are discovered by type assertion; they register from `init()` like filer stores. Viewers return a plan (a rendered document or an extent number) and the server executes it, so streaming stays on the optimized path and adapters stay pure functions. A `formattest` kit holds every adapter to no-panic parsing of truncated input, since indexers parse untrusted bytes inside a storage daemon.

The layout is advisory: a stale or corrupt one 404s its views while plain reads stay untouched. It is also bound to a digest of the chunk list it described, so a write through any other path (offset writes, appends, mounts) invalidates the views until re-ingest or repack, even when the file size is unchanged.

## Limitations

- Repack refuses hard-linked, remote, and server-side-encrypted entries. Versioned entries are fine: every object version owns its chunk list. Within a filer, writes serialize on the per-path entry lock - gRPC writers, renames, plain-HTTP overwrites, and repack all take it, and WORM is revalidated under it. The lock is filer-local, so repack also re-reads the entry from the store at commit time and aborts with 409 if anything that fed the repack changed - chunk fingerprint, file size, TTL and both expiry anchors, the S3-expiry flag, hard-link or remote state - or WORM was enabled. The cross-filer window shrinks to the swap itself, inside which repack races like any ordinary writer. Closing it entirely needs owner routing like the S3 gateway's, which is the follow-up; until then route writes for a path to one filer. TTL'd entries repack with their remaining lifetime, anchored the way expiry actually works (Mtime for S3-expiring entries, Crtime otherwise) and rounded up to a volume-representable TTL so chunks never expire before their entry.
- Ingest is explicit; nothing sniffs uploads on the write path.
- S3 surface (per-bucket repack policy, align hints on PUT) and a background repack worker are follow-ups; this PR is the storage and serving foundation they build on.

Tests cover the layout codec and cutter, playlist parsing/rendering/rejections, parquet extent derivation against footer metadata, truncation fuzzing for both adapters, and the full existing weed/server suite passes.

items.title: fix(filer): opt-in chunk-list optimistic concurrency in UpdateEntry (RFC)
items.body:
> **RFC / DRAFT** — opening this for design feedback before hardening. The proto field shape, error/retry semantics, and which call sites should populate the precondition are open questions (see below). Companion to the read-side defense-in-depth in #10367; both address #10366.

## Motivation

A filer entry can end up referencing a volume needle that has been deleted and vacuumed, so reads 404 even though the object is intact in a remote-storage mount. The root cause is a last-write-wins race in the filer's `UpdateEntry`.

`UpdateEntry` (`weed/server/filer_grpc_server.go`) is a read-modify-write:

1. `FindEntry` reads the current stored entry.
2. `validateUpdateEntryPreconditions(entry, req.ExpectedExtended)` — guards **only** the `Extended` map, **not** the chunk list.
3. `cleanupChunks(entry, req.Entry)` diffs stored-vs-incoming chunks to compute garbage needles.
4. the incoming entry is written, then `DeleteChunksNotRecursive(garbage)` fire-and-forget queues the garbage for deletion.

Because the precondition ignores the chunk list, two concurrent RMWs on one entry are last-write-wins on chunks. The stranding interleaving:

1. entry `chunks=[F]`, needle F live.
2. **R** (a chunk-preserving RMW — S3 tag/attr/copy, FUSE setattr, another controller) reads the entry and prepares a metadata-only change that keeps `chunks=[F]`.
3. **D** (eviction/uncache) commits `UpdateEntry chunks=[]`: garbage = `[F]`, F is enqueued for deletion.
4. **R** commits its stale snapshot last: stored is now `[]`, so its garbage diff is empty, and it writes `chunks=[F]` — **resurrecting the reference to F**, which is already queued for deletion.
5. the deletion queue tombstones F; vacuum reclaims it → the entry references a dead needle. `IsInRemoteOnly()` is false (the entry still has chunks) so there is no remote re-pull → **404**.

This has been reproduced deterministically and via a real eviction/uncache path in a testcontainers harness against a released build.

## Overview

Add **opt-in optimistic concurrency on the chunk list** to `UpdateEntry`, mirroring the existing `ExpectedExtended` mechanism:

- **Proto** (`weed/pb/filer.proto`): a new optional `repeated string expected_chunks = 6` on `UpdateEntryRequest`. It carries the client's expected current chunk set as fid strings (`FileChunk.GetFileIdString()`). A fid-string list was chosen as the lightest faithful representation: needle liveness — the thing this bug is about — is keyed exactly by fid `(volume, key, cookie)`, and fid strings are already the identity used throughout chunk diffing (`DoMinusChunks`, `SeparateGarbageChunks`). Regenerated with `make gen` in `weed/pb` (protoc + go + go-grpc + vtproto).
- **Handler**: `validateUpdateEntryPreconditions` now also takes `expectedChunks` and delegates to a new `validateExpectedChunks`. When `expected_chunks` is non-empty, the stored entry's current chunk set is compared (order-independent, multiset by fid) against it, and a mismatch returns a retryable `codes.FailedPrecondition`. This makes R's stale chunk-preserving write fail cleanly so the caller can re-read the emptied state instead of resurrecting F.
- **Backward compatible / opt-in**: empty or nil `expected_chunks` ⇒ no check ⇒ current behavior is preserved exactly. No existing call site changes behavior until it starts populating the field.

### Related: `CreateEntry`

`CreateEntry` shares the same `cleanupChunks` → `DeleteChunksNotRecursive` pattern and the same class of race on overwrite. It is intentionally **not** changed here to keep this PR focused; covering it is a candidate follow-up (see open questions).

## Test

`weed/server/filer_grpc_server_chunk_cas_test.go`:

- `TestValidateExpectedChunks` — unit coverage of the precondition: nil/empty disables, exact match and reordering pass, and every mutation (stored emptied, chunk added/removed/replaced, duplicate-count mismatch) is rejected with `FailedPrecondition`.
- `TestUpdateEntryChunkCASPreventsStrand` — drives the real `UpdateEntry` gRPC handler through the #10366 interleaving:
  - **without** the precondition, R's stale write resurrects `chunks=[F]` (demonstrates the current buggy behavior);
  - **with** `expected_chunks=[F]` against the concurrently-emptied entry, R's write is rejected and the stored entry correctly stays `chunks=[]` (no resurrected reference — the strand does not occur);
  - a fresh RMW whose precondition still matches is applied normally.

`go build ./...`, `go vet`, and `go test ./weed/server/ ./weed/pb/filer_pb/` all pass.

## Open questions for maintainers

1. **Field shape / name.** Is `repeated string expected_chunks` (fid strings) the representation you'd want, or would you prefer a compact fingerprint (e.g. a hash of the sorted fid set) or a structured `repeated FileId`? Fid strings are simple and debuggable but grow with chunk count for large/manifest objects.
2. **Should `CreateEntry` get the same precondition?** It has the same overwrite race. Happy to extend it here if the shape is agreed, or split it into a follow-up.
3. **Which upstream RMW call sites should populate the precondition?** Candidates: the S3 API metadata/tagging/copy paths, FUSE `setattr`, and other filer-client read-modify-write callers. This PR only adds the mechanism; wiring the producers is deliberately deferred pending direction.
4. **Error type / retry semantics.** `FAILED_PRECONDITION` mirrors the existing `ExpectedExtended` behavior and signals "re-read and retry". Is that the contract you want, or should this be a distinct/typed error (or `ABORTED`, which gRPC conventionally marks retryable) so callers can auto-retry without conflating it with object-lock / If-Match precondition failures?

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.title: filer: keep empty folders that are s3tables catalog entries
items.body:
Fixes #11094.

The empty-folder cleaner was deleting S3 Tables catalog entries. A namespace, table or view is a filer directory whose extended attributes *are* the catalog record, and its files may live somewhere else entirely: a rename moves only the catalog pointer and leaves the data at the old path, and a view has no files at all. An empty one is still a live entry.

`DROP TABLE person` followed by `ALTER TABLE t RENAME TO person` hits this every time. The drop's recursive delete queues `person/metadata` and `person`; the rename then recreates `person` as the new catalog entry, which is empty because the data stayed under `t`. Two minutes later the cleaner pops the queue, finds `person` empty and deletes it, cascading up into the namespace. The table is gone from the catalog while the metadata it points at is still on disk — exactly what the report shows, including the `deleting empty folder .../person/metadata (triggered by v2.metadata.json)` line.

`executeCleanup` now reads the folder's own extended attributes and leaves it alone if any of them is a catalog attribute. Ordinary `data/`, `metadata/` and partition directories still get cleaned; the cascade simply stops at the table and at the namespace above it.

There is a second way in, on the queue side: a cleanup is queued against the folder that was found empty, but `OnCreateEvent` only cancelled the queue entry for the *parent* directory. When the drop removes `<ns>/person` and the rename puts a new one back under that name, the stale queue entry outlives the folder it was about and the next pass deletes the replacement. `OnCreateEvent` now drops the queue entry for the recreated path too. The attribute check still covers the other route, the cascade from a child folder up into a table or namespace that was never queued.

Also names the `s3tables.` attribute prefix once in `s3_constants` and builds the catalog keys from it, so the cleaner can recognize an entry without the filer package depending on `s3api/s3tables`.

Reproduced against `weed mini` with the Iceberg REST catalog:

```
== drop table person (purge): 204
== rename person_with_concept_name -> person: 204
== load person right after rename: 200 {"metadata-location":"s3://warehouse/pedsnet/person_with_concept_name/metadata/v1.metadata.json",...}
== waiting 170s for the empty folder cleaner ==
== load person after the cleanup delay: 404 {"error":{"message":"Table does not exist: person",...}}
== list tables: 200 {"identifiers":[]}
```

```
EmptyFolderCleaner: deleting empty folder /buckets/warehouse/pedsnet/person (triggered by metadata)
```

With the fix the same run keeps the table:

```
== load person after the cleanup delay: 200 {"metadata-location":"s3://warehouse/pedsnet/person_with_concept_name/metadata/v1.metadata.json",...}
== list tables: 200 {"identifiers":[{"namespace":["pedsnet"],"name":"person"}]}
```

```
EmptyFolderCleaner: skipping /buckets/warehouse/pedsnet/person (triggered by metadata), s3tables catalog entry
```

The new unit test drives the same cascade through `executeCleanup` and fails without the guard, deleting `person/metadata`, `person` and the `pedsnet` namespace.

items.title: `s3.bucket.create` on an existing bucket replaces it: lifecycle configuration, owner, versioning and Object Lock are lost
items.body:
### Description

Running `s3.bucket.create -name <bucket>` in `weed shell` against a bucket that **already exists** prints `created bucket <bucket>` and reports no error, but it replaces the bucket's filer entry with a fresh one. Every extended attribute of the bucket is lost:

- the stored lifecycle configuration: `GetBucketLifecycleConfiguration` answers `404 NoSuchLifecycleConfiguration` right after;
- the bucket owner set with `-owner`;
- versioning;
- **Object Lock**, which is documented as irreversible ("Once enabled, Object Lock cannot be disabled on a bucket"), comes back `Disabled`.

We hit it because a provisioning script creates its bucket with `s3.bucket.create` and was expected to be safe to re-run. It was not: every re-run silently removed the bucket's lifecycle rules.

### Version

Measured on `chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.42` and `chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.47` (`weed server -s3`, single node). The code path is the same on `master`.

### Reproduction

Lifecycle configuration (3 of 3 runs on 4.42, 3 of 3 on 4.47):

1. `weed shell`: `s3.bucket.create -name my-bucket`
2. Put any lifecycle configuration on `my-bucket` with an S3 client (`PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration`, e.g. `aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration`). `GetBucketLifecycleConfiguration` returns it.
3. `weed shell`: `s3.bucket.create -name my-bucket` again. It prints `created bucket my-bucket`.
4. `GetBucketLifecycleConfiguration` now returns `404 NoSuchLifecycleConfiguration`.

Owner, versioning and Object Lock (3 of 3 runs on 4.47), all in `weed shell`:

```
s3.bucket.create -name locked-bucket -owner alice -withLock
s3.bucket.owner -name locked-bucket        # Owner: alice
s3.bucket.lock -name locked-bucket         # Versioning: Enabled, Object Lock: Enabled
s3.bucket.create -name locked-bucket       # prints "created bucket locked-bucket"
s3.bucket.owner -name locked-bucket        # Owner: (none - admin access only)
s3.bucket.versioning -name locked-bucket   # Versioning: Unconfigured
s3.bucket.lock -name locked-bucket         # Versioning: Disabled, Object Lock: Disabled
```

For contrast, a repeated `s3.bucket.lifecycle.fastpath -name my-bucket -disable` keeps the lifecycle configuration (3 of 3 runs on 4.42).

### Cause

`weed/shell/command_s3_bucket_create.go` builds a fresh `filer_pb.Entry` for the bucket, with no `Extended` unless `-owner`/`-withLock` are given, and sends `CreateEntry` with `OExcl` unset. In `Filer.CreateEntry` (`weed/filer/filer.go`), an existing path with `o_excl == false` goes to `UpdateEntry(oldEntry, entry)`, which carries over only `Crtime` and `Inode` and stores the new entry whole. The lifecycle XML (`s3-bucket-lifecycle-configuration-xml`), the owner, the versioning and the Object Lock keys all live in `Extended`, so they are all replaced.

`s3.bucket.lifecycle.fastpath` does not have the problem because it looks the entry up, changes one key and writes the same entry back.

### Expected

`s3.bucket.create` on an existing bucket should not modify it. It could refuse, as the S3 `CreateBucket` API does with `BucketAlreadyOwnedByYou` / `BucketAlreadyExists`, e.g. by sending `CreateEntry` with `OExcl: true` and reporting that the bucket already exists. Or it could leave the existing entry untouched and say so. Either way a re-run should not be able to drop Object Lock from a bucket.

### Workaround

Check for the bucket first (for example, `s3.bucket.lifecycle.fastpath -name <bucket>` without flags fails with `no entry is found` when it is absent) and call `s3.bucket.create` only when it does not exist.

items.title: filer.remote.sync deletes the live chunks of a file that was rewritten while its upload was in flight
items.body:
**Describe the bug**

`filer.remote.sync` stamps an entry after each upload by writing the event's entry back to the filer (`updateLocalEntry` → `UpdateEntry`, no write condition). The filer deletes every stored chunk absent from an updated entry. When the file is rewritten while its previous upload is still in flight, or when the event is a `-timeAgo` replay, that write-back is a stale snapshot and it deletes the rewrite's chunks:

1. the daemon starts uploading `f` at version A and reads A's chunks;
2. a client rewrites `f` through the filer (version B); the filer stores B's chunk and drops A's;
3. the upload of A completes and the daemon writes snapshot A back; the filer deletes B's chunk;
4. the event for B arrives; its chunk is gone, the upload fails, `isSuperseded` (#11149) sees the entry no longer references B's chunk and skips it.

The entry now points at B's fid with no needle behind it, and the remote holds A. Reads still succeed until the next vacuum (deleted needles are served with `readDeleted`), then fail. The last write is lost on both sides. #11149 only consults the filer after a failed upload, so a successful upload of a stale event still writes back.

**System Setup**

Docker, `chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.47` (also reproduced on master d848b8e), three containers on one network:

```
weed server -dir=/data -ip=cluster -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -master.volumeSizeLimitMB=64 -master.defaultReplication=001 -filer
weed volume -dir=/data -ip=vol2 -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -port=8080 -mserver=cluster:9333
weed server -dir=/data -ip=remote -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -master.volumeSizeLimitMB=64 -s3      # stands in for the cloud
```

```
remote.configure -name=r -type=s3 -s3.endpoint=http://remote:8333 -s3.access_key=any -s3.secret_key=any -s3.region=us-east-1
remote.mount -dir=/buckets/mount -remote=r/archive/
```
(filer restarted after the mount)

```
weed filer.remote.sync -filer=cluster:8888 -dir=/buckets/mount
```

Steps: `docker pause remote` (holds the in-flight upload); `POST /buckets/mount/race.txt` with content `v1`; wait 3 s; `POST /buckets/mount/race.txt` with content `v2`; `docker unpause remote`; wait for the daemon to settle. Then `GET /buckets/mount/race.txt?metadata=true` shows the v2 chunk fid, and `GET <volume server>/<that fid>` is 404 on both volume servers. `volume.vacuum -garbageThreshold=0` makes the filer read fail.

OS: Docker Desktop on macOS, linux/arm64 images. `weed version`: `version 30GB 4.47 c50733600 linux arm64`. filer.toml: the image default (leveldb2).

**Expected behavior**

A stale stamp write must not delete the live chunks. The filer already evaluates `WriteCondition IF_CHUNKS_EQUAL` under the path lock; if the stamp write carried the event's chunk fids, a stale snapshot would be refused with `FailedPrecondition` and could be skipped like a superseded upload. #11435 does this and makes the reproduction pass. It is one way to close the gap; if you prefer a different shape, happy to rework it or leave it to you.

**Additional context**

Hit in production with a workload that rewrites a ~50 MB SQLite file every 60 s through a tmp + rename cycle: three files lost their newest generation. Related recent fixes in the same code path: #11149, #11146, #11261.
