items.title: tarantool: fix upsert data corruption and missing context propagation
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?
The Tarantool filer store had two bugs:

1. Upserts silently corrupted stored data. `InsertEntry`/`UpdateEntry`
   (`tarantool_store.go`) and `KvPut` (`tarantool_store_kv.go`) upsert the
   `data`/`value` field using `crud.Insert` as the update operator. That
   operator maps to Tarantool's `"!"` op ("insert a new field before this
   position"), not "assign/replace". Since every update to an existing
   entry goes through this same upsert path, each write against an
   existing key inserted an extra `data`/`value` field instead of
   overwriting the old one — the tuple grew by one field on every update,
   leaving stale copies of every prior value behind indefinitely.
2. Caller cancellation/timeouts were silently ignored. None of the store's
   methods (`InsertEntry`, `FindEntry`, `DeleteEntry`,
   `DeleteFolderChildren`, `ListDirectoryEntries`, `KvPut`, `KvGet`,
   `KvDelete`) attached the `context.Context` they were given to the
   underlying Tarantool/CRUD request, so only the pool-wide `Opts.Timeout`
   applied and a caller's own timeout/cancellation had no effect.

# How are we solving the problem?
- Replaced `crud.Insert` with `crud.Assign` (`"="`) for the upsert
  update-operations in both `tarantool_store.go` and
  `tarantool_store_kv.go`, so an upsert against an existing key correctly
  replaces the field value in place instead of appending a new one.
- Added `.Context(ctx)` to every request built in the store (CRUD requests
  and the `filer_metadata.*` call requests), so the caller's context is
  propagated to the driver and cancellation/timeouts are honored.

# How is the PR tested?
```bash
make -C docker test_tarantool
RUN_TARANTOOL_TESTS=1 go test -tags=tarantool ./weed/filer/tarantool
```

# Checks

items.title: redis: remove orphaned directory index members on listing
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

The `redis` (v1) store has the same defect #10735 fixes in `redis2`: the listing's not-found branch logs and continues without removing the directory-index member, so a member whose value key is gone — TTL expiry, eviction, an out-of-band `DEL` — stays in the parent's SET forever. v1 is worse off than redis2 here, because `ListDirectoryEntries` loads the whole member set with no pagination, so every dead member inflates every single listing of that directory.

# How are we solving the problem?

Same shape as the redis2 fix, with the sharp edges found in its review already filed off:

- `SRem` the member, re-check the value key, and `SAdd` it back when the value is present again — a concurrent recreate's `SAdd` can land before our `SRem`, and this is what keeps that entry listed. Converges in both interleavings for the same reason as in #10735: `InsertEntry` writes the value before the member.
- A member whose value is gone but whose own child index still exists is kept, not stripped: empty sets self-delete in Redis, so a present index means live children, and detaching it would leave the subtree unreachable to a later recursive delete.
- The repair runs on `context.WithoutCancel` so a client disconnect mid-listing cannot tear it half-done, and a failed restore is logged instead of discarded.

Single-key commands only, so behavior is identical on all `UniversalClient` transports.

# How is the PR tested?

`weed/filer/redis/universal_redis_store_test.go`, gated on `RUN_REDIS_TESTS=1` like the redis2 suite (`REDIS_ADDR` defaults to `127.0.0.1:6379`): orphan removal through the listing, a recreated entry surviving the repair, and a directory with live children keeping its member. All pass with `-race` against redis-server 8 (docker `redis:7` as well); the orphan test fails on master.

items.title: s3api: fix PutObjectAcl permission scoping and owner grants
items.body: ## Summary `PutObjectAcl` had four authorization and ownership bugs: - **Double-scoped action**: the handler embedded the resource path into the action (`WriteAcp:bucket/object`), and `authRequest`/`CanDo` scoped it to the request's bucket/object a second time. A bucket-wide `WriteAcp:bucket` grant could never match, so legitimate object owners received `403 AccessDenied`. - **Policy-authorized requests denied**: after `authRequest` succeeded via an IAM or bucket policy, a leftover `identity.CanDo` gate re-checked only the legacy `Actions` list, denying identities authorized purely by policies. - **Wrong FULL_CONTROL grantee**: for canned and default ACLs, `ExtractAcl` generated the `FULL_CONTROL` grant for the requesting account instead of the stored object owner. An admin setting `private`/`public-read` on another account's object left the owner metadata in place but reassigned full control to the admin. Per AWS, canned ACLs grant the resource owner full control. - **Ownerless object takeover**: objects without stored owner metadata (e.g. written via the filer outside S3) fell back to treating the requester as the owner, letting any user with a `WriteAcp` grant modify the ACL and claim ownership. Non-admins are now denied; admins keep the existing takeover fallback. Grantee validation also accepts the object's stored owner even when that account has been removed from the account registry, so canned/XML ACLs for retired owners keep working; other unknown grantees are still rejected. ## Test plan - [x] New `TestPutObjectAclPermissions` with 26 signed-request subtests covering legacy scoped actions (bucket-wide/prefix/out-of-scope), IAM and bucket policy allow/deny, canned ACLs, XML ACLs, retired owners, and missing/empty owner metadata for both regular users and admins - [x] Confirmed the new test fails on unfixed master (wrong grantee, 403 on valid grants, ownerless takeover) and passes with the fix - [x] `go test ./weed/s3api -count=1` passes - [x] `gofmt` and `git diff --check` clean --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Corrected object ACL updates so default and canned grants are assigned to the object owner. * Non-admin callers can no longer update ACLs when an object has no stored owner. Admins can still proceed using the requesting account as the fallback owner. * Improved consistency of permission checks for object ACL updates.

items.title: filer: close the empty-folder race by checking after each mutation
items.body:
Follows #10782 and #10783.

#10782 stopped the empty-folder cleaner from destroying an entry that arrives between the emptiness check and the delete. #10783 put back the directory that such an entry loses, by watching the metadata stream for its create event. That narrowed the window rather than closing it, and the restore only ran on the cleaner's next pass, so the entry stayed out of listings for up to a ticker interval.

The question on #10783 was whether `ListObjectsV2` can still return nothing for a prefix that has children. It can, and it is worth being precise about why, because the answer decided the shape of this change.

## Every listing starts at the parent

`normalizePrefixMarker` splits a prefix at its last slash, after trimming a trailing one when there is no marker: the part before becomes the directory to list, the part after a name filter. So `data/abc/` lists `data` looking for `abc`, and the traversal has to see `abc` there before it can descend into it. A directory whose own entry is gone is therefore invisible to every prefix shape, including one that points straight at it, and everything it holds goes with it.

That matters most for object storage disks that derive their filesystem from listings rather than from local metadata. There a missing directory is not one absent key, it is a directory that loads with no files at all. Those layouts also tend to empty and refill the same directory name repeatedly, which is exactly the churn the cleaner acts on.

## Both sides act, then look

The cleaner now re-lists a folder once it has removed it, and puts it back if something is in there.

The writer now creates the directories holding an entry *after* the entry rather than before it. A parent checked first can be taken before the entry lands, and nothing looks again; a parent created afterwards cannot be undone by a delete that was authorised before the insert.

Either alone is another narrowing. Together they close it. Call the writer's insert `Tc` and its parent creation `Tp`, the cleaner's delete `Td` and its re-list `Tr`. The writer creates the parent if `Tp > Td`, the cleaner restores it if `Tr > Tc`. For an entry to be orphaned both have to miss, which needs `Tp < Td` and `Tr < Tc`; with `Tc < Tp` and `Td < Tr` that gives `Tr < Tc < Tp < Td < Tr`. Whichever of the two acts second sees what the other did.

This does not depend on the event stream, on the observation window holding, or on a watched set surviving a restart, which were the three ways the previous fix could still be beaten. The deferred path stays as the retry route for a re-check or a restore that fails. Nothing is added to the write path: it is the same single parent lookup as before, on the other side of the insert.

Going second has a cost. The entry is already stored when the parent fails, and it is left there: deleting it by path would destroy a concurrent create that has already succeeded through the update branch, and nothing can tell the two apart, since the update keeps the inode and crtime and mtime only survives the store to the second. A failed create leaving an entry behind is within what a write is allowed to do; deleting an acknowledged one is not.

That entry is not announced. `MetaAggregator` replicates create events straight into a peer's store when the stores are not shared, so emitting one for a write that failed would put the same parentless row on every filer in the cluster rather than leaving it on the one whose next write into that folder repairs it. The row stays local and unlogged, which also means a later delete of it reaches peers with no matching create - a no-op there, since they never had the row.

The order of the events that are emitted is unchanged: the directory events still precede the entry's, because the entry's is emitted at the end of `CreateEntry` in both arrangements. What does change is that the entry is in the store before its parent's event goes out, so anything that lists a directory on seeing it created can now find it already occupied.

A filer that dies between the two steps also leaves the entry without its parent, where before it would have left an empty directory. The entry stays readable by path, and the next write into the same folder recreates the parent.

## A restore should not widen a directory

A writer creating a missing parent has only the entry it is inserting to go on, so a `0700` directory comes back `0751` - `os.ModeDir | 0640 | 0111`. That is not new, it is what implicit parent creation has always done, but the change above means it now happens on the racing path too.

The cleaner reads the real attributes before deleting, so `EnsureDirectoryEntry` now intersects the restorable bits with the ones it saved rather than replacing them - replacing would grant a bit the current directory denied whenever the two modes are not nested, `0705` against a saved `0750` coming back as `0750`. A directory tightened deliberately since is therefore left alone. It cannot tell a deliberate widening from an inferred one and narrows either way, which is the safe direction to be wrong in. The mode bits a restore carries over are named once now and shared with `DirectoryAttributes`, since `Perm()` alone would drop setgid, setuid and sticky.

## Tests

`TestEmptyFolderCleaner_restoreIfWrittenTo` covers the cleaner half: an entry that landed during the delete is restored without waiting for its event, a restored folder does not cascade into its parent, a folder that really is empty still does, and a re-check that fails leaves the folder under observation.

`TestCreateEntryCreatesParentAfterTheEntry` drives the writer half over leveldb2, deleting the folder from the store while the entry is landing and asserting the entry is reachable by listing afterwards. `TestCreateEntryRollsBackWhenTheParentCannotBeCreated` covers the error path. `listHookStore` grew an `afterInsert` hook for this and became `hookStore` rather than gaining a sibling type.

`TestEnsureDirectoryEntryNarrowsAWiderRestore` and `TestEnsureDirectoryEntryKeepsATightenedDirectory` cover the mode. Each test above fails with its own production change disabled.

items.title: fs.configure -apply does not reload filer.conf on the local filer
items.body:
## What happens

On SeaweedFS 4.41, running `fs.configure ... -apply` through a filer updates `/etc/seaweedfs/filer.conf`, but the same filer can keep using its old in-memory `FilerConf` until restart.

Peer filers do reload the config when they receive the metadata event, so the behavior differs between the filer that handled the write and remote filers that subscribe to it.

## Reproduction

With a single filer:

1. Start SeaweedFS 4.41 with a filer.
2. Run a shell command such as:

   ```sh
   fs.configure -locationPrefix=/data/ -collection=hot -apply
   ```

3. Observe that `/etc/seaweedfs/filer.conf` is updated.
4. Continue using the same filer and observe that the in-memory path configuration can remain unchanged until the filer restarts.

## Root cause

`fs.configure -apply` writes the config with `filer.SaveInsideFiler(...)`, which calls `CreateEntry` or `UpdateEntry` for `/etc/seaweedfs/filer.conf`.

The reload hook exists in `Filer.onMetadataChangeEvent()` via `maybeReloadFilerConfiguration()`, but the only caller is the peer metadata subscription path in `MetaAggregator.doSubscribeToOneFiler()` after receiving events from `SubscribeLocalMetadata`.

That means a remote peer receives the metadata event and reloads `filer.conf`, while the local filer that created/updated the entry only logs the local metadata event and never runs the same metadata-change side effects.

## Expected behavior

The filer that handles the local metadata update should process the same `onMetadataChangeEvent()` side effects as remote peers, so local updates to `/etc/seaweedfs/filer.conf` reload `FilerConf` immediately.

items.title: iceberg: make a table commit a compare-and-swap
items.body:
The catalog validated the caller's version token, ran its authorization checks, and only then wrote the new metadata xattr. Two engines committing against the same base both passed that check and both wrote, so the second silently dropped the first one's snapshot. This is the case where Spark and Trino, or an engine and the maintenance worker, write the same table.

The metadata file had the same problem from the other side: both commits derive the same `v{N}.metadata.json` name from the base version, and the write overwrote, leaving the surviving catalog pointer aimed at the loser's metadata. The loser's conflict cleanup then deleted that file — the winner's.

Two changes:

- Write the new metadata file with an exclusive create. A commit that lost the race finds the name taken, has nothing of its own on disk to clean up, and re-reads to rebuild on top of the winner.
- Update the catalog pointer conditionally on the xattr bytes the handler read, using the filer's `ExpectedExtended` precondition — the same compare-and-swap the maintenance worker has always used for its own commits (`weed/worker/tasks/iceberg/filer_io.go`). The filer validates it under the per-path lock, so the read and the write are atomic.

Out of attempts, a losing writer gets 409 `CommitFailedException`, which is what Iceberg clients retry on.

`TestUpdateTableRejectsLostUpdate` drives a competing write into the handler's read-to-write window through the in-memory filer, which now enforces `ExpectedExtended` the way the real one does; it reports success on master with the first commit's snapshot gone. `TestSaveNewMetadataFileRefusesToOverwrite` covers the file side.

Views commit through the same path and get the same treatment.

items.title: filer: route exclusive and conditional creates to the entry's ring owner
items.body:
Stacked on #11108 — review that one first.

## The problem

`CreateEntry` with `o_excl` is a FindEntry-then-Insert. The per-path lock makes that atomic only on the filer running it, and the store's insert is an upsert on every backend, so with several filers two callers both pass the existence check and both report success. `mkdir(2)` then succeeds twice for the same path, which is what #11079 reports and measures (18/30 races on a 3-filer cluster).

The same hole sits under the `condition` precondition. Its proto comment already told callers to route the key's writes to the owner filer themselves — a contract nothing enforced and most callers cannot honour.

## Why not fix it in the store

Every shared store has an atomic insert available and throws it away: `AbstractSqlStore.InsertEntry` catches the duplicate-key error on `PRIMARY KEY (dirhash, name)` and downgrades to UPDATE, `MongodbStore.InsertEntry` is literally `UpdateEntry`, etcd does a bare `Put` where a version-0 txn was available, redis3 does `SET` instead of `SET NX`. Teaching each of them an exclusive insert would work — for shared stores.

It does nothing for `leveldb`, `leveldb2`, `leveldb3` and `rocksdb`. Those filers hold a private store each and cluster through `MetaAggregator` replicating peer metadata logs, so there is no shared constraint to lean on and an exclusive insert is not merely unimplemented but unimplementable. Routing covers them: if every exclusive create for a path lands on one filer, that filer's own store is the arbiter and its writes are immediately visible to itself, so the check is exact even though the cluster is eventually consistent.

It also fails in the wrong direction. A store whose "atomic insert" turns out not to be atomic fails open, silently — precisely the current bug.

## What this does

Resolve the entry's ring owner and forward one hop, bounded by `is_moved`, reusing `forwardToWriteOwner` from #11108. The ring's membership comes from the master, so it tolerates a stale view and reassigns when a filer dies — neither of which a client's configured filer list can do.

Every creator gets this: mount, S3, the filer's own HTTP surface, the Java client. Not only the ones that opted in.

Plain creates are upserts whoever applies them, so they stay local and pay nothing — no extra hop on the write path that matters for throughput.

The route key shares the S3 gateway's namespace (`s3_constants.ObjectWriteRouteKeyPrefix`, whose comment already says the filer is meant to hash the same key), so an object's `ObjectTransaction` and its `CreateEntry` resolve to the same owner and land on that filer's one per-path lock. The name is S3-flavoured for what is now a general filer key; renaming it is a separate cleanup.

## Scope

Routing exclusive creates alone is enough for "at most one exclusive create wins". A concurrent *non*-exclusive upsert on another filer can still clobber the winner's entry, but it cannot make two exclusive creates both succeed, which is the POSIX contract at stake. Routing every write would serialize all namespace mutation through one filer per path — a throughput decision this does not make.

The mount half of #11079 (set `OExcl`, map `ErrEntryAlreadyExists` to `EEXIST`, let the structured code survive `doUnary`) rebases cleanly on top of this and no longer needs its client-side owner ring.

## Tests

New: an exclusive create for a peer-owned path leaves this filer and does not also write locally; a plain create stays local; an `is_moved` create is applied locally even when the ring says otherwise; an owner applies its own exclusive create. Existing `TestCreateEntryOExclSerialized` and `TestCreateEntryConditionEnforced` still pass.

`go test ./weed/server/ ./weed/filer/... ./weed/s3api/...` passes.

- [x] I have added unit tests if possible.
- [ ] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging.

items.title: s3: make RenameObject idempotent for a retried request
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

Addresses #10661.

`RenameObject` is not idempotent. When a rename commits but its response is lost, the client has no safe move left: resending the identical request returns 404, because the source it names is already gone. A retry that succeeded and a rename that never happened look the same from outside.

This matters most where retries are automatic. An SDK that retries on a dropped connection turns one successful rename into a client-visible failure.

# How are we solving the problem?

A rename records what it was, on the object it produced.

The destination carries `x-seaweedfs-rename-token` in its extended attributes: the client's token, the source key, and the time. A retried request is then classified against what it finds there.

- Same token, same source, same destination: the rename already committed here, answer 200 and touch nothing.
- Same token, different rename: answer 409 rather than silently doing something the client did not ask for.
- Token older than 24 hours, or none at all: unrelated, behave exactly as before.

The header is an internal one, so it does not leak back out through GET or HEAD. A request that sends no token takes the unchanged path.

A third choice belongs here rather than in the code alone: if the token write fails and the rename commits anyway, the rename goes ahead and only logs. A retry then finds no token, sees the source gone and gets today's 404, which is exactly where a client stands without this feature. Aborting instead would turn a transient metadata write failure into a failed rename that would otherwise have succeeded, so this fails in the direction that cannot make an existing caller worse off. Say so if you would rather the gateway refuse a rename it cannot make idempotent.

Two more limits are worth naming rather than hiding. The token is written to the destination, so an ordinary rename now carries one extra attribute; a copy of a renamed object inherits it, which is why the classification checks the destination key as well and treats a mismatch as unrelated. And the 24 hour window is a deliberate bound, not a correctness guarantee: past it, a retry falls back to today's 404 behaviour instead of a key answering for a request indefinitely.

# How is the PR tested?

`weed/s3api/s3api_object_handlers_rename_test.go` covers the classification directly: a rename that answers its own retry, the same token sent for a different source refused as reused, a different token treated as unrelated, a copy of a renamed object not answering for the original, an expired token, and the assertion that the header is internal so it cannot reach a GET or HEAD response.

items.title: filer.remote.sync: do not pin the sync offset on completed work
items.body:
## What problem are we solving?
Fixes #11568. The processor holds the persisted sync offset at the oldest failed job, and `util.Retry` gives a job one attempt unless its error is transient. Three failures that leave nothing to do pin the offset for the life of the process, so every restart replays from the pin (seven days observed): a delete of a remote object that was never uploaded (GCS `ErrRemoteObjectNotFound`), the stamp of an entry deleted after its upload (filer `not found`), and a GCS 429 `rateLimitExceeded` on a hot object the replay itself re-uploaded in a burst.

## How are we solving the problem?
- `processDeleteEvent` (the delete branch of the event processor, now a function) and `syncDeleteMarker` treat an absent remote object as deleted, as `processUpdateEvent` already does for the old key of a rename.
- `updateLocalEntry` skips a filer `not found` the way it skips a failed precondition: the delete that superseded the stamp follows in the log.
- `retriedWriteFile` asks `isSuperseded` before the first attempt as well as after a failed one, so a backlog uploads only the version the filer still holds. This also removes the burst that triggers the per-object rate limit. The caller's duplicate "create" log line is dropped; the attempt log inside `retriedWriteFile` remains.
- `util/retry.go`: `ratelimitexceeded`, `rate limit`, `too many requests` are transient.

## How is the PR tested?
- `go test ./weed/command/ ./weed/util/`: new `TestDeleteEventAbsentRemoteObjectIsSuccess` (absent object, other failure, delete marker), `TestUpdateLocalEntrySkipsDeletedEntry` (plain, gRPC, other failure), `TestRetriedWriteFileStopsWhenSuperseded` gains "superseded before the first attempt, no write" and "superseded during the attempt, one write"; `TestIsTransientErrorMessage` gains the GCS 429 text. The two rename tests' stub filer now holds the renamed entry (the pre-upload check reads it).
- Docker, against a filer + S3 remote: a backlog of three rewrites of one path uploads once (was three); a create + delete processed after the fact leaves no `holding sync offset` line and a restart resumes past them (was pinned).

## Checks

- [ ] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging.

items.title: filer: retry and surface metadata replay failures from peers
items.body:
## Problem

When peer filers don't share a store, `doSubscribeToOneFiler` replicates their entries locally via `Replay`. A `Replay` failure was logged and swallowed, then the offset advanced anyway:

```go
if err := Replay(f.Store, event); err != nil {
    glog.Errorf(...)
    return          // <- processEventFn returns nil, processOne advances lastTsNs
}
```

So a failed event is dropped permanently: that entry diverges between filers forever, with no retry and no signal.

Querying three filers on independent `leveldb3` backends directly, they reported `131072MiB`, `131072MiB` and `65536MiB` for the same bucket's quota. The S3 gateway enforced the stale value while another component read the current one, and a quota increase applied to fix it stayed ineffective for three days. A swallowed `Replay` failure is the only mechanism that explains it, though that's a diagnosis — nothing in logs or metrics pointed at replication either way, which is the gap this closes.

## Change

`replicateMetadataChange` retries through `util.Retry`, which already classifies transient failures with bounded backoff. The success path is unchanged.

A non-transient or retry-exhausted failure is deliberately **not** retried further — blocking the subscribe stream would stall every later event from that peer. Instead it becomes visible: a `SeaweedFS_filer_meta_aggregator_replay_failures` counter labelled by peer, and an error log that now names the diverged entry rather than only its parent directory, which was `/buckets` for every bucket.

**Tradeoff:** the retry is synchronous inside the per-peer `stream.Recv()` loop. One poison event costs a bounded ~13s (five attempts: 1 + 1.5 + 2.25 + 3.375 + 5.06s). But if the *local* store is degraded and every event fails transiently, each pays that ~13s plus an unrate-limited `Errorf` — a peer replaying thousands of events/sec drops to a fraction of one. That trades fast-but-silent for slow-but-loud, and it's slowest under exactly the outage this targets. A per-peer circuit breaker or a rate-limited log would fix it; I'd rather disclose it than guess which you'd prefer.

## Tests

`meta_aggregator_replay_test.go` covers both paths — a transient failure retried past, and a permanent one that gives up and increments the counter. Both were verified to fail against the old one-shot body.

`go build ./...`, `go test ./weed/filer/... -race`, full suite (144 packages), `gofmt` and `go vet` on amd64 and 386: all clean.

Related: #10368 → #10382 (earlier `UpdateEntry` race, same reporter); #9923, #10224, #10310 (the bucket-quota work that surfaced this).

items.title: filer sink rename updates the old name instead of moving the entry
items.body:
The filer sink's `UpdateEntry` builds its final request from `existingEntry` (looked up at the old key, so it carries the old name) with `Directory: newParentPath`, then calls the filer `UpdateEntry` RPC. That RPC updates in place at `Directory/Entry.Name` and cannot move entries, so:

- same-directory renames rewrite the old name (the new name never appears),
- cross-directory renames target `newParentPath/oldName` and leave the source path stale.

Both drivers reach this:
- `replication/replicator.go`: the delete-old + create-new branch is gated on `r.sink.GetName() != "filer"`, so filer sinks fall through to `UpdateEntry` even when `oldSinkKey != newSinkKey`.
- `command/filer_sync.go`: the rename branch returns as soon as `UpdateEntry` reports `foundExisting`, without creating the new key or deleting the old one.

Fix: handle a rename as delete-old + create-new (or `AtomicRenameEntry`) in both drivers, with an end-to-end rename test.

Surfaced during review of #9886; kept out of scope there since that change only skips superseded/deleted corrupt chunks.

items.title: s3tables: add the maintenance configuration APIs
items.body:
Rebased onto master now that #10772 has merged; this PR is the remaining three commits.

Adds the five maintenance APIs the S3 Tables control plane was missing: `Get`/`PutTableBucketMaintenanceConfiguration`, `Get`/`PutTableMaintenanceConfiguration`, and `GetTableMaintenanceJobStatus`. Until now the worker took a single global plugin config with wildcard bucket/namespace/table filters, so there was no per-table override and no way to read back what a run did.

### One idea

Iceberg table properties, the AWS maintenance settings, and our plugin config are three vocabularies for the same handful of numbers, so the whole thing is one resolver plus the storage to feed it.

| Knob | AWS setting | Worker field |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compaction target | `icebergCompaction.targetFileSizeMB` | `TargetFileSizeBytes` |
| Snapshot age | `icebergSnapshotManagement.maxSnapshotAgeHours` | `SnapshotRetentionMs` |
| Snapshot floor | `icebergSnapshotManagement.minSnapshotsToKeep` | `MaxSnapshotsToKeep` |
| Orphan age | `icebergUnreferencedFileRemoval.unreferencedDays` | `OrphanOlderThanHours` |

Resolution order is table property, then per-table configuration, then per-bucket configuration, then plugin config. Detection pays nothing for the two new attributes — `scanTablesForMaintenance` already has the entries and their `Extended` maps in hand.

### The one call worth arguing about

Properties beating the maintenance configuration means `PutTableMaintenanceConfiguration` is advisory for knobs the table also declares: you Put 256, Get returns 256, and the worker still uses the table's 512. That diverges from AWS, and the reason is mechanical — a writer honouring `write.target-file-size-bytes` and a compactor rewriting to a different size rewrite each other's output forever. `table_properties_override` (default on) flips the two layers for anyone who wants the control plane authoritative.

`status` is deliberately outside that contest. Iceberg has no property for "don't compact this table", so a disabled type drops its operations and nothing can re-enable them. The kill switch always holds.

### Storage

Two new extended attributes. `s3tables.maintenance` holds the configuration verbatim in its wire shape, so `Get` is a passthrough and no translation layer can drift; Put merges a single type so configuring compaction does not drop snapshot management. `s3tables.maintenanceStatus` is written only by the worker, kept separate so operator and worker writes never contend on one attribute.

Both writes assert the attribute's prior value. Worth flagging: `validateUpdateEntryPreconditions` does per-key CAS but `UpdateEntry` rewrites the whole entry, so writers asserting *different* keys can still clobber each other. `persistPlanningIndex` already lives with this; separate keys plus bounded retries narrow it, and the real fix is partial-xattr update semantics in the filer, which belongs in its own issue.

### Divergences from AWS

Dispatch is by `X-Amz-Target` rather than REST paths, inherited from the existing thirty actions rather than introduced here. `Get` on an unconfigured resource returns an empty `configuration` map instead of synthesised defaults, since our effective defaults live in a layer this API cannot express. Job status is last-run only — there is no retained history behind it. Manifest and delete-file rewrites have no AWS equivalent and ride with `icebergCompaction`, so disabling compaction stops all rewriting.

The encryption trio is still missing and nothing here depends on it.

items.title: Lazily-created remote-mount entries carry no TTL and accumulate without bound
items.body:
All references are to `master` @ `db5a086d0` (4.41).

## Problem

Under a lazy remote mount, filer entries are created on demand: `maybeLazyFetchFromRemote` on a miss in `FindEntry` (`weed/filer/filer_lazy_remote.go:30-117`) and `maybeLazyListFromRemote` on a directory listing (`weed/filer/filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:32-173`). Both create remote-only mappings — a path pointing at an object in the remote store — and neither sets `TtlSec`, so it stays `0` and nothing ever expires them.

They therefore accumulate one entry per distinct object ever touched, and are never reclaimed. On one of our filers that is currently **11,142,152 entries, growing by roughly 330,000/day**, with no upper bound short of the object count of the bucket.

The mount's own cache TTL does not help: `ListingCacheTtlSeconds` only decides how often a directory is re-listed from the remote (`filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:60-76`), and re-listing an existing entry takes the merge path at `:107-120`, which updates it. Nothing removes anything.

This is a real operational ceiling for anyone fronting cloud storage with a shared filer store. The entries are trivially reconstructible — the remote is authoritative, and a filer that lacks an entry re-derives it on the next access via exactly the code that created it.

## Why plain TTL is the right mechanism

The filer already has expiry machinery that does precisely what a cache wants, and — importantly — the *plain* TTL path never touches the remote:

- `FindEntry`: `f.Store.DeleteOneEntry(ctx, entry)` then `ErrNotFound` (`weed/filer/filer.go:434-437`);
- `doListDirectoryEntries`: expired entries collected at `:473-476` and deleted via `f.Store.DeleteOneEntry` at `:496-500`.

Both go to the store and nothing else. Neither reaches `doDeleteEntryMetaAndData`, so `maybeDeleteFromRemote` — which is gated on `!isFromOtherCluster` inside it (`weed/filer/filer_delete_entry.go:144-152`) — is not on that code path at all. Expiring a cached entry **cannot** propagate a delete to the remote object.

Worth having on the record: the S3-lifecycle branch a few lines above behaves differently. It calls `f.doDeleteEntryMetaAndData(ctx, entry, true, false, nil)` (`filer.go:429` and `:492`) with `isFromOtherCluster: false`, so it *does* reach `maybeDeleteFromRemote` and *does* propagate. Whatever is decided here, those two expiry paths are not interchangeable for remote-mounted content.

No new job, no sweep, no schedule — the reclamation is already written.

## Two things have to be fixed first

### 1. `Crtime` is stamped with the remote object's mtime

Both creation sites set `Crtime` to the remote mtime, not to the creation time:

- `filer_lazy_remote.go:84-95` — `mtime := time.Unix(remoteEntry.RemoteMtime, 0)`, then `Mtime: mtime, Crtime: mtime`;
- `filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:137-146` — same, defaulting to `time.Now()` only when `RemoteMtime` is absent.

The expiry check is `Crtime + TtlSec < now`. Stamping a TTL as the code stands would expire every object older than the TTL window the instant its entry is created. And in `FindEntry` the expiry branch `return`s at `filer.go:436`, before the lazy-fetch fallback at `:440-446` — so the caller gets `ErrNotFound` for an object that demonstrably exists in the remote. The next request re-creates the entry, which is immediately expired again: objects would alternate 200/404 forever.

So `Crtime` has to mean "when this entry was created", with `Mtime` keeping the remote mtime. That split is arguably just correct on its own merits, independent of TTLs — `Crtime` is currently reporting a fact about the remote object rather than about the entry, and `entryInitialAtime` (`filer.go:395-400`) already prefers `Mtime` where the distinction matters.

### 2. Expiring a directory's last child can delete the remote prefix

This one I did not expect, and it is the reason I am opening an issue rather than a PR.

The entry deletion itself is store-only, as above. But `doListDirectoryEntries` does not stop there — when the expiry pass leaves no valid entries it calls `DeleteEmptyParentDirectories` (`filer.go:502-507`), and that path *does* propagate:

- `IsDirectoryEmpty` (`filer.go:585-592`) calls `f.Store.ListDirectoryPrefixedEntries` directly, bypassing `maybeLazyListFromRemote` — so it sees only the local store and reports the directory empty even though every object is still sitting in the remote;
- it then calls `f.doDeleteEntryMetaAndData(ctx, dirEntry, false, false, nil)` (`filer.go:573-574`) — `isFromOtherCluster: false`;
- for a directory entry, `maybeDeleteFromRemote` calls `client.RemoveDirectory` (`filer_lazy_remote.go:139-148`);
- `RemoveDirectory` on S3 (`weed/remote_storage/s3/s3_storage_client.go:429`) and GCS (`weed/remote_storage/gcs/gcs_storage_client.go:222`) lists the prefix and **deletes every object under it**.

The only guard is the depth check at `filer.go:550-555`, which protects `/buckets/<bucket>` but nothing below it. So a TTL on lazy entries, added naively, turns "this directory's cached metadata went cold" into "wipe that prefix from the bucket".

It is latent today only because lazy entries carry `TtlSec: 0` and so never reach that code. (The same `isFromOtherCluster: false` call is reachable from the scheduled empty-folder cleaner — `weed/filer/empty_folder_cleanup/empty_folder_cleaner.go:360` — which suggests the interaction between remote mounts and empty-directory cleanup deserves a look regardless of this proposal.)

The fix that fits the existing design is to make `maybeDeleteFromRemote` decline to remove a directory whose emptiness was never confirmed against the remote, or to skip `DeleteEmptyParentDirectories` when the entries were reclaimed by cache expiry rather than deleted by a client. I would rather agree the shape with you than pick one.

## Proposal

Three parts:

1. `Crtime` = creation time at both lazy-creation sites, `Mtime` unchanged. Small and independently defensible.
2. Do not propagate a remote directory removal that originates from cache expiry (see above).
3. Give lazy-created entries a configurable TTL.

For (3), the machinery already exists and I would rather reuse it than add a flag: `FilerConf.PathConf.ttl` (`weed/pb/filer.proto:758`) is already parsed by `needle.ReadTTL` and turned into the entry's `TtlSec` on the upload path (`weed/server/filer_server_handlers_write.go:289-295`). Having the two lazy-creation sites do the same `f.FilerConf.MatchStorageRule(path).GetTtl()` lookup would mean a lazy mount is configured with the command that already exists:

```
fs.configure -locationPrefix=/buckets/mybucket/ -ttl=7d -apply
```

no new proto field, no new flag, and it composes with everything else `filer.conf` already scopes per path. The alternative — a `remote.mount -entryTTL` flag mirroring `-listingCacheTTL` (`weed/shell/command_remote_mount.go:73,93`) — keeps the setting next to the mount it belongs to, at the cost of a second place TTLs come from. I lean towards the `filer.conf` route but have no strong attachment.

## Related

Under a store that expires values natively, there is a second half to this. `redis2`'s directory index leaks a member for every entry whose value key expires, because the listing loop only cleans up on the logical-expiry branch and not on the not-found branch that TTL entries actually take — so TTL-based reclamation frees the values but not the index. Fix in #10735. The two changes compose: TTLs here, and a store that stays clean when they fire.

Background: #8391, #8454, #8522, #8568 are the lazy remote-mount work this builds on. Happy to implement all three parts if the approach sounds right — particularly keen for a steer on (2) before writing anything.

items.title: mount: use the kernel-resolved node id in Link, not the persisted attribute
items.body:
Fixes #8404.

## Problem

`weed/mount/weedfs_link.go`'s `Link()` used `oldEntry.Attributes.Inode` in three places: `inodeToPath.AddPath`, `syncHardLinkSiblings`, and the `outputPbEntry` call that fills the FUSE `LinkOut` reply's node id. `Attributes.Inode` is a persisted filer attribute, not the mount's own node id space, and for an entry that never went through the mount it can be 0. A `LinkOut` reply with `NodeId 0` is rejected by the kernel as EIO, which is the reported error.

`in.Oldnodeid` is available in the same function, already resolved by the kernel and already used to look up the source path (line 43). It is the correct value at all three sites regardless of what the filer happens to have stored, since `inodeToPath` is keyed by the node ids handed to the kernel, not by the persisted attribute, and the two can diverge (`Lookup`'s collision probe can move them apart even for an entry that does carry a stored inode).

## Second bug found while fixing the first

The old `AddPath(oldEntry.Attributes.Inode, newEntryPath)` call, when the attribute was 0, wrote `path2inode[newLink] = 0`. A LOOKUP reply with node id 0 means "negative dentry" (ENOENT) to the kernel, so within the same mount session, a later `Lookup` on the freshly created hardlink name would fail too, independent of the LINK reply itself. Fixed by the same change, since all three sites now consistently use the real node id.

As a side effect of the same root cause: under the old code the real inode's `nlookup` was never incremented for the new dentry even though the kernel holds a reference for it. A later FORGET could over-decrement and trip the `kernel forget over-decrement` guard in `inode_to_path.go`, dropping the inode early.

## Reproducing this

The steps in #8404 (upload with the S3 API, then `ln`) may not fail on current master. Since #9067 added `weed/filer/filer_inode.go` and #9724 reworked it, `Filer.CreateEntry` calls `ensureEntryInode` (`weed/filer/filer.go:268`), which fills in a non-zero `Attributes.Inode` for an entry that arrives without one, for a plain S3 upload that is `FullPath.AsInode(crtime)`. A file uploaded today therefore usually reaches `Link()` with the stored inode already equal to the node id the mount handed the kernel, and the old code happens to pick the right number.

That changed how easy the bug is to hit, not whether it is there. `ensureEntryInode` runs on create and on update (`filer.go:268` and `:482`), never on read, so an entry written before that code landed keeps `inode: 0` for as long as nothing rewrites it, and `ln` on it still returns EIO, which is the state the original report's `fs.meta.cat` dump shows. Any writer that reaches the store without going through `Filer.CreateEntry`/`UpdateEntry` leaves the same hole.

The added test reproduces the failure deterministically: reverting the three call sites makes `TestLinkReportsKernelNodeIdWhenEntryHasNoPersistedInode` fail with `Link replied with NodeId 0`.

## Scope checked and left alone

`Rename` and both `Unlink` call sites were checked for the same class of bug. Neither returns an `EntryOut`, so neither can produce this specific EIO. One of the two `Unlink` sites does have its own, separate precedence quirk (checks the persisted attribute before falling back to the live-resolved inode, the reverse of the other three call sites), but it degrades to a silent no-op on sibling nlink sync rather than an error, and is out of scope here.

## Testing

New `weed/mount/weedfs_link_test.go`, using the existing in-process gRPC test harness (`newCreateTestWFS`, already used by several other mount tests) to drive `Link()` over a real RPC path: one case for an entry with no persisted inode (the bug), one regression case for an entry that already has one. `go build ./weed/mount/...`, `go vet`, and `go test -race ./weed/mount/` are clean.

items.title: log_buffer: bound the flush queue in bytes, not in copies
items.body:
Follow-up to #10430. That PR stopped an oversized metadata event from wedging the change feed; this one stops the flush queue from multiplying such an event through memory.

## The bug

`flushQueueDepth = 16` is a memory bound only while a window is `BufferSize`. An entry larger than that grows its window to fit, and the depth then multiplies straight through — sixteen queued copies of a 100 MB window is 1.6 GB of flush data on its own.

Queued bytes are now accounted against the ceiling the depth was chosen for (`16 * BufferSize`). Ordinary windows still queue sixteen deep, so nothing changes below the threshold.

Three details that matter:

- **Charge the slab, not the window.** `copiedBytes` backs each queued window with `mem.Allocate`, which rounds up to a power-of-two size class. Charging `len(data)` would let the queue hold up to twice the stated ceiling.
- **Admit in seal order.** A producer can now park for seconds. Letting a later window overtake an earlier one would hand `loopFlush` the windows out of order, persisting an older window after a newer one and walking `lastFlushedOffset` / `lastFlushTsNs` backwards.
- **An oversized window goes through alone** once the queue drains, so it is never stuck behind its own size.
- **Large writers wait for headroom before they seal.** A window is copied into its slab under the write lock, *before* the reservation is taken, so a burst of concurrent oversized writers would each be holding a full copy in hand by the time they queue up — memory the budget never sees. This throttles the burst rather than bounding it: a writer that passes the check still seals unconditionally.

A grown window is also sized to the entry rather than twice it — the extra room only bought space for a second oversized record in the same window, doubling both the flush copy and the snapshot taken of it. The overflow guard halved its bound for that doubled allocation and is raised to match what is now allocated.

## Measured

40 sequential `CreateEntry` calls carrying 30 MB of inline `Content` each, paired runs on the same host:

| | peak filer RSS |
|---|---|
| master | 3256 MB |
| this branch | 2641 MB |

## What this does not fix

The budget covers the flush queue only. A sealed window stays reachable through `prevBuffers` for `PreviousBufferCount` more seals and readers may snapshot it, so an oversized entry still costs several times its size before it falls out of the ring — that is most of the remaining 2641 MB, along with the gRPC receive buffer and protobuf decode of the 30 MB requests themselves. Bounding those means bounding `Entry.Content` at the point it enters the filer, which is a separate change.

The copy-before-reserve ordering above is throttled, not bounded — a hard bound would mean reserving before the window is copied, which is a larger change to the seal path.

A shutdown that races a producer whose queue is already full can still drop that sealed window. This change takes any room in the queue before the shutdown escape, which removes the common case; eliminating it entirely needs the flush loop's lifetime reworked and is out of scope here.

Backpressure is the intended behaviour change: with a stalled flush, producers now block instead of queueing more copies. A single window over the whole budget serializes producers behind it where sixteen windows of headroom used to absorb the same outage. That trade is deliberate — blocking beats an OOM.

## Tests

Budget accounting (bounds queued bytes, admits an oversized window once drained, admits strictly in seal order, releases waiters on shutdown), that `queueFlush` charges the slab rather than the window, that a sealed window survives a shutdown racing the hand-off while the queue has room, that a stalled flush blocks producers — asserted on how many producers get through, independently of the counter `reserve` maintains — and that they all drain once the flush resumes.

Each new test was checked to fail against the unfixed code. Suite passes under `-race`.

## Note on an earlier revision

This PR previously also chunked oversized inline `Entry.Content` in the gRPC `CreateEntry`/`UpdateEntry` handlers. Review found that change unsound and it has been dropped: `filer.ReadInsideFiler` reads `Entry.Content` with no chunk fallback, so config blobs over `-maxMB` (`filer.conf`, `/etc/iam/identity.json`, MQ `topic.conf`) would have saved fine and read back empty; and routing `UpdateEntry` through `detectStorageOption` made it return `ErrReadOnly`, breaking metadata-only updates on over-quota buckets. Bounding inline content is still worth doing — at a layer that has neither problem — but not here.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved log flushing backpressure using a bytes-based flush budget for queued windows.
  * Ensured sealed-window admission happens strictly in seal order, even with stalled or racing shutdown hand-offs.
  * Prevented flush-loop wedging by correctly admitting oversized windows when capacity allows.
  * Corrected queue accounting to charge the pooled slab capacity, and improved shutdown release behavior.

items.title: Fix PutObjectAcl writing back to the wrong object for nested keys
items.body:
`PutObjectAclHandler` authorizes against the full requested object key, but then wrote the updated entry back to the bucket root for regular objects (non-versioned, and the null / pre-versioning latest version). For a key like `allowed/protected.txt` the fetched entry name is `protected.txt`, so `UpdateEntry` targeted `protected.txt` at the bucket root instead of the intended object.

Because the update carries the full entry, a principal scoped to `allowed/protected.txt` could overwrite the content, metadata, owner, and ACL of a different `protected.txt` at the bucket root that it has no write or ACL permission for. The trigger is two keys sharing a basename where one is nested under a prefix.

Fix: resolve the object's own parent directory instead of falling back to the bucket root. The `.versions` paths for versioned objects already carry the full key and are unchanged.

Verified end to end: a writer scoped to `allowed/protected.txt` overwrote a root `protected.txt` it cannot write directly before the change; after it, the ACL update lands on the correct object and the victim is untouched. Added a unit test covering the directory resolution for nested, root, deep, null-version, and versioned keys.

items.title: fix(s3): fall back to remote on local chunk 404 for remote-mounted objects
items.body:
## Motivation

Fixes #10366.

When a remote-storage mount is used as a read-through cache over an object store, an S3 `GetObject` can fail with `404 Not Found` even though the object is intact in the remote store.

Objects are dual-populated (app writes to both the object store and SeaweedFS), and a local eviction process later clears local chunks and stamps a remote-only `RemoteEntry` so reads re-pull. That remote-only re-pull path works. The bug is the case where a filer entry **still has local chunks** (so `IsInRemoteOnly()` is false) but the referenced volume needle has been reclaimed by vacuum-compaction/deletion — the chunk read 404s and there is no fallback to the remote copy.

Production log evidence (generalized):

```
stream.go: read chunk <VID>,<NEEDLE> failed, invalidating cache and retrying: ...?readDeleted=true: 404 Not Found
reader_at.go: fetching chunk {FileId:<VID>,<NEEDLE> ...}: 404
s3api_object_handlers.go: streamFromVolumeServers: streamFn failed after writing 0 bytes: ...404
s3api_object_handlers.go: GetObjectHandler: failed to stream <bucket>/<key> from volume servers: ...404
```

## Overview

`streamFromVolumeServers` now detects a not-found chunk read (via `errors.Is(err, util_http.ErrNotFound)`), and — only when no response bytes have been written yet and the entry is remote-backed — recovers instead of failing:

1. **Drop the stale chunks** (`dropLocalChunks`) so the filer entry becomes remote-only again. This is required because `CacheRemoteObjectToLocalCluster` short-circuits as "already cached" while chunks are present, and it also makes future reads self-heal through the existing, well-tested remote-only path.
2. **Re-pull from the remote** via the existing `cacheRemoteObjectForStreamingWithShortTimeout` → `CacheRemoteObjectToLocalCluster` mechanism.
3. **Stream** the requested range from the freshly cached chunks (`streamEntryRangeToResponse`, mirroring the existing reader setup).

The recovery is guarded on `entry.RemoteEntry` being present, so non-remote buckets are completely unaffected. Since `Content-Length` has already been sent and no bytes were written, streaming exactly the requested range still yields a valid response.

All new code lives in `weed/s3api/s3api_object_handlers.go`.

## Status: Draft / WIP

- The SSE-encrypted read path (`streamFromVolumeServersWithSSE`) is not yet covered — only the plain `streamFromVolumeServers` path (where the production 404 occurred).
- Only a guard-level unit test is included (`TestRecoverFromStaleRemoteChunksGuards`), asserting the recovery is skipped for non-remote entries and canceled requests without touching the filer. **TODO:** a full integration test with fake volume servers exercising the drop-chunks → re-pull → stream flow end to end.

## Testing

- `go build ./...` passes.
- `go vet ./weed/s3api/` reports only pre-existing warnings in unrelated test files.
- `go test ./weed/s3api/ -run 'TestRecoverFromStaleRemoteChunksGuards|TestCacheRemoteObjectForStreaming'` passes.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.title: fix(filer.sync): replicate a rename as an atomic move, not a no-op update
items.body:
Fixes #9891

A rename arrives as a single metadata event carrying both the old and new entry. The filer sink routed it to `UpdateEntry`, which cannot move an entry, so a rename was silently dropped: the old path lingered and the new path never appeared. Affects `filer.sync` and `filer.backup` (shared `genProcessFunction`) and the `filer.replicate` driver.

## Approach

Replicate a real move (the path changed) through a native atomic move, not create-then-delete:

- New optional `sink.EntryMover` capability: `MoveEntry(oldKey, newKey, newEntry, signatures)`.
- The filer sink implements it via the filer's `AtomicRenameEntry` — one atomic, metadata-only transaction that relocates a whole subtree server-side.
- Sinks without a native move (s3/local/etc.) keep create-then-delete (create-before-delete, so a crash leaves the entry visible under both names rather than gone).
- In-place updates (same path) still route to `UpdateEntry`.

A directory rename emits the parent event before its per-descendant events; the parent's atomic move relocates the whole subtree, so each descendant event then finds its old path already gone — `MoveEntry` re-checks existence with a lookup and creates the new path, which `CreateEntry` short-circuits (ETag match) into a no-op. With deletes disabled (backup/incremental) a rename creates the new entry and keeps the old.

### Why a native move over create-then-delete for the filer sink

create-then-delete is unsafe there: `FilerSink.CreateEntry` returns nil without creating on a transient chunk-copy error, so a paired delete could remove the only valid destination copy; a directory rename also deleted the old subtree before descendants were recreated; and `deleteIncludeChunks=false` leaked the old chunks. The atomic move closes all three — atomic (no silent-fail loss), single-transaction subtree move (no descendant gap), metadata-only (no chunk leak, no re-replication).

Loop prevention is preserved via `Signatures` (threaded through `AtomicRenameEntry` into the emitted events). Covered by recording-sink routing tests in both drivers (mover -> `MoveEntry`; non-mover -> create-then-delete; deletes-disabled -> keep-old; in-place -> `UpdateEntry`). No real-filer integration harness exists in the repo.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Optional atomic "move" capability for sinks; filer sink will attempt an atomic rename when supported and otherwise fall back to create/delete behavior.
* **Bug Fixes**
  * Renames now create the destination before removing the source; same-path updates use update calls and fall back to delete-then-create when the existing entry is missing. Deleted-file handling respects deletion-enabled/disabled modes.
* **Tests**
  * Added and strengthened tests covering rename ordering, native moves, deletion-disabled cases, and update fallback sequencing.

items.title: feat(filer): TouchAccessTime handler + atime flags (server wiring) [2/2]
items.body:
> **Part 2 of 2** of the `AtimePolicy` work. Depends on #9898 (the policy primitive).

# What problem are we solving?

Filers fronting remote/cloud storage need to evict their local cache by
*least-recently-accessed* (true LRU) rather than least-recently-synced, but the filer
does not track access time. This PR wires the `AtimePolicy` primitive (#9898) into the
filer, completing the **server-side** half of the work begun in #9556.

No read-path bumpers are wired here — those follow once the client-side Toucher helper
lands (see the roadmap in #9899). The feature stays opt-in and defaults to `off`.

- **`TouchAccessTime` gRPC handler**: runs each request through the configured policy,
  clamps a future client-supplied atime to server-now, and persists via the canonical
  `Filer.UpdateEntry` path. Best-effort by design (documented on the handler): relatime
  debouncing keeps the read-modify-write race window small, and only read paths bump atime.

  and the `-filer.atime*` equivalents on `weed server`.
- **`buildAtimePolicy()`** tolerates nil flag pointers so embedders that construct
  `FilerOptions` without registering the flags (`weed mini`, integration tests) do not

items.title: filer: replicate RECOMPUTE_LATEST pointer updates to peers
items.body:
On a multi-filer cluster, `mc du` / ListObjects on a versioned bucket returns only ~1/N of the objects right after a write or mirror, even though the data is intact (per-key GET/HEAD work, and ListObjectVersions sees every version).

Root cause: `applyRecomputeLatest` wrote the `.versions` latest-version pointer (and the demoted prior version's stamp) through `filer.UpdateEntry`, which only touches the local store, with no following `NotifyUpdateEvent`. The pointer never entered the metadata log, so peer filers never replicated it. ListObjects served by any other filer then can't resolve the current version and drops the object. Confirmed with `weed filer.meta.tail`: zero events carry `Latest-Version-Id`, while the version-file creates (which do notify) replicate fine.

Emit `NotifyUpdateEvent` after both `UpdateEntry` calls, the way the `PATCH_EXTENDED` mutation case already does, keeping a pre-update image for the notification diff.

Verified on a 2-filer cluster: 8 versioned PUTs, pointer now present on both filers 8/8, ListObjectsV2 = 8 on both endpoints (was 3). New `weed/server/filer_grpc_server_recompute_test.go` asserts the pointer flip and the demote both emit events; both fail without the change (event count 0). Full `weed/server` suite passes.

items.title: fix(filer.backup): prevent silent backup data loss on transient not-found
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

**`filer.backup` can consume a metadata event — advancing the persisted subscription offset — without ever replicating the file to the sink, with no error logged.** Under a checkpoint write burst, small inline-content files (e.g. configs) land on the destination while sibling manifest-backed files (large `.pt` checkpoints) are silently dropped: partial landing, permanent data loss on the backup.

Three defects combine into the swallow:

1. **filersink `CreateEntry`/`UpdateEntry` swallow replicateChunks errors.** Any failure that is not `errChunkSizeMismatch` is logged with `glog.Warningf` and reported as success (`return nil` / `return true, nil`), so the offset advances past an entry that was never written.
2. **The manifest-chunk branch of `replicateChunks` has no retry.** It resolves via `ResolveOneChunkManifest`/`LookupFileId`, which can transiently fail during a write burst (`volume id ... not found` before the volume registers). The data-chunk branch retries such errors forever inside `fetchAndWrite`; the manifest branch let them escape — which is exactly why large manifest-backed files vanished while small files survived.
3. **`isIgnorable404` over-matches.** It classified `"LookupFileId"` / `"volume id ... not found"` substrings as genuine source 404s, so even a propagated transient error was re-swallowed at the backup layer under the default `-ignore404Error=true`. The `LookupFileId` prefix also wraps pure network failures (`weed/replication/source/filer_source.go` wraps any `LookupVolume` RPC error, including timeouts), so a connection blip was classified as "file is gone". The substring matching was added by #7889 for genuinely-gone volumes replayed from old events — a legitimate case this PR keeps covering, by consulting the live source instead of guessing from error text.

# How are we solving the problem?

Replace error-string guessing with a check of the live source: a failed event may be skipped only when the source has provably moved past the replayed version (entry deleted, or strictly-newer mtime) — lossless, because a later event carries the current content. Otherwise the error propagates, the offset stays put, and the event is retried (`RetryForeverOnError` already provides the retry loop; the sink just never honored the error contract).

- `FilerSink.onReplicateChunkError`: on a non-size-mismatch `replicateChunks` failure, skip only when `hasSourceNewerVersion` confirms supersession; otherwise propagate. Wired into `CreateEntry` and both `UpdateEntry` paths. `errChunkSizeMismatch` → `onCorruptChunk` unchanged.
- `replicateOneManifestChunk`: retry the manifest resolve via `util.RetryUntil`, gated by `manifestResolveRetryGate` — keep retrying only transient errors (volume-lookup races, network interruptions); stop when the source supersedes (skipped as lossless); stop immediately on non-transient errors (corrupt manifest data, bad file ids) so the configured metadata error policy applies (`-disableErrorRetry` included); stop after a few attempts when supersession cannot be checked at all (incremental dated target keys don't map back to a source path), letting `filer.backup` decide with the event's real source key instead of spinning inside the sink.
- `isIgnorable404`: narrowed to genuine source 404s (`http.ErrNotFound`, and the S3 `"404 Not Found: not found"` status string).
- Non-filer sinks (local/S3/GCS/...) and the initial-snapshot walk relied on the broad match as their only lossless-skip valve; they now make the same live-source decision via the newly exported `filersink.SourceSupersedes` (+ `filersink.EntryMtimeNs`), instead of retrying forever on a permanently gone volume (e.g. a dropped bucket collection). The supersession probe derives the source path with `filer_pb.MetadataEventTargetFullPath`, so legacy events with an empty `NewParentPath` fall back to the event directory instead of probing a wrong path.

# How is the PR tested?

- New unit tests:
  - filersink: `TestOnReplicateChunkErrorPropagatesWhenSupersessionUnconfirmed` (a transient/partial not-found propagates, never swallowed); `TestManifestResolveRetryGateUnverifiableSupersessionBounded` (incremental dated keys stop after the bound and propagate); `TestManifestResolveRetryGateNonTransientPropagates` (corrupt-manifest errors propagate immediately, lookup races keep retrying); the supersession decision itself is covered by the existing `TestSourceSupersedes`.
  - command: `TestIsIgnorable404_TransientLookupNotSwallowed` (lookup races are not ignorable and classify for live-source resolution), `TestIsSourceLookupError_NonLookupErrors` (genuine 404s / network errors are not lookup errors), `TestEventSupersessionProbe_PathDerivation` (legacy empty-`NewParentPath` events fall back to the event directory), `TestEventSourceSuperseded_Guards` (no event, no NewEntry, or no source filer never skips).
- `go test ./weed/replication/sink/filersink/ ./weed/command/` pass.
- The filersink hardening ran as the backup binary on our dev cluster, where checkpoint bursts previously reproduced the partial landing; burst-window events that used to be dropped were recovered and re-verified with `filer.sync.verify`.

items.title: mount: refresh open file handles from the metadata event entry
items.body:
Fixes #10394

The invalidation callback looked the path up again after a subscription event touched an open handle. A transient lookup failure, or a stale cached result, left the handle pinned to its old entry with no retry: the cursor had already advanced, so only another event for the same path would recover it. An open reader then kept observing the obsolete size and chunk list indefinitely, and a metadata mutation through that handle could write the stale entry back to the filer.

Apply the entry the event itself carries instead. Each invalidation now attaches the entry that lives at the invalidated path — NewEntry for in-place updates, rename destinations, and creates; nil when the path was vacated — and the handle refresh clones it, applies the filer-to-local uid/gid mapping, and sets it directly, with no filer round-trip. A nil entry keeps the last entry so unlinked-but-open reads still work. Self-originated events cannot clobber local write state through this path: the local apply seeds the dedup ring, so the subscription's redelivery is dropped before invalidation.

Reproduced in a test that delivers an update event to a mount whose filer address has no listener, so any secondary lookup fails like a transient error: before, the open handle stayed at the old 88-byte entry; after, it refreshes to the event's 180,020-byte entry. A second test pins the per-event-shape invalidation payloads for update, rename, create, and delete.

items.title: fix(filer.backup): repair chunk-incomplete and stale destination entries
items.body:
<!--
Upstream seaweedfs PR body for the filer.backup chunk-truncation repair fix.
Format follows seaweedfs/.github/pull_request_template.md.
Suggested title: filer.backup: repair chunk-incomplete and stale destination entries
Internal analysis / design notes: pr-filer-backup-chunk-truncation-repair.md
-->

# What problem are we solving?

`filer.backup` (filersink) can leave a destination **chunk-incomplete**: it holds only a subset of the source's chunks while `attr.file_size` keeps the full value. Every skip/repair decision in `chooseUpdateAction` and `CreateEntry` keys on `filer.FileSize`/`filer.ETag`, so the missing range is invisible and the only repair branch (gated on `FileSize(existing) < FileSize(incoming)`) never fires — the copy never self-heals. It is only visible via an MD5/ETag comparison (`filer.sync.verify`).

Concrete cases in the current code that this fixes:

1. **Truncated destination, full size, never repaired (event path).** `mtime(existing) <= mtime(incoming)` → `updateNormal`, whose `compareChunks` diff never backfills a gap predating `oldEntry`; `updateRepair` needs a strictly-newer *and* smaller destination, but the copy reports full size.
2. **`attr.Md5`-backed ETag equality skips a truncated destination (snapshot path).** `filer.ETag()` returns `attr.Md5` when set (e.g. S3 PutObject), so `CreateEntry`'s ETag-equal check passes a short chunk list as "already replicated" — even on `-initialSnapshot`.
3. **Range gap at full total size.** `FileSize(dst) >= FileSize(src)` treats a destination as complete even when its chunks sum to the size at the wrong offsets (a missing range plus an extra chunk elsewhere).
4. **Stale superseded chunk at full coverage.** A missed same-range overwrite leaves an old-version chunk; size and even coverage look full.
5. **Out-of-order replay rolls a newer destination back.** `updateRepair` fires on strictly-newer-but-smaller, so an older, larger replayed event overwrites a legitimately newer truncate.

(**A truncated copy first appears when a transient `replicateChunks` failure is acked without retry.** That is best left to a separate change, if needed at all: simply propagating the error would stall the offset on the failing event, so a permanently failing chunk would retry forever and head-of-line-block the stream. This PR instead lets a diverged destination self-heal through detection — on the next event or an `-initialSnapshot` pass — so truncation is eventually-consistent rather than permanent.)

# How are we solving the problem?

Decide on the chunk lists, never on `attr.FileSize`/`attr.Md5`:

- **`coversReference`** — does the destination cover every byte *range* the reference covers? Range-by-range over merged intervals, so equal totals at different offsets don't pass (fixes 1–3). Manifests count by their own span.
- **`hasStaleBackupChunk`** — does the destination hold a chunk this backup wrote (`SourceFileId` set) that the reference no longer lists (fixes 4)? Chunks without `SourceFileId` (rsync/direct seed) are ignored.

Applied at:

- `chooseUpdateAction(existing, oldEntry, incoming)` (event path): a strictly-newer destination is always `updateSkip` (fixes 5). Otherwise an allocation-free positional match short-circuits the in-sync case; on its failure, `updateRepair` when `!coversReference`, or — only when strictly older — `hasStaleBackupChunk`.
- `destinationSatisfiesSource` (`CreateEntry` / `-initialSnapshot`): keeps a strictly-newer destination, else checks coverage and (older-only) identity **before** ETag, so an `attr.Md5`-backed ETag match can't skip a bad copy.

The fast path keeps normal replication allocation-free; the `O(n log n)` checks run only on divergence. Change is confined to `weed/replication/sink/filersink/`.

# How is the PR tested?

- Unit tests in `filer_sink_test.go`: `TestCoversReference`, `TestHasStaleBackupChunk`, `TestDestinationMatchesReference`, `TestDestinationSatisfiesSource`, `TestChooseUpdateAction` — covering the in-sync fast path, range gaps, `attr.Md5`-backed truncation, older/equal-mtime stale chunks, newer out-of-order replay (no rollback), and rsync-seeded destinations. `go test ./weed/replication/sink/filersink/...`, `gofmt`, `go vet` clean.
- **On a live pair, `filer.sync.verify` flagged 13 chunk-incomplete files; the event path and a `-initialSnapshot` pass re-replicated them in full, 13 → 0.** Correct files short-circuit on coverage/ETag.
