items.title: S3: let a key that is a prefix of other keys be an object
items.body:
Fixes #10910. Fixes #10660.

## The problem

S3 keys are flat, so `collision/foo` and `collision/foo/bar` are independent keys
that coexist on AWS in either write order. SeaweedFS stores a key as a filer path,
so those two keys want the same path - one as an object, one as a directory.

```
$ aws s3api put-object --bucket coll --key "collision/foo/bar" --body data.bin
{"ETag": "..."}
$ aws s3api put-object --bucket coll --key "collision/foo" --body data.bin
An error occurred (InternalError) when calling the PutObject operation
(reached max retries: 2): We encountered an internal error, please try again.
```

The opposite order returns 200 for both PUTs and is not better. The promotion in
`ensureParentDirectoryEntry` turns the file into the directory and keeps its chunks
- but an empty object leaves no chunks, no content and no mime, so nothing marks
the directory as still being a key, and it disappears from listings and answers 404.
One with data survives and lists as `collision/foo/`, a key with a trailing slash
the client never wrote.

## Approach

The representation already existed and was half-built: a directory entry can carry
an object's chunks, and `IsDirectoryKeyObject()` recognises one. What it could not
do is say *which* key that directory stands for, because it inferred the answer
from whatever data happened to be on the entry:

- an empty object leaves nothing to infer from, so the key is lost;
- it cannot tell `PUT foo/` (key ends in a slash) from `foo` with `foo/bar` under
  it (key does not), so it listed both with a trailing slash;
- and the write path never produced one deliberately - `CreateEntry` refused.

So the fix is to stop inferring. A directory that also holds a key gets marked -
`x-seaweedfs-prefix-object`, read through `Entry.IsPrefixObject()` - and every
surface that meets one consults the mark rather than guessing from chunks or mime.

The write path has to be able to produce that state, which is where the reported
500 comes in. `Filer.CreateEntry` flattened the `%w`-wrapped sentinel that
`Filer.UpdateEntry` returns, so `errors.Is` stopped matching and the S3 mapper fell
through to `ErrInternalError`; `ErrExistingIsDirectory` had been unreachable since
#8767 added the mechanism. With the wrap restored the sentinel is not just an honest
409, it is the signal `putToFiler` retries on: the object is written onto the
directory the nested keys already live in. That costs nothing on the normal path -
no extra lookup per PUT - because it only runs after a write has actually collided.

Everything else follows from the mark:

| surface | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| PUT, nested key written first | retryable 500 | 200, object stored on the directory |
| PUT, nested key written second | 200, key silently lost when empty | 200, key survives |
| GET / HEAD | 404 when the object is empty | serves it |
| LIST | `collision/foo/` | `collision/foo`, plus `collision/foo/` as a CommonPrefix |
| ListObjectVersions | disagreed with ListObjectsV2 | same keys, same prefixes |
| DELETE key | worked | worked; the mark goes with the data |
| DELETE `?versionId=null` | retryable 500 | 204 |
| COPY, either end | 404 / retryable 500 | 200 |
| RENAME, either end | 404 / 409 | 200 |
| empty-folder cleaner | would delete an empty one | leaves it alone |

A directory SeaweedFS keeps its own state in - `.uploads`, a key's `.versions`
history - is not a prefix a key can be stored on, and still answers 409. A *bare*
prefix, a directory holding no object of its own, is still not a key: it stays a
404 as a copy or rename source.

## Decisions worth arguing with

**A TTL comes off the directory rather than onto it.** An expired entry is deleted
one row at a time, so expiring a directory removes it and strands every key under
it. The promotion has been carrying the object's TTL across since #8767, which is
that landmine already armed. Dropped on promotion, and one an older build wrote is
no longer acted on. The lifecycle worker still expires the object, through the S3
delete that leaves the directory behind.

**Rename copies instead of moving.** `AtomicRenameEntry` moves a directory by moving
everything under it, and the nested keys are not part of what is being renamed. When
either end of a rename is such a key, the object's own data is copied across and
then stripped off the source key, whose entry survives as the directory those keys
live in. Both keys are held under their write locks for the whole move. It is not
atomic across a crash - the destination can land with the source still there, and a
retry settles it - which is what the operation costs when the source entry cannot go
away. Plain renames still take the atomic path.

**A page can run one item over `MaxKeys`.** A prefix object spends two slots on one
filer entry, its key and the CommonPrefix its nested keys fold into, and the budget
is only checked between entries. Both come off the same entry, which a marker names
as a whole: `adjustMarkerForDelimiter` maps a `<key>/` marker to "that subtree is
done", so a page cannot end between them and resume at the prefix. I tried it, and
the deferral dropped CommonPrefixes from every page. Overrunning by one is the
better failure. `TestS3PrefixObjectKeys/Paged` asserts the bound and that every key
and prefix comes back exactly once.

**One existing test changed meaning.** `TestRenameObjectOntoDirectory` asserted 409
on the grounds that an object must not replace a directory. It does not replace it -
the directory and its children survive and the key becomes an object too, exactly as
PutObject now does - so it asserts that instead.

## Commits

1. `filer: keep the sentinel when CreateEntry reports an update failure` - the
   one-character fix the issue points at.
2. `s3: let a key that is a prefix of other keys be an object` - the mark, the write
   retry, and the read, list and delete surfaces that consult it.
3. `filer: keep a TTL off a directory that stands for an object`.
4. `s3: delete the null version of a key other keys are nested under` -
   `routedDeleteNullVersion` had no fallback to the lock path, which the unversioned
   routed delete has for exactly this case, and `deleteSpecificObjectVersion` passed
   a whole key where a name was expected. Both pre-existing, both affecting
   trailing-slash directory markers with children too.
5. `filer: keep the sentinel when MkFile and Mkdir report a create failure` - the
   same flattening one layer out, which is why a CopyObject onto such a key answered
   a 500 where a PutObject of it answered 409.
6. `s3: copy and rename a key that other keys are nested under` - closes #10660.

## Verified

`test/s3/normal/s3_prefix_object_test.go` covers both write orders, empty objects,
delimiter listings, pagination across max-keys 1 to 5, versioned and suspended
buckets, deleting either key or a specific version, reserved directories, copy and
rename in every direction, and that ListObjectVersions and ListObjectsV2 name the
same keys and prefixes over six prefix/delimiter combinations. Every assertion was
run against the unfixed code first. Wired into the S3 authenticated integration
workflow, which already gates on `weed/s3api/**` and `weed/filer/**`. The 27 tests
in `test/s3/copying` pass.

Against a live `weed mini`, both orders return 200 and listings match AWS:

```
$ aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket deep --delimiter / --prefix "x/"
  Contents:       ['x/a', 'x/a2']
  CommonPrefixes: ['x/a/']
$ aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket deep --delimiter / --prefix "x/a/"
  Contents:       ['x/a/b', 'x/a/b2']
  CommonPrefixes: ['x/a/b/']
```

items.title: restore: weed nfs gateway (NFSv3) with opt-in inode index scoping
items.body:
## What

Restores the `weed nfs` (NFSv3 gateway, built on `github.com/willscott/go-nfs`) that was removed in #9724, with an **opt-in inode index scoping** flag to address the index bloat, plus fixes that make the gateway fully functional out-of-the-box.

## Why #9724 removed it

`weed nfs` needs an inode-to-path reverse-lookup to decode fixed-length NFS file handles. The original wrote one KV row per filer entry on every create/update/delete, regardless of NFS usage — reaching ~1.1B rows / 30GB on S3-heavy deployments. Since the index only benefits NFS, it was removed.

## Changes (3 commits)

**1. Restore the gateway** from 4.29, adapted to current APIs (WithGrpcClient ctx arg, NewReaderCache invalidator, UploadWithRetry callback removal). No change to NFS protocol logic or filehandle format.

**2. Opt-in index scoping** — filer flag `-nfs.inodeIndexPrefixes=/exports`:
- Only entries under the configured prefixes get an index row
- Default empty = index disabled = zero KV rows = identical to current master
- Directory-boundary matching (`/exports` matches `/exports/x` not `/exportsx`)

**3. Bug fixes from real kernel-client testing**:
- `lookupGeneration` fell back to initial generation when index absent (mount no longer hard-fails)
- `mountproto` hint corrected to `udp` (MOUNT responder is UDP-only)
- **`weed nfs` now self-manages its index via the filer KV RPC** — it writes the inode→path row itself on create, so the gateway is fully functional with default filer config (no `-nfs.inodeIndexPrefixes` needed for a working export). This is additive: when the filer flag IS set, both writers produce byte-identical records and converge.

## Verification

**Unit**: `go build ./weed/...` passes (CGO_ENABLED=0); `go test ./weed/server/nfs/...` 64+2 tests pass; `go test ./weed/filer/ -run TestInodeIndex` both scoping tests pass.

**Real kernel-client E2E** (privileged container, Linux 5.10 NFSv3 client, live single-node cluster):

Default filer config (no index flag):
- `mount -t nfs -o nfsvers=3,nolock,noacl,port=2049,mountport=2049,proto=tcp,mountproto=udp` — mount OK exit 0
- Write + read back — content matches, VERIFY OK
- mkdir + nested write — OK
- `dmesg | grep nfs` — zero kernel errors

With `-nfs.inodeIndexPrefixes=/exports`:
- All operations pass — no regression

The 4.29-era kernel-client interop bugs do NOT reproduce.

## Non-goals

NFSv3 + MOUNTv3 only; no NLM/NSM (mount with `-o nolock`); AUTH_SYS only; no pNFS.

## For maintainers

Default config is fully functional. The opt-in flag adds filer-side index writes for deployments wanting broader index coverage; nfs self-manages index for its own export subtree regardless. Index bloat is bounded by NFS export volume, not total cluster objects.

items.title: fix(filer.sync): scope filesystem key sanitization to the local sink
items.body:
Fixes #9892

`destKey` ran every sink key through `escapeKey`, whose Windows build strips colons. Colons are illegal in NTFS filenames so the **local** sink needs that, but s3/filer/azure/gcs/b2 accept colons as ordinary key bytes — stripping them silently diverged the destination key (a source `a:b` replicated as `ab`). The escaping was also inconsistent within a run: the in-place-update branch built keys that bypassed `escapeKey`, so on Windows an update wrote an escaped create key but deleted the unescaped old key.

Move the sanitization out of the command layer into the local sink, behind a Windows build tag, applied at every entry point (`CreateEntry`/`UpdateEntry`/`DeleteEntry`). `LocalIncSink` inherits it via embedding.

- Non-local sinks now receive the raw key (colons preserved).
- Non-Windows builds are byte-identical to before for every sink (`sanitizeFsKey` is identity).
- A leading drive-letter colon (`C:\...`) is preserved so absolute target paths stay valid — the old `escapeKey` stripped it, corrupting absolute Windows paths.

Verified host build/test/gofmt and `GOOS=windows` build/vet (which compiles the Windows-tagged source and tests).

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Sync destination keys preserve colon characters for non-local sinks.
  * Local filesystem sinks now sanitize keys on Windows (preserving drive-letter prefixes) to avoid illegal path characters; non-Windows behavior is unchanged.

* **Tests**
  * Added platform-specific tests verifying key sanitization and that destination keys preserve colons where expected.

items.title: s3api: retry a transient failure when listing multipart uploads/parts (RFC on layering)
items.body:
Fixes #7221. References #7235 (same underlying gap, see the caveat below on why I'm not claiming it outright).

Opening this as more of an RFC than a drop-in fix, since neither issue has had a maintainer reply yet and the right layer for this retry is a real open question I'd like your take on before anyone spends more time on it.

## The problem

`ListMultipartUploadsHandler` / `ListPartsHandler` list through `(*S3ApiServer).list` → `filer_pb.List` → `DoSeaweedListWithSnapshot`, which opens a streaming `ListEntries` call and drains it with `stream.Recv()`. Neither the initial call nor the `Recv` loop retries a transient gRPC error. #7221's log shows the initial call failing with `Unavailable`; #7235's shows `Recv` failing mid-stream. Both currently turn one blip from a restarting filer into a 500 for the S3 client.

## What this does

A small bounded retry (`listWithRetry` in `weed/s3api/filer_util.go`, 3 attempts, 100ms backoff doubling) wrapped around both `listMultipartUploads` and `listObjectParts`'s calls to `s3a.list`. Only classified-transient errors are retried (gRPC `Unavailable`, plus a message-based fallback since `DoSeaweedListWithSnapshot` wraps the `ListEntries` failure with `%v`, which drops the gRPC status code, so a pure `status.Code` check alone would silently miss #7221's exact failure shape while still catching #7235's). A not-found answer is never retried, and no other error is either.

## Why here and not lower

`DoSeaweedListWithSnapshot` is shared by mount's meta cache, the shell, and other object listings. A retry inside it, after a stream fails partway through, would re-deliver entries a streaming callback had already consumed, corrupting state for those callers. `weed/mount/meta_cache/meta_cache_init.go` already establishes the pattern this codebase uses for exactly that hazard: retry above the streaming primitive and explicitly reset the accumulator. `(*S3ApiServer).list` fits that pattern, since it collects into a fresh slice on every call.

## A caveat I'd rather raise myself than have found later

That "a replay can't duplicate or drop entries" guarantee holds within one call to `list`, but not past it. `withFilerClientFailover` already re-runs its callback against the next filer in the cluster on any non-`NotFound` error, and it does not reset the caller's accumulator between attempts. On a multi-filer gateway, a `Recv` failure partway through a listing (#7235's exact scenario) can hit this path and produce a silently duplicated result with `err == nil` rather than an error `listWithRetry` could catch. Pre-existing, not introduced by this PR, and out of scope to fix here, but it's the reason I'm not claiming this closes #7235 outright, and it's also an argument for retrying at a lower, shared layer eventually rather than per call site.

## Two questions for you

1. **Right layer**: keep the retry scoped to the 2 multipart call sites (as here), move it inside `(*S3ApiServer).list` itself so all 17 call sites benefit, or would you rather see a gRPC service-config retry policy on the dial options, which would cover `ListEntries` globally without new Go code but wouldn't help the `Recv`-mid-stream case? I have opinions but no strong attachment to this shape.
2. Is the `withFilerClientFailover` accumulator issue above worth its own issue, or is it already known/accepted?

## Testing

`weed/s3api/filer_util_list_retry_test.go` scripts a fake filer client and stream against the real `filer_pb.List` / `DoSeaweedListWithSnapshot` code path (not a reimplementation), covering: recovery from a transient `ListEntries` failure, recovery from a transient `Recv` failure, giving up after the bound, and correctly *not* retrying permission-denied, invalid-argument, and not-found. `go build ./weed/s3api/...`, `go vet`, and `go test ./weed/s3api/...` are clean.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved reliability of multipart upload and object-part listings by automatically retrying transient filer errors.
  * Preserved not-found and other non-transient errors without unnecessary retries.
  * Added bounded backoff and clear error reporting when retries are exhausted.

* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for transient failures, stream interruptions, retry limits, and error propagation.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

items.title: filer.sync: repair a destination shorter than the source
items.body:
A file left truncated by a failed replication is never corrected, because `FilerSink.UpdateEntry` treats a newer destination mtime as last-writer-wins and skips the update. The trap (seen in #9330): the source kept the file's original mtime while the partial copy on the destination was written recently, so the destination looks "newer" forever. `filer.sync.verify` already flags exactly this as `late_updates_skip_likely` (B_NEWER).

When the mtime guard would skip but the destination is strictly shorter than the source (`filer.FileSize`), re-replicate the full source content and replace the chunk list instead of skipping. The same shorter-than-source bypass is added to `CreateEntry`'s skip. Only the previously-skipped path changes behavior; the normal catch-up path is untouched.

The skip/repair/normal decision is factored into `chooseUpdateAction` and unit-tested.

Note: the repair fires on the next metadata event for the path, so an already-truncated file under a stable source still needs the source to re-emit (touch / re-copy). This stops the trap going forward and repairs on the next change.

Ref: #9330


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved file replication to better detect and repair truncated or incomplete copies encountered during sync; now avoids skipping necessary overwrites when destination is newer but smaller.
  * Enhanced conflict resolution for files with mismatched timestamps and sizes to ensure genuine updates are applied reliably.

* **Tests**
  * Added targeted tests covering replication decision logic to validate normal, skip, and repair behaviors.

items.title: filer: add RECOMPUTE_LATEST mutation to ObjectTransaction
items.body:
Replaces #9642 (auto-closed, same cascade fallout).

A RECOMPUTE_LATEST mutation scans a directory under the transaction lock, picks the child that sorts last (descending) or first by name, and copies mapped extended keys into a pointer entry (clearing them when empty). Mechanical and S3-agnostic: the caller supplies the sort direction and key mappings. Covers re-pointing the latest version after a specific version is deleted.

items.title: s3api: 修复 PutObjectAcl 的权限范围检查和拥有者授权
items.body:
# 解决的问题

`PutObjectAcl` 的权限范围和拥有者处理存在以下问题：

- 非管理员对象拥有者具有 `WriteAcp:acl-bucket` 授权时，修改 `allowed/image.png` 的 ACL 仍返回 `403 AccessDenied`。处理器将资源路径放入 action，随后 `authRequest` 和 `CanDo` 再次拼接资源路径，导致正常的桶级授权无法匹配。
- 只有 IAM 或桶策略授权的对象拥有者，也会被处理器额外的旧 `CanDo` 检查拒绝；该检查只读取旧 `Actions`，无法识别已通过统一授权的策略。
- 管理员为其他账号拥有的对象设置 `private` 或 `public-read` 时，拥有者元数据仍指向原账号，但预定义 ACL 的 `FULL_CONTROL` 授权被错误地生成给请求账号。预定义 ACL 应授予资源拥有者完全控制权限，见 [AWS ACL 说明](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/acl-overview.html#canned-acl)。
- 对象缺少拥有者元数据时，处理器把当前请求账号当作拥有者。有旧 `WriteAcp`、IAM 或桶策略授权的普通用户因此能修改 ACL，并将自己写为拥有者；非 S3 的 Filer 写入路径可以产生这类对象。

# 实现方式

- 处理器仅传入基础 `ACTION_WRITE_ACP`，由现有授权逻辑处理资源范围。
- 去除策略授权成功后的旧 `CanDo` 门禁，保留统一授权路径和对象拥有者检查。
- `ExtractAcl` 的预定义/默认 ACL 分支使用已有资源的 `ownerId` 生成授权，XML ACL 分支继续验证不可更改的拥有者。
- 授权验证允许保留元数据内的不可变历史拥有者 ID，即使该账号已从当前 IAM 注册表删除；其他未知授权账号仍按原逻辑拒绝。

items.title: fix(filer.sync): resolve manifest chunks against source filer
items.body:
## Summary

`FilerSink.UpdateEntry` was resolving source-side manifest chunks against the **sink** filer, causing `404 Not Found` on cross-cluster syncs whenever the two clusters had overlapping volume IDs hosting unrelated content. The 404 aborts `compareChunks`, the manifest chunk never gets replicated, and the target is left with whatever flat chunks landed from earlier partial syncs — visible as `SIZE_MISMATCH` in `filer.sync.verify` on files large enough to use manifest chunks (~150 GB+ in practice).

```
compare chunks error: fail to read manifest 631,0babe7a0a8718478:
  http://<sink-volume>:8082/631,0babe...?readDeleted=true: 404 Not Found
```

`oldEntry`/`newEntry` arrive from the source cluster's metadata stream, so manifest resolution must use the source filer's volume map. Switching `compareChunks(... filer.LookupFn(fs) ...)` to `filer.LookupFn(fs.filerSource)` matches what the flat-chunk path already does in `fetchAndWrite` (`fs.filerSource.ReadPart`).

Reported in #9330.

## Test plan

- `go build ./weed/replication/sink/filersink/`
- Cross-cluster active-active sync of a >150 GB file no longer 404s on the source's manifest chunk, and `filer.sync.verify` reports size agreement.

items.title: fix(filer.backup): skip replay events whose source chunk was superseded or deleted
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

* #9883

`filer.backup` (and the shared filer sink used by `filer.sync`) can get permanently stuck on a single metadata event and stop all replication.

**When the backup replays the source metadata log from a checkpoint, an event may reference a chunk whose needle was overwritten or deleted and garbage-collected on the source volume.** Fetching it now returns 0 bytes, correctly flagged as a permanent `errChunkSizeMismatch` — but the sink returned that error to the subscription, so the same offset was retried forever and replication never advanced. Restarting resumes at the same offset and wedges again.

# How are we solving the problem?

Let the sink **skip** such an event, but only when it can prove the event is stale; otherwise keep refusing so genuine loss of a still-live file halts loudly instead of being dropped silently.

- `onCorruptChunk` centralizes the three `errChunkSizeMismatch` sites (`CreateEntry`, `UpdateEntry` repair/default) into one decision.
- `sourceSupersedes` re-reads the entry's current state on the source: **gone** (`ErrNotFound`, including wrapped / gRPC-string forms) or a **strictly-newer mtime** than the replayed version ⇒ skip; any other lookup error or a same/older version ⇒ keep (refuse).
- `getEntryMtimeNs` compares mtime at nanosecond precision so versions rewritten within the same second are ordered correctly.
- `targetPathToSourcePath` reports "unmappable" for incremental sinks (their date-prefixed keys cannot be reversed to a real source path), so a mis-mapped not-found never skips a live entry.

**Skipping is lossless because metadata events are full-entry snapshots, not deltas: a later event re-carries the current chunk set, and a delete event reconciles a removed file.** Only the provably-superseded case is auto-skipped; genuine loss of a live chunk still halts replication by design.

# How is the PR tested?

Unit tests in `weed/replication/sink/filersink` (`go test ./weed/replication/sink/filersink/`):

- `TestSourceSupersedes` — not-found (sentinel / wrapped / gRPC string) and nil entry → skip; network error → keep; source newer → skip; same/older → keep.
- `TestGetEntryMtimeNs` — nanosecond precision, same-second ordering, nil safety.
- `TestOnCorruptChunkRefusesWhenSupersessionUnconfirmed` — never skip silently when supersession is unconfirmed.
- `TestTargetPathToSourcePath` — incremental sink is reported unmappable.

Also verified end to end on a green→blue `filer.backup`: the run that previously wedged for 45+ minutes now skips the stale events (663 skips, 0 refuses), passes the stuck offset, and drains the backlog.

We also confirmed that, in the actual filer.backup production environment, processing continued successfully beyond that checkpoint.

# Checks

items.title: feat(s3api): add bucket quota S3 extension via ?seaweedfs-quota
items.body: ## Summary - Adds a SeaweedFS-specific S3 subresource for bucket quota management: `PUT /{bucket}?seaweedfs-quota` and `GET /{bucket}?seaweedfs-quota` - Request/response body is JSON: `{"quota_size": 100, "quota_unit": "GB", "quota_enabled": true}` - Quota is stored on the bucket's filer entry (positive = enabled, negative = disabled but retained, zero = no quota), matching the existing admin REST API behavior - When quota is cleared, the bucket's read-only flag is also lifted - Authentication uses the existing S3 SigV4 flow — no new global secret needed - Authorization uses two new dedicated IAM permissions: `s3:PutBucketQuota` and `s3:GetBucketQuota` ## Motivation This enables integrations like Apache CloudStack to manage per-bucket quotas through the S3 endpoint with a scoped credential, without exposing the broad admin REST API or requiring a separate admin token. The credential can be limited to `s3:PutBucketQuota`/`s3:GetBucketQuota` only, preventing bucket deletion, user management, or cluster topology changes. This replaces the earlier approach in #11278 (closed), which added bearer-token auth to the broad admin REST API. After review, that was unnecessary for this integration — static S3 config plus standard S3 APIs plus one scoped quota mutation API is sufficient. ## Usage ```bash # Set a 100GB quota on a bucket curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 ..." -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"quota_size":100,"quota_unit":"GB","quota_enabled":true}' http://s3endpoint:8333/mybucket?seaweedfs-quota # Get the current quota curl -H "Authorization: AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 ..." http://s3endpoint:8333/mybucket?seaweedfs-quota ``` ## IAM policy example ```json { "Statement": [ { "Action": ["s3:PutBucketQuota", "s3:GetBucketQuota"], "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::*" } ] } ``` ## Changes | File | Change | |------|--------| | `s3_constants/s3_action_strings.go` | Add `S3_ACTION_PUT_BUCKET_QUOTA` and `S3_ACTION_GET_BUCKET_QUOTA` | | `s3_constants/s3_actions.go` | Add coarse-grained `ACTION_PUT_BUCKET_QUOTA` and `ACTION_GET_BUCKET_QUOTA` | | `s3_action_resolver.go` | Map `seaweedfs-quota` query param to fine-grained s3: actions | | `s3api_bucket_quota_handlers.go` | New — PutBucketQuotaHandler and GetBucketQuotaHandler | | `s3api_bucket_quota_handlers_test.go` | New — tests for unit conversion, validation, and error paths | | `s3api_server.go` | Register the two routes in the bucket subrouter | #### Test plan - [x] `go build ./weed/s3api/...` — compiles clean - [x] `go test ./weed/s3api/ -count=1 -short` — all existing + new tests pass - [ ] Manual: verify SigV4 auth and IAM policy enforcement against a live deployment - [ ] Manual: verify quota enforcement (read-only flag) after setting quota via S3 extension --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **New Features** - Added SeaweedFS-specific S3 bucket quota management through `GET` and `PUT` requests. - Supports quota units from bytes through terabytes. - Added authorization for reading and updating bucket quotas. - Disabling a quota restores bucket write access. - Quota responses provide the configured bucket limit in JSON format. - **Bug Fixes** - Added validation for malformed requests, unsupported units, invalid sizes, overflow, trailing data, and missing bucket names. - **Documentation** - Updated Apache CloudStack integration guidance for IAM endpoint configuration.

items.title: fix(shell): mergeVolumes hard-link safety and cleaner cleanup logging
items.body:
Follow-up to #9160 addressing two post-merge review comments from coderabbit.

## Summary

- **Hard-link safety** (1st commit). Hard-linked entries share a chunk list with their siblings, but the filer's \`UpdateEntry\` only rewrites one entry at a time. Moving a chunk here leaves every other hard-linked sibling pointing at a fid that either gets deleted by the filer's own garbage step after \`UpdateEntry\` or by \`deleteMovedSourceNeedles\` — either way, siblings end up with dangling references. Detect \`entry.HardLinkId\` and skip the entry with a visible log line.
- **404 suppression in cleanup warnings** (2nd commit). \`BatchDelete\` also returns \`StatusNotFound\` (404) for an already-deleted needle in the cookie-check path, not only \`StatusNotModified\` (304). Both are benign races against concurrent fsck/vacuum, so both should be suppressed.

items.title: fix(redis2): remove orphaned directory index members on listing
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

The `redis2` per-directory child index — the ZSET at `<dir>\x00` — accumulates members whose value key no longer exists, and nothing ever removes them.

`ListDirectoryEntries` reads the members, then calls `FindEntry` per member (`weed/filer/redis2/universal_redis_store.go:189-231`). Two outcomes matter:

- the value key is gone → `filer_pb.ErrNotFound` → the loop logs and `continue`s, **leaving the member in the index** (`:205-211` before this change);
- the value key is there but the entry is logically expired (`Crtime + TtlSec < now`) → `DEL` the value **and `ZREM` the member** (`:213-219`).

The second branch is the intended behaviour — the code already means to keep the index consistent. The first branch is the one that actually runs for TTL entries, because the two expiry deadlines are on different clocks:

- `doInsertEntry` writes `SET <key> <value> EX <TtlSec>` (`:86`), so Redis drops the key at `set_time + TtlSec`;
- the filer's logical check is `Crtime + TtlSec < now`.

`Crtime` is stamped before the store write, so `Crtime <= set_time` and the logical deadline is the *earlier* of the two — by the sub-millisecond gap between stamping the attribute and Redis processing the `SET`. The `else` branch can therefore only run if a listing lands inside that gap. Every listing after it finds `GET` returning `redis.Nil` and takes the not-found branch, the one that leaves the member behind. (An entry that is later *updated* re-arms the Redis TTL from the update time while `Crtime` stays put, which is the only case where the working branch is reliably reachable — so the leak is specific to entries created once and never touched again, which is the common TTL case.)

Under a TTL workload the index therefore grows without bound, and two things get worse with it:

- `LIST` costs one `GET` round trip per name *ever created* in that directory, not per live entry;
- the skip logs at `glog.V(0)`, which is on by default, so every listing emits one log line per dead member.

The same orphan is produced by any other route that removes a value key without the matching `ZREM` — an out-of-band `DEL`, `maxmemory` eviction, or a `DeleteEntry` that fails between its `DEL` and its `ZREM` (`:119-143`). TTL is just the one that does it continuously.

# How are we solving the problem?

`ZREM` the member in the not-found branch, mirroring what the expiry branch already does below and against the same `dirListKey` variable — guarded against a concurrent recreate, per the review point below.

Things I checked rather than assumed:

**A member cannot legitimately outlive a missing value.** `InsertEntry` writes the value first and adds the member second (`:56-74`): `doInsertEntry`'s `SET` has returned before `ZAddNX` is issued. So "member present" implies "value was written at some point", and a member returned by `ZRangeByLex` whose value is absent has had that value deleted or expired — it is never an entry mid-creation. The opposite window (value written, member not yet added) does exist, but a listing cannot observe it, because it only iterates members.

**The value can, however, come back before the `ZREM` lands** — which the paragraph above does not cover, and which both review bots caught. If an `InsertEntry` for the same path completes between `FindEntry` returning `ErrNotFound` and the `ZREM`, its `ZAddNX` is a no-op, because the member is still in place; the `ZREM` then strips the index member off a live value. `UpdateEntry` only calls `doInsertEntry` (`:92-95`) and never re-adds the member, so the entry stays invisible to `ListDirectoryEntries` and `DeleteFolderChildren` until another `InsertEntry` hits that exact path. That is a real regression, so the cleanup compensates rather than removing unconditionally: `ZREM`, re-check the value key, and `ZAddNX` the member back when the value is present again or when the check itself failed.

That converges in both interleavings. If the insert's `SET` lands before the re-check, the re-check sees it and restores the member; if it lands after, the insert's own `ZAddNX` is necessarily after our `ZREM` and restores the member itself. Only a positively confirmed absent value leaves the member removed, so the repair still converges for genuine orphans at the cost of one extra `EXISTS` — on the repair path only, which is one-time per orphan.

The remedy both reviews suggested — a Lua script or `MULTI` spanning the value key and the index key — is not available here. `RedisCluster2Store` embeds `UniversalRedis2Store`, and the two keys (`<prefix></dir/name>` and `<prefix></dir>\x00`) carry no hash tag, so a multi-key script would be `CROSSSLOT` under `redis_cluster2`. The compensating form uses only single-key commands and behaves identically on all three transports.

**`keyPrefix`.** `dirListKey` is `store.getKey(genDirectoryListKey(...))` at `:178` — already prefixed — and the new `ZREM` reuses that variable instead of rebuilding the key. Rebuilding it unprefixed would have been a silent no-op for every deployment that sets `keyPrefix`, which is why the test runs both with and without one.

**Transient errors cannot trigger it.** `FindEntry` returns the bare `filer_pb.ErrNotFound` sentinel only for `redis.Nil` (`:99-102`); every other failure is wrapped with `fmt.Errorf`. The branch guard is `err == filer_pb.ErrNotFound` — identity, not `errors.Is` — so a connection blip cannot match it and still breaks out of the loop as before.

**Super-large directories.** `isSuperLargeDirectory` makes `InsertEntry` skip the `ZAdd` and `DeleteEntry` skip the `ZRem`, so the index key does not exist for those directories at all. `ZRangeByLex` returns nothing, the loop body never runs, and the new call is unreachable. The feature is unaffected.

Cleanup failures still do not fail the listing — a failed repair is simply retried on the next one — but the errors are no longer discarded outright, since the restore decision depends on them: a `ZREM` that errors removes nothing and returns, and a re-check that errors restores the member, so the failure modes bias towards a stale member rather than a lost one.

**Deliberately not included:** making the physical TTL a backstop behind the logical one (`SET ... EX TtlSec + grace`) so the logical branch wins the race and performs the clean two-part delete. That changes when data actually disappears from Redis for every `redis2` user, and it would not remove the need for this fix, since the non-TTL routes above produce the same orphan. Happy to raise it separately if you want it.

**Also deliberately not included:** the expiry branch at `:214-219` has a pre-existing instance of the same race, with a worse outcome — a concurrent `InsertEntry` landing between `FindEntry` and the `DEL` loses the freshly written value, not just the index member. Closing it needs a compare-and-delete on the value rather than the compensating restore used here, so it is a separate change and not one I want to smuggle into this one.

# How is the PR tested?

New `weed/filer/redis2/universal_redis_store_test.go`. It needs a live Redis, so it follows the existing convention for store tests that need a server — `tarantool_store_test.go` gating on `RUN_TARANTOOL_TESTS=1`, `foundationdb_store_test.go` skipping when the cluster is absent — and skips unless `RUN_REDIS_TESTS=1`, with `REDIS_ADDR` defaulting to `127.0.0.1:6379`. Each test works inside a uniquely named directory and cleans up after itself, so it is safe against a shared instance.

I did try the in-tree `tempredis` helper used by `redis3/kv_directory_children_test.go` first. It hangs on any current `redis-server`: it blocks waiting for the literal line `The server is now ready to accept connections`, which Redis stopped printing years ago. That helper is only reachable from a `Benchmark` today, so nothing noticed. Worth knowing if anyone tries to build on it.

- `TestListDirectoryEntriesRemovesOrphanedIndexMembers` — two entries, one's value key dropped; asserts the listing returns only the live entry *and* that the index is left holding only the live name. Run with `keyPrefix` empty and set.
- `TestListDirectoryEntriesRemovesIndexMembersExpiredByRedis` — inserts with `TtlSec: 1`, waits past it, asserts Redis has already dropped the value key, then asserts the listing empties the index. This is the reported path end to end.
- `TestRemoveOrphanedDirectoryListMemberKeepsRecreatedEntry` — added for the review point above. It drives the cleanup with the value key present, which is exactly the state a concurrent recreate leaves behind, and asserts the member survives and the entry still lists. Asserted at the helper rather than through `ListDirectoryEntries`, because the window between the `GET` and the `ZREM` cannot be hit deterministically from outside. It fails if the restore is removed.

Against `redis-server 8.2.1`, the first three cases fail on master and pass with the change:

```
--- FAIL: TestListDirectoryEntriesRemovesOrphanedIndexMembers/keyPrefix=
        directory index holds [alive orphan], want [alive]
--- FAIL: TestListDirectoryEntriesRemovesOrphanedIndexMembers/keyPrefix=sw:
        directory index holds [alive orphan], want [alive]
--- FAIL: TestListDirectoryEntriesRemovesIndexMembersExpiredByRedis
        directory index holds [ttl], want none
```

`go build ./weed/...`, `go vet ./weed/filer/redis2/`, `gofmt` all clean, and `go test ./weed/filer/redis2/... -race` passes against a live Redis.

## Note on `redis3`, which I am not touching

`redis3` has the same shape at `universal_redis_store.go:140-166`, and is worse off: its not-found branch removes nothing at all, and its expiry branch calls `ZRem` on `<dir>\x00` — which in `redis3` is a **string** holding the serialised skiplist root (`kv_directory_children.go:43`), not a ZSET. That returns `WRONGTYPE`, the result is discarded, and it has therefore never removed anything.

Flagging rather than fixing, because `weed/filer/redis3/README.md` reads `Desuppported.` and the store has no section in `weed/command/scaffold/filer.toml`, so any fix there would be to a store nobody is being pointed at. Say the word if you would like it repaired anyway.

## Related

#10736 proposes giving lazily-created remote-mount entries a TTL so the filer's existing expiry machinery reclaims them. The two compose: that change makes TTL entries the normal case for a whole class of deployment, and this one is what stops the directory index growing anyway when they expire.

items.title: feat(shell): fs.mergeVolumes deletes source needles after filer update
items.body:
## Summary

Before this change, \`fs.mergeVolumes\` only copied chunks to the destination volume and updated the filer — the source needle sat untouched on its original volume as a silent orphan. Operators had to run a separate \`volume.fsck\` + \`volume.vacuum\` pass to actually reclaim the space, and #9116 ([comment](https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/9116#issuecomment-4282692876)) showed how that pipeline can look exactly like \"mergeVolumes did nothing\": the source volume keeps reporting its original size even though every chunk has been logically moved out.

Clean up the source inline. For each entry, track the pre-move fids as they're captured, and after the \`UpdateEntry\` RPC commits, issue \`BatchDelete\` on every replica of each source volume.

Key invariants:

- Source fids are only deleted **after** \`UpdateEntry\` succeeds. If the filer write fails we skip cleanup for that entry, so we never delete data the filer still references.
- \`rewriteManifestChunk\` grew a fourth return value so nested manifest rewrites and sub-chunk moves propagate their moved-source list back to the top-level callsite. The outer manifest needle is recorded at the callsite, since only the callsite sees the pre-rewrite fid.
- \`deleteMovedSourceNeedles\` logs errors but never returns them. Propagating would abort \`TraverseBfs\` mid-merge and strand remaining entries; logging leaves the existing fsck fallback intact.
- \`StatusNotModified\` from the volume server is expected whenever a concurrent fsck purge beat us to the delete or a replica already reconciled — not warned on.

Readonly source volumes are already rejected up front by \`createMergePlan\`, so by the time we reach the delete the source is writable. If a replica's readonly bit has flipped since then the delete will fail and get logged; the user can re-run once they've fixed the replica (same failure mode as today's fsck purge).

Fixes the space-not-reclaimed half of #9116. Related design discussion in #8589.

## Test plan

- [ ] \`go build ./weed/shell/...\` — passes

items.title: filer: add ObjectTransaction for atomic multi-entry object writes
items.body:
Third of the filer-primitive stack. Stacked on #9640 (write precondition).

A versioned object write touches several entries that must change together: the main object, a delete marker or version file, and the latest pointer on the `.versions` directory. Holding a distributed lock across separate RPCs to do this is exactly what the per-path lock was meant to replace, but a single `CreateEntry` only covers one entry.

`ObjectTransaction` carries:
- `lock_key` — the object path; the filer holds its per-path lock for the whole call,
- an optional `WriteCondition`, checked against the entry at `lock_key`,
- an ordered list of `ObjectMutation` (`PUT` / `DELETE` / `PATCH_EXTENDED`).

The filer locks `lock_key`, evaluates the condition, then applies the mutations in order. Callers route the object's writes to its owner filer so the one lock is authoritative across all of the object's entries (main + `.versions/*`) — the same routing invariant the rest of the stack relies on.

`DELETE` and `PATCH` of an absent entry are no-ops, so a replayed transaction is idempotent. `PUT` entries are metadata-scoped; data-bearing writes (chunks) are written before the transaction, as the version-file pattern does today.

This generalizes the special-cased versioned-finalize op into one reusable primitive. New RPC, so `filer.pb.go` + `filer_grpc.pb.go` regenerated (protoc-gen-go-grpc 1.6.2, matching the repo).

items.title: S3 versioned copy object can lead to file corruption
items.body:
With S3 versioning on, simply updating the mtime creates a new version that shares the chunks with the original. The problem is that the refcount is not updated, so if you deleted one version the other would lose all its data. This is especially dangerous when combined with S3 lifecycle rules, which automatically delete older versions, and automatic vacuuming, which cleans up the deleted data permanently.

I ran into this issue with rclone, which updates the mtime after every upload. The rest of this issue description is from AI but I did at least fact check the most important details, and there are files on my cluster that actively exhibit these symptoms.

Repro (present since 4.20)

```sh
weed server -dir=/tmp/sw -filer -s3 -master.volumeSizeLimitMB=1024 -volume.max=10
head -c 16777216 /dev/urandom > blob.bin
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8333/repro
curl -X PUT "http://localhost:8333/repro?versioning" \
  -d '<VersioningConfiguration xmlns="http://s3.amazonaws.com/doc/2006-03-01/"><Status>Enabled</Status></VersioningConfiguration>'
curl -X PUT --data-binary @blob.bin -D - http://localhost:8333/repro/blob
curl -X PUT -D - \
  -H 'x-amz-copy-source: /repro/blob' \
  -H 'x-amz-metadata-directive: REPLACE' \
  -H 'x-amz-meta-mtime: 1653465360' \
  http://localhost:8333/repro/blob
```

Then confirm the two versions have identical chunks with `fs.meta.cat`

```weedshell
> fs.meta.cat /buckets/repro/blob.versions/v_6736fb618f225b190c06e5b4fb63c83b
      "fileId": "4,0443236f67"      "fileId": "1,01721254cd"
      "fileId": "5,02879dca88"      "fileId": "3,036c5a29f5"
  "hardLinkId": ""

> fs.meta.cat /buckets/repro/blob.versions/v_6736fb6180893a6e671022aed7e0d1f2
      "fileId": "4,0443236f67"      "fileId": "1,01721254cd"
      "fileId": "5,02879dca88"      "fileId": "3,036c5a29f5"
  "hardLinkId": ""
```

Then delete one of the versions

```sh
curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:8333/repro/blob?versionId=6736fb618f225b190c06e5b4fb63c83b"
204
```

```weedshell
> volume.list
volume Id:1, ... FileCount:1, DeleteCount:1, DeletedByteCount:4194349
volume Id:3, ... FileCount:1, DeleteCount:1, DeletedByteCount:4194349
volume Id:4, ... FileCount:1, DeleteCount:1, DeletedByteCount:4194349
volume Id:5, ... FileCount:1, DeleteCount:1, DeletedByteCount:4194349

> volume.fsck -findMissingChunksInFiler -cutoffTimeAgo 0
/buckets/repro/blob.versions/v_6736fb6180893a6e671022aed7e0d1f2
/buckets/repro/blob.versions/v_6736fb6180893a6e671022aed7e0d1f2
/buckets/repro/blob.versions/v_6736fb6180893a6e671022aed7e0d1f2
/buckets/repro/blob.versions/v_6736fb6180893a6e671022aed7e0d1f2
```

After vacuuming, the read still succeeds:

```
curl -o out -w '%{http_code} %{size_download}\n' \
    "http://localhost:8333/repro/blob?versionId=6736fb6180893a6e671022aed7e0d1f2"
200 0

curl "http://localhost:8333/repro?versions&prefix=blob"
<Key>blob</Key>
<VersionId>6736fb6180893a6e671022aed7e0d1f2</VersionId>
<IsLatest>true</IsLatest>
<Size>16777216</Size>
```

HTTP 200 with a zero-byte body, while `ListObjectVersions` still advertises the
object as the current version at its full 16 MiB. No error is returned at any
point in the sequence.

Extra details:
<details>

### Root cause

`CopyObjectHandler` takes the metadata-only self-copy branch
(`weed/s3api/s3api_object_handlers_copy.go`, the `sameDestination && (replaceMeta || replaceTagging) && canUseMetadataOnlySelfCopy(...)` guard). With versioning enabled `routeInPlace` is false, so it takes the clone path:

```go
updatedEntry := cloneProtoEntry(currentEntry)   // carries currentEntry's chunk fids
...
dstVersionId, etag, finErr = s3a.finalizeCopyDestination(dstBucket, dstObject, dstVersioningState, updatedEntry)
```

`finalizeCopyDestination`'s `VersioningEnabled` branch writes a new version file via `mkFile(..., dstEntry.Chunks, ...)` with:

```go
func copyEntryToTarget(dst, src *filer_pb.Entry) {
	...
	dst.Chunks = src.Chunks     // same fids, no data copy, no refcount
```

Reusing chunks is correct **without** versioning — the clone replaces the entry it came from, so one entry owns the needles throughout. The in-code comment says as much ("it is still metadata-only (reuses the source chunks)"). Under versioning the clone becomes a *second live entry*, and the assumption no longer holds.

### Why it turns into data loss

The filer already refcounts shared chunks, but only for hard links
(`weed/filer/filer_delete_entry.go`):

```go
if len(entry.HardLinkId) != 0 && entry.HardLinkCounter > 1 {
	// if the file is a hard link and there are other hard links, do not delete the chunks
} else {
	f.DeleteChunks(ctx, p, entry.GetChunks())
}
```

Copy-created versions have `HardLinkId == ""`, so they fall through to `DeleteChunks`.

Deleting a specific non-current version is a routine, documented S3 operation,
and SeaweedFS performs it *automatically* for anyone with a
`NoncurrentVersionExpiration` lifecycle rule
(`weed/s3api/lifecycle_xml/types.go`, `weed/s3api/s3lifecycle/noncurrent_since.go`).
No API-surface hint exists that two versions might be entangled.

Two triggers we hit in production:

1. **Deleting a version.** Removing one twin frees needles the other needs.
2. **`fs.mergeVolumes`.** `deleteMovedSourceNeedles` (`weed/shell/command_fs_merge_volumes.go`) tombstones source needles after moving them, with no refcount — its comment states the assumption directly ("the source data is already orphan at this point"). With twins, it frees needles the untraversed twin still points at. `moveChunk` reads with `?readDeleted=true` so the twin is repairable until vacuum compacts the tombstone; after that `moveChunk` fails, the loop logs and `continue`s, and the entry keeps pointing at the source volume. Once the source is vacuumed empty, `volume.deleteEmpty` removes it and the reference dangles permanently.

That chain cost us three volumes and four unrecoverable object versions.
</details>

Suggested changes:
<details>

```diff
diff --git a/weed/s3api/s3api_object_handlers_copy.go b/weed/s3api/s3api_object_handlers_copy.go
index ed44cf4a4..337b801bc 100644
--- a/weed/s3api/s3api_object_handlers_copy.go
+++ b/weed/s3api/s3api_object_handlers_copy.go
@@ -271,6 +271,22 @@ func (s3a *S3ApiServer) CopyObjectHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request
 				return s3err.ErrNone
 			}
 			updatedEntry := cloneProtoEntry(currentEntry)
+			// The clone carries currentEntry's chunk fids verbatim. Without
+			// versioning that is exactly right: the clone replaces the entry it
+			// came from, so one entry owns the needles throughout. Under
+			// versioning the clone becomes a SECOND live entry alongside the
+			// source version, and nothing refcounts a plain shared chunk list --
+			// deleting either version, or relocating its chunks with
+			// fs.mergeVolumes, frees needles the other still references. Put
+			// both under one hard link id so the filer's existing refcount
+			// (see filer_delete_entry.go: HardLinkCounter > 1 skips DeleteChunks)
+			// governs the shared needles.
+			if dstVersioningState == s3_constants.VersioningEnabled {
+				if linkErr := s3a.linkSelfCopyVersions(dstBucket, dstObject, currentEntry, updatedEntry); linkErr != nil {
+					glog.Errorf("CopyObjectHandler: link self-copy versions %s/%s: %v", dstBucket, dstObject, linkErr)
+					return filerErrorToS3Error(linkErr)
+				}
+			}
 			updatedEntry.Extended = mergeCopyMetadata(updatedEntry.Extended, updatedMetadata)
 			if updatedEntry.Attributes == nil {
 				updatedEntry.Attributes = &filer_pb.FuseAttributes{}
@@ -511,6 +527,52 @@ func copyEntryETag(entry *filer_pb.Entry) string {
 	})
 }
 
+// linkSelfCopyVersions puts an existing version and the clone about to be
+// written beside it under a single hard link id, so the needles they share are
+// refcounted instead of owned twice. It mirrors the sequence in
+// weed/mount/weedfs_link.go: stamp the id on the entry that already exists and
+// persist it, then hand the same id and counter to the new entry, which the
+// caller writes via mkFile.
+//
+// A "null" version predates versioning and lives at the bare object key with no
+// .versions file to update; there is nothing to link it to, so leave it be and
+// let the caller fall back to the current behaviour.
+func (s3a *S3ApiServer) linkSelfCopyVersions(bucket, object string, currentEntry, newEntry *filer_pb.Entry) error {
+	if len(currentEntry.GetChunks()) == 0 {
+		return nil
+	}
+	versionId := string(currentEntry.Extended[s3_constants.ExtVersionIdKey])
+	if versionId == "" || versionId == "null" {
+		return nil
+	}
+
+	normalizedObject := s3_constants.NormalizeObjectKey(object)
+	versionsDir := s3a.bucketDir(bucket) + "/" + normalizedObject + s3_constants.VersionsFolder
+
+	if len(currentEntry.HardLinkId) == 0 {
+		currentEntry.HardLinkId = filer.NewHardLinkId()
+		currentEntry.HardLinkCounter = 1
+	}
+	currentEntry.HardLinkCounter++
+	// Address the version by the name derived from its own version id rather
+	// than trusting Entry.Name, which getLatestObjectVersion may have filled
+	// from a different lookup path.
+	currentEntry.Name = s3a.getVersionFileName(versionId)
+
+	if err := s3a.WithFilerClient(false, func(client filer_pb.SeaweedFilerClient) error {
+		return filer_pb.UpdateEntry(context.Background(), client, &filer_pb.UpdateEntryRequest{
+			Directory: versionsDir,
+			Entry:     currentEntry,
+		})
+	}); err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("stamp hard link on version %s: %w", versionId, err)
+	}
+
+	newEntry.HardLinkId = currentEntry.HardLinkId
+	newEntry.HardLinkCounter = currentEntry.HardLinkCounter
+	return nil
+}
+
 func copyEntryToTarget(dst, src *filer_pb.Entry) {
 	dst.IsDirectory = src.IsDirectory
 	dst.Attributes = src.Attributes
```

</details>

items.title: filer: serialize same-path mutations with a per-path lock
items.body:
First of a small stack that builds the filer-side primitives for serializing object mutations on the owner filer, so S3 (and other) writes can drop the distributed lock.

`CreateEntry` is a `FindEntry`-then-write with no lock, so concurrent creates to the same path race: `OExcl` can admit two creators, and a conditional check-then-act has no atomicity. This adds a per-path exclusive lock (`util.LockTable`, which evicts idle keys so it stays bounded) on the `FilerServer` and takes it in `CreateEntry`, making the existence check and the write atomic on this filer.

This is the local serialization point that lets a caller route a key's writes to its owner filer and drop the distributed lock for that key. Strictly additive — `CreateEntry` had no lock before.

`AppendToEntry` keeps its distributed lock for now; it can move to the per-path lock once its callers route to the owner.

items.title: filer: serialize same-path mutations with a local lock
items.body:
First of a three-part series that takes the S3 object-write path off the distributed lock and onto route-by-key + filer-local serialization.

## Problem

`Filer.CreateEntry` is an unlocked `FindEntry`-then-`InsertEntry`/`UpdateEntry`. Two concurrent creates to the same path race: `OExcl` (create-if-absent) can admit two creators, and there is no atomic check-then-act for conditional writes. This is exactly why the S3 path and `AppendToEntry` reach for the distributed lock — the filer can't serialize a key on its own.

## Change

Add a per-path exclusive lock to the `CreateEntry` gRPC handler using the existing `util.LockTable[util.FullPath]`, which already evicts idle keys so the table stays bounded. The read and the write now run inside one exclusive critical section on the filer.

This local lock is the authoritative serialization point only once a key's writes are routed to its owner filer (the follow-up gateway PR does that, using the lock-ring view from #9626). On its own, this PR already removes the single-filer check-then-act race.

`AppendToEntry` — itself a read-modify-write that previously borrowed the distributed lock — switches to the same per-path lock. There are no in-tree callers constructing `AppendToEntryRequest`; the operation now serializes within the owner filer, consistent with the route-by-key model.

## Test

`TestCreateEntryOExclSerialized` fires concurrent `OExcl` creates for one path through the real handler (with a widened check-then-act window) and asserts exactly one winner.

## Series

1. **this PR** — filer serializes same-path mutations locally
2. add a `Condition` field to `CreateEntryRequest` so the filer evaluates `If-Match`/`If-None-Match`/time conditions under the lock
3. S3 gateway routes non-versioned object writes to the owner filer and uses these instead of the distributed lock

items.title: refactor(filer): remove the inode->path index and the NFS gateway
items.body:
## Problem

The filer kept an inode->path secondary index, writing a `filer.inode.path.<inode>` KV row on every `InsertEntry`/`UpdateEntry`. In an S3-only deployment the SQL KV layer keys every such row under one directory hash (`base64("filer.in")` = `ZmlsZXIuaW4=`) and always lands in the default store, so `filemeta` grew by one row per object — observed at ~1.1B rows / 30 GB.

That index existed solely so the experimental NFS gateway (`weed nfs`) could reverse-resolve a filehandle back to a path. Nothing else reads it: a fixed-size NFS filehandle can't carry an arbitrary-length key, so NFS needs a persisted reverse map, but S3/FUSE/HTTP never do.

## Change

- **Derive inodes by hash.** `ensureEntryInode` now computes the value the FUSE mount would otherwise derive — the mount already treats a non-zero `entry.Inode` as the source of truth. A non-hard-linked entry hashes path + crtime (`FullPath.AsInode`); a hard link hashes its shared `HardLinkId` so every link resolves to one inode (the value is already shared through the hard-link blob). The snowflake `inodeSequencer` and `SEAWEEDFS_FILER_SNOWFLAKE_ID` are removed; inodes are now deterministic across filers.
- **Remove the NFS gateway.** Deletes the `weed/server/nfs` package, the `weed nfs` command and its registration, the integration test harness, and the CI workflow; `go mod tidy` drops `willscott/go-nfs` and `willscott/go-nfs-client`.
- **Drop the inode->path index.** With NFS gone nothing reads it, and inodes are derivable on demand, so the secondary KV index and its write/remove hooks are removed. No filer store writes a per-object index row.

Existing entries keep their inode (only `Inode == 0` is assigned), so there is no churn on upgrade. The FUSE mount (`st_ino`) and server-side copy preconditions still consume `entry.Inode` unchanged.

Operators with an already-bloated table can reclaim the rows after deploying:

```sql
DELETE FROM filemeta WHERE directory = 'ZmlsZXIuaW4=' LIMIT 50000;  -- repeat until 0 rows
```

## Tests

- Inode derivation matches the FUSE formula and is deterministic; two links with the same `HardLinkId` share one inode.

Fixes #9718

items.title: s3api: replay a delete the filer's transport dropped, and classify by status code
items.body:
References #7204 and #7224.

Both issues bottom out in the same place: `doDeleteEntry` in `weed/s3api/filer_util.go` issues `DeleteEntry` once and turns any failure into an error the client sees. For #7204 that becomes a 500, boto3 resends the DELETE, and the second one finds the bucket already gone and answers `NoSuchBucket`. For #7224 it becomes a per-key `InternalError` inside a 200 response, which no SDK retries, so the object silently survives.

`doDeleteEntry` is the only `DeleteEntry` call in `weed/s3api` proper, so a replay there covers every delete path in both handlers without touching any of the 23 `rm`/`rmObject` call sites.

## What this actually recovers, and what it does not

It recovers a transport blip: a filer restart, a GOAWAY, a single reset stream, anything where the channel is reconnecting underneath the call and a fresh attempt lands on a working transport.

It does not help when a filer is genuinely down. Once the channel is in TRANSIENT_FAILURE every attempt returns `Unavailable` immediately and the handler still emits the 500 or the in-200 `InternalError`. **If you test this with `docker stop filer` you will see no change at all.** In a multi-object delete the loop holds one filer client for the whole batch and `receiveTrackingConn` blocks failover once any reply has arrived, so a filer dying mid-batch means the remaining keys each replay and none of them recover.

That is why this says "references" and not "fixes". The complete answers are different changes: not mapping a transient filer failure to 500, and using a retryable per-key code. Both are behaviour changes I did not want to bundle here.

## The replay is immediate, and bounded anyway

No backoff. What clears a transient failure here is the channel reconnecting, not the passage of time, and a sleep would be paid once per key in handlers that delete up to 1000 entries per request.

Immediate is still not free, though. When a pick finds no ready subconn the picker waits for the balancer to publish one, and `WaitForReady(false)` does not shorten that wait; only the context does. So replaying multiplies that stall by the attempt count. There is a single bounded context shared by the replays to cap it.

The first attempt deliberately keeps the caller's own context. A recursive delete of a large bucket is legitimately slow, and putting a deadline on it here would fail deletes that succeed today. Only the attempts this change adds are bounded, so it cannot make anything slower than it already is.

## Classification is by status code only

The previous shape of this classified by message text through `util.IsTransientError`, which substring-matches. That is spoofable here, because the filer formats the object path into the error before the gateway sees it: `weed/filer/filer_delete_entry.go` wraps with `delete file %s: %v` and `weed/server/filer_grpc_server.go` copies that verbatim into `resp.Error`. A `PermissionDenied` on a key named `logs/transport.log` would have been replayed, and an object named after the not-found sentinel would have suppressed a legitimate replay. Stripping a prefix does not fix it either, since a recursive delete names the child entry it stopped on, which is another client-chosen key.

So this classifies by gRPC status code and never reads message text. `FilerServer.DeleteEntry` has exactly one return statement, `return resp, nil`, and reports failure through `resp.Error`, so everything the classifier sees came from the gRPC stack and carries no client-controlled text by construction.

The consequence is a deliberate narrowing worth seeing plainly: a `resp.Error` whose text happens to read transient is no longer replayed at all. Against current master nothing that works today stops working, since master never replayed anything.

The retryable set is `Unavailable`, `Internal` and `ResourceExhausted`, matching what `pb.shouldInvalidateConnection` treats as a broken channel, less `Aborted`. `Aborted` reports a conflict the filer decided on rather than a channel that broke. `ResourceExhausted` is unreachable today and is there for symmetry; if a filer-side load shed is ever added, an immediate replay would be the wrong answer to backpressure.

## Same class of bug, still open nearby

Two places still match against a message with the object path formatted in, both identical on current master so neither is a regression, but a reader should not take the claim above as broader than it is: `deleteObjectEntry`'s `MsgFailDelNonEmptyFolder` check, and `pb.shouldInvalidateConnection`'s substring fallback. `isRetryableListError` has the same shape and came in with #10886 and #10890, which is my own earlier contribution. I filed the general problem as #10994.

## Testing

Verified by reverting each property separately: removing the replay fails 5 tests, restoring free-text classification fails the classifier tests, removing the context check fails 1, and removing the replay bound fails 1. Several of the other tests pin invariants rather than demonstrating a change, and pass under both the old and new shape; they are there to stop a future edit from reintroducing the spoof.

Not verified: no cluster here, so this rests on unit tests and code reading rather than on reproducing the reporters' setups.

  * Stops retrying when the request is cancelled or the retry time limit is reached.
  * Preserves immediate handling for permanent failures and filer-reported errors.
  * Ensures delete operations use consistent request context and error handling.

items.title: fix(mount): keep periodic metadata flush from dropping concurrent chunk uploads
items.body:
## Problem

Large sequential writes through a FUSE mount can silently corrupt the file. A `cat` of two 15 GiB files into a third produces a file whose md5 differs from the streamed input, reproducibly. The file is full size and reads back stably, but contains zero-filled holes at 2 MiB chunk boundaries.

The corrupted regions correspond to gaps in the file's chunk list. The chunk data is still present on the volume servers; the file just lost the references to it.

## Cause

`flushFileMetadata` (the periodic metadata flush, every 2 min) does a read-modify-write on `entry.Chunks` that is not safe against the async uploader goroutines:

1. read `entry.Chunks`
2. run `CompactFileChunks` + `MaybeManifestize` — seconds-long, the manifest upload is a network round trip
3. `entry.Chunks = append(compactedChunks, manifestChunks...)`

While step 2 runs, uploader goroutines append freshly uploaded chunks via `entry.AppendChunks` (which locks). Step 3 overwrites the slice without re-reading, discarding every chunk appended during the window. A multi-minute write hits several flush cycles, each dropping a batch of references.

The close-path flush (`flushMetadataToFiler`) is unaffected: it runs after `FlushData()` has drained all uploads and holds the same exclusive file-handle lock as the periodic flush.

## Fix

Snapshot the chunk list under the entry lock and record its length, do the slow compaction/manifestization on the snapshot, then re-acquire the lock and splice the processed prefix in front of any chunks that arrived after the snapshot. The filer request is cloned inside the same critical section so it can't observe a half-merged state.

## Verification

Repro (2x15 GiB cat) corrupts on master, passes with `-metadataFlushSeconds=0`, and passes with the fix and the periodic flush enabled. `go test ./weed/mount/...` passes.

items.title: fix(mount): make a concurrent duplicate mkdir fail with EEXIST instead of both succeeding
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

The mount's `Mkdir` sends `CreateEntryRequest` without `OExcl`, 
so the filer treats a concurrent duplicate as an update and both callers get rc=0 — `mkdir(2)` must fail with `EEXIST`. 

Setting `OExcl` alone is not enough with multiple filers: the per-path lock (#9639) is filer-local and the store insert is an upsert, so two mounts streaming to different filers both pass the existence check. 

Measured 18/30 both-success on a 3-filer cluster under a barrier-synchronized cross-node race; 
the losers also saw `EIO` because the stream client collapses a failed create's structured error code into a generic errno.

# How are we solving the problem?

Set `OExcl` on the mkdir create and map `ErrEntryAlreadyExists` to `EEXIST`. 
Route exclusive creates to a deterministic owner filer — fnv32a of the path over the sorted filer list — the routing contract the per-path lock's comment already assumes; the mutation stream is kept when it already targets the owner, and used as fallback when the owner is unreachable. 

Let `doUnary` hand failed creates to `CreateEntry` so the structured error code survives. 

# How is the PR tested?

`go test ./weed/mount/...` passes. On a live 3-filer cluster, 30 barrier-synchronized cross-node mkdir races of the same fresh path: before, 18/30 ended with both succeeding and the losers got `EIO`; after, 30/30 had exactly one winner and every loser got `EEXIST`. Deployed mount-only against an unmodified 4.40 server — the server prerequisites (#9639 lock, #8767 error codes) are long present.

items.title: mount: keep metadata operations working on a removed open directory
items.body:
Fixes #11065.

Same shape as #10989, but for directories. An unlinked open file lives on through its file handle, so maybeReadEntry can answer from there. A removed directory has nothing like that: OpenDir hands out only a listing cursor, so once rmdir drops the name, fchmod/fstat/futimens/f*xattr on the still-open descriptor hit ENOENT.

Now rmdir keeps the directory's last-known entry in memory, keyed by inode, whenever the kernel still holds lookup references, and maybeReadEntry falls back to it the same way it falls back to a file's open handle. Metadata mutations publish a changed copy back rather than editing in place, so a concurrent reader never sees a half-applied change. The kernel's final forget drops the entry along with the other per-inode overlays.

Reproduced with the issue's program (plus fstat/futimens/xattr checks) against `weed mini` + `weed mount`, with tmpfs as the control. Before, on the mount:

```
FCHMOD: -1 (No such file or directory)
FSTAT: -1 (No such file or directory)
FUTIMENS: -1 (No such file or directory)
FSETXATTR: -1 (No such file or directory)
```

After, identical to tmpfs:

```
FCHMOD: 0 (Success)
FSTAT: 0 (Success) mode=40770 nlink=0
FUTIMENS: 0 (Success)
FSETXATTR: 0 (Success)
FGETXATTR: 1 (Success)
FREMOVEXATTR: 0 (Success)
```

readdir on the removed descriptor already returns an empty stream, so it is left alone.

items.title: fix(mount): sanitize non-UTF-8 filenames; keep marshal errors per-request
items.body:
## Summary

- Sanitize kernel-provided filenames at every FUSE entry point (Create, Mknod, Mkdir, Unlink, Rmdir, Rename, Lookup, Link, Symlink) via a new `sanitizeFuseName` helper (`strings.ToValidUTF8` with `?` replacement — matches the existing `util.FullPath.DirAndName` convention). Also scrub `AssignVolumeRequest.Path` as a backstop in the upload path for async-flush handles that may have captured a pre-sanitization path.
- Teach `pb.shouldInvalidateConnection` to recognize a **client-side proto marshal failure** and keep the shared cached `grpc.ClientConn` alive: the TCP/HTTP2 connection is healthy, only the one request is unmarshalable.

## Why

Reported on [#9139 (comment 4301184231)](https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/9139#issuecomment-4301184231): a single GNOME Trash "partial" file whose name contained raw binary bytes (`\x10\x98=\\\x8a\x7f...`) would cause every FUSE-initiated filer RPC to fail with

```
rpc error: code = Internal desc = grpc: error while marshaling:
string field contains invalid UTF-8
```

and then trigger an avalanche of `code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing` errors on unrelated `LookupEntry` / `ReadDirAll` / `UpdateEntry` calls — visible as volume-server QPS dips.

Two bugs in series:

1. Proto3 `string` fields require valid UTF-8, but the FUSE kernel passes raw name bytes. The mount forwarded them directly into `Entry.Name`, `DeleteEntryRequest.Name`, `StreamRenameEntryRequest.{Old,New}Name`, and `AssignVolumeRequest.Path`.
2. `shouldInvalidateConnection` treated the resulting `codes.Internal` as a connection problem and dropped the **shared** cached `ClientConn`, canceling every concurrent RPC on it. This is what made one ill-named file destabilize the whole mount.

## Test plan

- [x] `go build ./...`
- [x] `go test ./weed/mount/ ./weed/pb/` (all green, including existing tests)
- [x] New unit tests:
  - `weed/mount/wfs_save_test.go` — reproduces the exact byte sequence from #9139, asserts `sanitizeFuseName` produces valid UTF-8, asserts valid inputs are passed through unchanged, asserts `checkName`'s length guard still fires after sanitization.
  - `weed/pb/grpc_client_server_test.go` — asserts a synthetic `codes.Internal` with the gRPC marshal-error message does **not** invalidate the cached connection, while genuine server-side `Internal` and transport errors still do.
- [ ] Manual: mount a filer, `touch $'foo\x80bar'` — create should succeed and no "connection is closing" cascade on concurrent readers.

Refs: #9139

  * Upload/assign paths are UTF-8–sanitized to prevent marshal/transport failures.
  * Certain gRPC client-side marshal errors no longer trigger unnecessary connection resets.

items.title: feat(filer): add atime to FuseAttributes + TouchAccessTime RPC
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

SeaweedFS filer entries currently have no access-time tracking. FUSE clients see `atime` aliased to `mtime` from a bounded, in-memory overlay (`weed/mount/weedfs_attr.go` `atimeMap`), and other surfaces (S3, WebDAV, the filer HTTP API, `weed shell fs.meta.cat`) have no notion of last-read time at all. Downstream tooling — read-LRU cache eviction for remote-mounted buckets, hot-data detection, audit — has no signal it can rely on.

Concrete use case: capacity-driven LRU eviction of cached objects for remote-mounted buckets. Today only last-cached time (`RemoteEntry.LastLocalSyncTsNs`) is available; we need last-read time.

# How are we solving the problem?

This PR is the foundational, behaviour-preserving step. It adds the on-the-wire shape required by follow-ups, with zero behavioural change:

- `FuseAttributes` gains `int64 atime = 22;` and `int32 atime_ns = 23;` in `weed/pb/filer.proto` (and the Java client proto kept in lock step).
- A new `SeaweedFiler.TouchAccessTime` RPC and its `TouchAccessTimeRequest`/`TouchAccessTimeResponse` messages are declared, ready for the policy/handler PR that follows.
- The in-memory `filer.Attr` struct grows an `Atime time.Time` field and the codec helpers (`EntryAttributeToPb`, `EntryAttributeToExistingPb`, `PbToEntryAttribute`) round-trip it. Zero atime decodes as Mtime so legacy entries report a sane value and on-disk records remain wire-compatible.
- `Filer.CreateEntry` and `Filer.UpdateEntry` stamp `Atime = Mtime` (or `Crtime` if Mtime is zero) when callers do not set it explicitly — POSIX semantics where a freshly written file has `atime == mtime`.

No storage migration is required: every filer backend (`abstract_sql`, `mysql{,2}`, `postgres{,2}`, `cassandra{,2}`, `ydb`, `mongodb`, `redis{,2,3}`, `leveldb{,2,3}`, `rocksdb`, `etcd`, `tikv`, `tarantool`, `hbase`, `arangodb`, `foundationdb`, `elastic`) stores attributes inside an opaque `meta` protobuf blob, so the additive proto fields are picked up automatically.

Follow-ups (planned as separate, minimal PRs):

1. `TouchAccessTime` server handler with a configurable relatime/strict/off policy and `-atime`, `-atime.relatime_threshold` flags.
2. Read-path hooks: a coalescing toucher invoked from S3 `GetObject` (incl. SSE), FUSE `Read`, WebDAV `Read` and the filer HTTP GET path. HEAD/List/304/internal scanners are explicitly excluded.
3. Mount refactor: replace the in-memory `atimeMap` with the filer-backed `Atime`.

# How is the PR tested?

- New unit tests in `weed/filer/entry_codec_atime_test.go`:
  - `TestEntryCodec_AtimeRoundTrip` round-trips a non-zero atime through `EntryAttributeToPb` → `PbToEntryAttribute`.
  - `TestEntryCodec_AtimeZeroFallsBackToMtime` asserts the zero-atime → mtime fallback for legacy entries.
- Existing tests under `weed/filer/` continue to pass (`go test ./weed/filer/...`).
- Project-wide build is green (`go build ./weed/...`).
