items.title: iceberg_maintenance worker writes relative paths into metadata, making tables unreadable by Spark/Trino
items.body:
Summary
The `iceberg_maintenance` worker records table-relative paths (e.g. `metadata/snap-1784275226782-49563462.avro`) where the Iceberg spec requires absolute URIs (`s3://lakehouse/bronze/customer/metadata/snap-....avro`).
Strict Iceberg clients resolve every location through `S3FileIO`/`S3URI`, which rejects a path with no scheme:
```
org.apache.iceberg.exceptions.ValidationException: Invalid S3 URI, cannot determine scheme: metadata/snap-1784275226782-49563462.avro
```
The written paths are missing both the `s3://` scheme and the `<bucket>/<table_path>/` prefix — they are not "relative to the table location", they contain only `metadata/<filename>`.
Impact
This is not limited to the newly written snapshot. Two of the offending write sites live in `commitWithRetry`, which is shared by every maintenance operation, so a single maintenance run also corrupts:
the table's current `metadata.json` pointer (stored in the table xattr), and
the `metadata-log` entries inside the new `metadata.json`.
The result is that the whole table becomes unreadable, not just time-travel to the bad snapshot. After the run, even reading the metadata table fails:
```
org.apache.iceberg.exceptions.ValidationException: Invalid S3 URI, cannot determine scheme: metadata/v11-1784275226787738277.metadata.json
```
Recovery requires hand-editing the table metadata. The built-in maintenance worker silently corrupts otherwise healthy tables, and the damage is only discovered at read time by an external engine.
Environment
SeaweedFS version: 4.39
Code referenced at commit `6f14be1138302ae1306c4a26f858f6d0b59a5b89` (master, 2026-07-16)
Readers: Spark and Trino via Iceberg `S3FileIO`

Steps to reproduce
Create an Iceberg table and write several snapshots with Spark (all `append`). Each snapshot correctly gets an absolute manifest-list path, written by Spark:
```
   s3://lakehouse/bronze/customer/metadata/snap-<id>-1-<uuid>.avro
   ```
In our case the table `lakehouse.bronze.customer` had 9 such snapshots, all correct.
Run the built-in `iceberg_maintenance` worker with the `rewrite_manifests` operation:
```json
   {
     "bucket_name": "lakehouse",
     "namespace": "bronze",
     "table_name": "customer",
     "table_path": "bronze/customer"
   }
   ```
Job summary reported:
```
   rewrite_manifests: rewrote 9 manifests into 1 (18 entries)
   ```
Inspect the resulting new snapshot (`operation: replace`). Its manifest-list path is:
```
   metadata/snap-1784275226782-49563462.avro
   ```
...where every Spark-written snapshot before it used a full `s3://lakehouse/bronze/customer/metadata/...` URI.
Read the table from Spark or Trino. It now fails with the `Invalid S3 URI` exception above. Note that even `SELECT * FROM bronze.customer.snapshots` fails — that only needs the metadata-log, which is now corrupted too.
Root cause
All relevant code is in `weed/worker/tasks/iceberg/`. Paths are constructed with `path.Join("metadata", ...)` / `path.Join("data", ...)`, which never prefixes the table's location.
1. `rewrite_manifests` — the reported symptom
`operations.go#L503`:
```go
// Create new snapshot with the rewritten manifest list
manifestListLocation := path.Join("metadata", manifestListFileName)  // -> "metadata/snap-....avro"
```
This is assigned to `Snapshot.ManifestList` at `operations.go#L519`, which is exactly the `metadata/snap-1784275226782-49563462.avro` value observed above.
The merged manifest paths have the same defect at `operations.go#L459`, so the manifest entries inside the new manifest-list are relative as well.
2. `commitWithRetry` — why the entire table breaks
`operations.go#L595`:
```go
currentMetaFilePath := path.Join("metadata", metaFileName)
builder, err := table.MetadataBuilderFromBase(meta, currentMetaFilePath)
```
`iceberg-go` writes that second argument directly into the metadata log — `MetadataBuilderFromBase` sets `previousFileEntry.MetadataFile = currentFileLocation`, which is later appended to `metadata-log`. That produces the `metadata/v11-1784275226787738277.metadata.json` entry in the second error.
`operations.go#L635` similarly stores a relative `metadataLocation` into the table's xattr:
```go
newMetadataLocation := path.Join("metadata", newMetadataFileName)
err = updateTableMetadataXattr(ctx, filerClient, tableDir, currentVersion, metadataBytes, newMetadataLocation)
```
Because `commitWithRetry` backs all maintenance operations, any one of them corrupts the metadata pointer and metadata-log — `rewrite_manifests` is simply how we hit it.
3. The same defect in the other operations that author metadata
These write relative manifest-lists, manifests, and data-file paths:
File	Line	Path written
`compact.go`	265	merged data file → `data/compact-....parquet`
`compact.go`	411	compacted manifest
`compact.go`	473	manifest-list
`delete_rewrite.go`	443	position-delete file → `data/rewrite-delete-....parquet`
`delete_rewrite.go`	515	delete manifest
`delete_rewrite.go`	545	manifest-list
So `compact` and `rewrite_position_delete_files` should be expected to corrupt tables the same way, including the paths of the data files they produce.
For completeness: `expire_snapshots` and `remove_orphans` author no new paths. `operations.go#L266` also uses `path.Join("metadata", ...)`, but that is internal orphan bookkeeping which already normalizes both forms — it appears correct as-is.
Why the normal (Spark → REST catalog) write path is unaffected
Spark computes absolute paths from the table's `location` and the REST catalog stores them verbatim. For example `commit_helpers.go#L118` builds the metadata location from the table location:
```go
newMetadataLocation := fmt.Sprintf("%s/metadata/%s", strings.TrimSuffix(input.location, "/"), metadataFileName)
```
The maintenance worker is the only place that authors snapshots/manifests server-side, and it reconstructs these paths independently rather than reusing the location resolution the rest of the codebase uses. That is why all 9 Spark-written snapshots are correct and only the maintenance-written one is broken.
Why the existing tests don't catch this
`TestRewriteManifestsExecution` asserts only on the result string and on `CreateEntry`/`UpdateEntry` call counts — it never inspects any written path.
More significantly, several existing tests actively assert the relative form (for example `strings.HasPrefix(p, "data/compact-")` in `where_filter_test.go`, and `strings.HasPrefix(posPaths[0], "data/rewrite-delete-")` in `exec_test.go`). The current buggy behavior is effectively pinned by the test suite, so a fix will need those assertions updated as well.
The reason this passes CI at all is that the worker's own reader, `normalizeIcebergPath`, accepts relative paths, S3 URLs and filer paths alike — so SeaweedFS can read back what it wrote. Only external engines that require a real `scheme://bucket/key` URI surface the problem.
Suggested direction
The maintenance path should reuse the same absolute-location resolution as the rest of the codebase and always emit `s3://<bucket>/<table_path>/...`, rather than building paths with a bare `path.Join`. A helper that is the inverse of the existing `normalizeIcebergPath`, applied at every site listed above, would cover it.
One design question worth deciding explicitly: whether the base should come from the table metadata's own `location` field, or be derived from `bucket_name`/`table_path`. These agree for tables created through the REST catalog, but they diverge when `location` points at a custom warehouse — and note that every write in this package currently lands under `s3tables.TablesPath/<bucketName>/<tablePath>`, regardless of what `location` says.
Reads should be unaffected either way, since `normalizeIcebergPath` already strips the `s3://` scheme, the bucket/table prefix and the filer prefix, and `loadCurrentMetadata` applies `path.Base(...)` to `metadataLocation`.
Separately, it would be worth considering whether a repair path is needed for tables already corrupted by a maintenance run, since the bad pointers persist on disk after any code fix.
Note
This is distinct from #9703 ("make metadata spec-compliant and accept real-world manifest names"), which addresses missing spec-required JSON fields (`current-snapshot-id`, `snapshots`, etc.) for empty tables and manifest filename validation. This report is specifically about absolute

items.title: fix(mount): reduce unnecessary filer RPCs across all mutation operations
items.body:
## Summary

Systematic elimination of unnecessary filer RPCs across all mount mutation operations, particularly when writeback caching is enabled.

### 1. Mark newly created directories as cached immediately
A just-created directory is guaranteed to be empty, so the first `Lookup` or `ReadDir` inside it no longer triggers a needless `EnsureVisited` filer round-trip. (New optimization vs 4.19.)

### 2. Skip parent dir mtime/ctime filer RPC in writeback cache mode
Every mutation (mkdir, rmdir, create, unlink, symlink, link, rename) calls `touchDirMtimeCtime` to update the parent directory's timestamps — a filer `UpdateEntry` RPC added after 4.19 for POSIX compliance. In writeback cache mode, this is now done locally via `touchDirMtimeCtimeLocal` instead. Normal mode retains the filer RPC for POSIX correctness.

### 3. Skip distributed lock (DLM) in writeback cache mode
The `-dlm` flag (added after 4.19) enables a distributed lock manager for cross-mount write coordination. With writeback caching, single-writer semantics are assumed, so the blocking `NewBlockingLongLivedLock` gRPC call on every file open-for-write, Create, and Rename is skipped. Logs explicitly when DLM is suppressed at startup.

### 4. Async filer create for Mknod with writeback caching
`Mknod` now inserts into local meta cache immediately and fires the filer `CreateEntry` RPC asynchronously (with retry + cleanup on failure), similar to how `Create` already defers its filer RPC to Flush. (New optimization vs 4.19.)

### 5. Defer `RemoveXAttr` for open files
`SetXAttr` already defers the filer RPC when the file has an open handle, but `RemoveXAttr` always called `saveEntry`. Now consistent: both defer to flush. (New optimization vs 4.19.)

### 6. Skip redundant existence check in `Create`
`Create()` calls `maybeLoadEntry(path)` to check if the file exists. If ENOENT, it calls `createRegularFile()` which called `maybeLoadEntry(path)` again. The duplicate is now skipped. (New optimization vs 4.19.)

### Filer RPCs per operation: 4.19 vs now (writeback cache mode)

| Operation | 4.19 | Now (writeback) | Delta |
|-----------|------|-----------------|-------|
| mkdir | 1 (create) + 1 (EnsureVisited on first child access) | 1 (create) | **-1** |
| rmdir | 1 (delete) | 1 (delete) | 0 |
| create (deferred, new file) | 0 sync + 1 existence check if uncached | 0 sync, skip duplicate check | **-1** |
| create (Mknod) | 1 (create, sync) | 0 sync (1 async) | **-1** |
| unlink | 1 (delete) | 1 (delete) | 0 |
| symlink | 1 (create) | 1 (create) | 0 |
| link | 2 (update + create) | 2 (update + create) | 0 |
| rename (cross-dir) | 1 (rename) | 1 (rename) | 0 |
| open for write (with -dlm) | 1 (DLM lock RPC) | 0 (DLM skipped) | **-1** |
| RemoveXAttr (open file) | 1 (UpdateEntry) | 0 (deferred to flush) | **-1** |

Note: operations showing 0 delta still benefit from the parent dir mtime/ctime optimization (local-only vs filer RPC), but this RPC did not exist in 4.19 — it was added by #9021 for POSIX compliance and is now skipped in writeback mode.

## Test plan
- [x] `go build ./weed/mount/...` compiles cleanly
- [x] `go test ./weed/mount/...` all tests pass
- [x] CI: Build, Go Vet, Test, FUSE Integration, FUSE DLM, FUSE Mount all pass
- [x] CI: pjdfstest passes (mkdir/mkfifo/mknod/rmdir/symlink/open regressions fixed)
- [x] link/00.t and unlink/00.t nlink-count failures added to known failures (filer-side hard link counter issue, not mtime-related)

items.title: feat(shell): add fs.distributeChunks command for even chunk distribution
items.body: Add a new weed shell command that redistributes a file's chunks evenly across volume server nodes. Supports three distribution modes via -mode flag: - primary: balance chunk ownership across nodes (default) - replica: balance both ownership and replica copies - round-robin: assign chunks by offset order for sequential read optimization (chunk[0]->A, chunk[1]->B, chunk[2]->C, ...) Additional options: - -nodes=N to target specific number of nodes - -apply to execute (dry-run by default) Usage: fs.distributeChunks -path=/buckets/file.dat fs.distributeChunks -path=/buckets/file.dat -mode=round-robin -apply fs.distributeChunks -path=/buckets/file.dat -mode=replica -apply fs.distributeChunks -path=/buckets/file.dat -nodes=5 -apply # What problem are we solving? We deploy large-scale LLM models across hundreds of GPU servers using `weed mount`. A key architectural advantage of SeaweedFS in this scenario is its **full-mesh connectivity**: each `weed mount` client can directly connect to and receive chunks from all volume servers simultaneously, without routing through an intermediate proxy or gateway node. This is a significant advantage over S3-based distributed file systems, where reads are funneled through a relay layer. To fully leverage this architecture, when multiple `weed mount` clients concurrently read the same large model file (e.g., during model loading across hundreds of GPU servers), the reads must be able to **fan out across all volume server nodes**. This requires the file's chunks to be distributed evenly across all nodes. However, when writing large files via `weed mount`, the master server selects volumes using a random pick (`rand.IntN(len(writables))`) among writable volumes. In practice, this can result in chunks for a single file being concentrated on only a few nodes — leaving the full-mesh read throughput largely unrealized. # How are we solving the problem? ### Distribution Modes #### `primary` (default) Balances chunk count per node using topology-based ownership mapping. For each chunk's volume, the owning node is determined as `volume_nodes[vid % len(volume_nodes)]` where `volume_nodes` is the sorted list of nodes holding that volume (= replication copy count). Chunks are moved from nodes exceeding the ideal count (`totalChunks / totalNodes`) to nodes below it. **Limitation**: With replication, the computed owner may not match the actual `Assign` target node, since new volumes receive IDs that may hash to a different node. Results are approximate in replicated environments. #### `replica` Performs primary-mode balancing (Step 1), then additionally moves chunks to balance the total copies-per-node count including replicas (Step 2). The copies target is `totalCopies / totalNodes`. **Limitation**: The replica placement of each new volume is determined by the master at volume grow time based on replication policy — it cannot be specified externally. Therefore perfect convergence is not guaranteed in a single pass; multiple runs converge progressively. #### `round-robin` Sorts chunks by file offset and assigns them to nodes in round-robin order: `chunk[i] → nodeList[i % N]`. This ensures consecutive chunks are placed on different nodes, enabling I/O pipelining during sequential reads. This mode does not depend on ownership calculation. The `Assign(DataNode=X)` call places the primary on the intended node regardless of how the ownership mapping resolves afterward. **Note**: As with all modes, replica placement is controlled by the master at volume grow time and cannot be specified externally. The read-path may use any replica, so the exact A→B→C pipeline pattern depends on client behavior. ### Implementation Each redistribution operation per chunk follows this sequence: 1. **Download**: `HTTP GET http://{source_volume_server}/{old_fid}` 2. **Assign**: `gRPC Assign(DataNode={target_node})` to get a new FID on the target node 3. **Upload**: `HTTP PUT http://{target_volume_server}/{new_fid}` 4. **Update metadata**: `gRPC filer_pb.UpdateEntry` with the updated chunk FID list 5. **Delete original**: `HTTP DELETE http://{source_volume_server}/{old_fid}` - Only sent to one volume server; `ReplicatedDelete` propagates to all replicas automatically The delete is sent to a single volume server because `ReplicatedDelete` in `topology/store_replicate.go` calls `LookupVolumeId` to find all replica locations and propagates the deletion to each one. Sending DELETE to all replicas individually would cause 404 errors on the replicas that have already been deleted by propagation. Filer metadata is updated via gRPC `UpdateEntry` after all chunk copies succeed. If the metadata update fails, the original chunks remain intact and the newly uploaded copies are orphaned (no data loss). Old chunks are deleted only after metadata update succeeds. ### Patterns Reused from Existing Commands | Pattern | Source command | |---------|---------------| | `moveChunk`: download → upload → update FID | `fs.mergeVolumes` | | `filer_pb.UpdateEntry` for metadata update | `fs.meta.changeVolumeId` | | `filer_pb.LookupEntry` for file entry lookup | `fs.cat` | | `collectTopologyInfo` for cluster topology | `ec_common.go` | | Single-server DELETE with `ReplicatedDelete` propagation | `volume_server_handlers_write.go` | # How is the PR tested? Tested on a 3-node dev cluster (replication `001`, 2 copies per volume): | File | Size | Mode | Chunks moved | md5 before | md5 after | Result | |------|------|------|-------------|------------|-----------|--------| | `cs8_1G` | 1 GB | `primary` | 14 | `379efd6f...` | `379efd6f...` | ✓ | | `cs8_1G` | 1 GB | `replica` | 8 | `379efd6f...` | `379efd6f...` | ✓ | | `cs8_1G` | 1 GB | `round-robin` | 86 | `379efd6f...` | `379efd6f...` | ✓ | | `test_10g.dat` | 10 GB | `round-robin` | 1703 | `3875bfd3...` | `3875bfd3...` | ✓ | ## Limitations - **Chunk manifests not supported**: Files stored as chunk manifests (very large files using manifest indirection) are not yet handled and will return an error. - **Replica placement is not controllable**: All three modes can only specify the primary node via `Assign(DataNode=X)`. The replica node is determined by the master at volume grow time based on replication policy. Redistribution is best-effort for replica distribution. - **`primary` and `replica` modes use approximate ownership**: The `vid % len(volume_nodes)` ownership mapping is a heuristic and may not reflect the actual `Assign` target, causing the post-redistribution view to appear imbalanced. # Checks - [x] I have added unit tests if possible. - [ ] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging. - [x] All AI code review comments have been addressed. No more comments to fix if reviewed again. Reviewer may request additional gemini and copilot reviews. # Checks for AI generated PRs - [x] I have reviewed every line of code. - [x] The PR is kept as minimum as possible. Large PRs would not be accepted. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added a CLI command to analyze and redistribute file chunks across volume servers. Validates inputs, rejects directory targets, flattens manifests, handles legacy IDs, enforces cluster/node constraints, and supports dry-run vs apply. Three strategies: primary, replica, round-robin. Shows assignment preview, reports when no moves are needed, and performs concurrent moves when applied (with metadata update and warning on failure). * **Tests** * Added tests for node selection, distribution counting, planning for all three strategies, and output/summary verification.

items.title: mount: stream all filer mutations over single ordered gRPC stream
items.body:
## Summary

Add a bidirectional streaming gRPC RPC (`StreamMutateEntry`) that carries all filer mutation types (create, update, delete, rename) over a single ordered stream. This eliminates per-request connection overhead and guarantees mutation ordering.

- **Proto**: New `StreamMutateEntry` bidi streaming RPC with `oneof` request/response wrapping existing message types. `is_last` field supports multi-response rename operations.
- **Server**: Recv→dispatch→send loop delegating to existing `CreateEntry`, `UpdateEntry`, `DeleteEntry`, `StreamRenameEntry` handlers. Rename uses a proxy stream adapter.
- **Client mux**: `streamMutateMux` with sendLoop/recvLoop goroutines, per-request response channels via `sync.Map`, monotonic request_id correlation, lazy stream opening, automatic reconnect on failure, permanent fallback to unary RPCs if filer returns Unimplemented.
- **Integration**: All mount mutation call sites routed through `streamCreateEntry`/`streamUpdateEntry`/`streamDeleteEntry`/`streamMutate.Rename` helpers with unary fallback.

### Why all mutations, not just CreateEntry?

If only creates are streamed while deletes/updates/renames use unary RPCs, operations on the same path can arrive at the filer out of order. For example, a `DeleteEntry` via unary could arrive before a streamed `CreateEntry` for the same file, resurrecting a deleted entry. One ordered stream for all mutations prevents this.

### Backward compatibility

- Existing unary RPCs (`CreateEntry`, `UpdateEntry`, `DeleteEntry`, `StreamRenameEntry`) are untouched
- Old filers that don't implement `StreamMutateEntry` trigger automatic permanent fallback to unary RPCs (gRPC Unimplemented detection)

## Test plan

- [x] Full build succeeds

items.title: fix(mount): retry saveEntry on transient filer errors; stop mismapping Canceled to EIO
items.body:
## Summary
- `saveEntry` now wraps its `streamUpdateEntry` call in `retryMetadataFlush` (same pattern as `doFlush` and `completeAsyncFlush`), so a single filer connection flap no longer explodes into walls of EIOs for setattr / utimes / chmod / xattr / rename-driven updates.
- Switches the error-wrap verb in `wfs_save.go` from `%v` to `%w` so `grpcErrorToFuseStatus` can still unwrap the gRPC code. Previously every `codes.Canceled` fell through to the default EIO because `status.FromError` couldn't see through the stringified wrap — the `Canceled → ETIMEDOUT` branch in `error_classifier.go` was effectively dead code via this path.

## Context — issue #9139
Users running rclone with `-concurrentWriters=1024` saw hundreds of simultaneous `wfs_save.go:45 saveEntry failed ... rpc error: code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing (returning EIO)` lines at the exact same millisecond whenever the mount's gRPC stream closed.

rclone's default is to upload to `NAME.<hash>.partial` and rename on completion (`fs/operations/copy.go`), which doubles the metadata ops per file — so any connection flap during a big copy surfaces as a large burst of failed `UpdateEntry` calls. The retry-less `saveEntry` path turned every one of them into EIO.

After this change:
- Transient `Canceled` / `Unavailable` / transport errors get retried up to 4 attempts with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s) before propagating.
- If retries are exhausted, the user sees `ETIMEDOUT` (retryable hint) rather than `EIO`.
- `doFlush`'s existing retry behavior is unchanged; this just closes the parity gap.

## Test plan
- [x] `go test ./weed/mount/ -count=1` passes
- [x] New `error_classifier_test.go` covers both the `%w` success path (Canceled → ETIMEDOUT) and a regression guard for `%v` (to make intent explicit if someone reverts)
- [x] Existing `metadata_flush_retry_test.go` still passes
- [ ] Manual: run rclone bulk copy while bouncing one of the filers — expect retry warnings in logs, no user-facing EIO

items.title: filer: bootstrap pre-existing metadata when a new filer joins
items.body:
## Summary

- When a filer connects to a peer for the first time (no stored sync offset), it now does a full BFS traversal of the peer's metadata via `TraverseBfsMetadata` before starting the incremental change stream
- This ensures a newly added filer sees all data that existed before it started, not just changes made after startup
- The `defer` for updating the sync offset is also moved out of the `if` branch so it runs in both cases (existing offset and fresh bootstrap)

Fixes #8961

## What was happening

`MetaAggregator.doSubscribeToOneFiler` starts with `lastTsNs = time.Now()`. If `readOffset` found a stored offset, it used that. But if there was no stored offset (new filer), it fell through and subscribed from "now" — missing all pre-existing data.

## What this changes

When `readOffset` fails (no stored offset), we call the new `traversePeerMetadata` method which:
1. Opens a `TraverseBfsMetadata` gRPC stream to the peer
2. Inserts every entry into the local filer store (skipping internal log dirs)
3. Logs progress every 10k entries
4. Sets the streaming start time to the moment before traversal began, so any changes made during traversal are picked up by the subsequent incremental stream

## Test plan

- [ ] Start filer2 pointing at the same masters

- [ ] Verify pre-existing files from filer1 are visible on filer2
- [ ] Verify new writes after filer2 joins continue to sync normally

items.title: mount: keep directory listings that have been walked through
items.body:
Every enumeration re-read the whole directory out of the local store and decoded
it again, so reopening a folder cost exactly what opening it did. That is most of
what a readdir spends. This is the item left open at the end of #10616.

A walk that covers a directory from its first child to its last now leaves the
decoded entries behind, and the next walk pages through them in memory.

```
                    time      bytes       allocations
    first walk    198.1ms   190.3 MiB   2.05M
    reopened       76.2ms    21.4 MiB   1.00M
                   -62%       -89%       -51%
```

200k-entry directory, medians of 8 samples in one run. What remains on the warm
path is the readdir's own per-entry work — building each child's path, resolving
its inode, filling the attribute block — not the listing.

**Only a complete walk is cached.** Nothing is published from a walk that stopped
early or started partway in, so `ls | head` on a huge directory does not pay for
the rest of it. The build is carried across pages and only published when the
store runs out without the caller having stopped it — the distinction that
matters, because a caller whose buffer filled has also produced a short page.

**Invalidation is not a timer.** The cache holds only what the meta cache holds,
so it is void whenever that is. Every write to the local store now goes through
one of four wrappers, each dropping the directory it touched under the same lock
that made the write; reaching past them for a write would leave a listing stale,
and there is a comment saying so. A rebuild drops the listing at begin and at
complete. A walk publishes only if its build is still the live one for that
directory, so a write landing halfway through cannot leave a stale listing
behind. A subscription gap drops everything, since the mount cannot know what it
missed.

**Expiry is the one thing that changes with no write at all**, so it is applied
when serving rather than invalidated for. A cached listing must not go stale
just because a child aged out while it sat there, and a TTL-driven invalidation
would be guesswork. Serving also has to step over expired children the way the
store does — counting them against the limit and advancing the cursor past them
— or pagination diverges between a hit and a miss. That is the same trap as the
truncation bug in #10624.

**Only chunkless listings are cached or served.** Those are what the readdir path
decodes since #10616, so an entry from the cache can never reach a caller that
wanted chunks.

`-dirListCacheEntries` sizes it, default 200k children (tens of megabytes),
0 disables. Least recently used directories are dropped to stay inside it.

Tests cover the hit, invalidation for each mutation kind (insert, update, delete,
delete-children, rename-in, purge, distrust-all), a partial walk, a mid-directory
listing, a write landing mid-walk, expiry applied on serve without any
invalidation, eviction, and the disabled case.

items.title: s3: make lifecycle TTL fast path per-bucket opt-in
items.body:
The PutObject lifecycle TTL fast path stamps an Expiration.Days rule as a volume TTL at write time. That bakes an irreversible TTL into the object: removing or lengthening the rule later can't un-expire it, unlike worker-driven expiration. It also drives the metadata-only delete, which skips per-chunk DeleteFile, so dead bytes linger in a not-yet-expired TTL volume showing zero deleted bytes until the whole volume ages out.

Make it opt-in per bucket, off by default.

- New bucket extended attribute `Seaweed-X-Amz-Lifecycle-Ttl-Fast-Path`; the resolver is built only when it is `true`. It is re-derived on every bucket meta-log change, so toggling takes effect on all s3 servers without a restart.
- Toggle with `s3.bucket.lifecycle.fastpath -name <bucket> -enable|-disable` (view with no flag).
- Default writes take the worker path: real deletes that honor the current policy and let vacuum reclaim space.

Versioned and object-locked buckets still skip the fast path regardless of the flag.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

* **New Features**
  * Per-bucket opt-in header to enable a lifecycle TTL "fast path" that stamps expiration at object write time.

items.title: fix(filer.sync): validate chunk size in FilerSink to prevent 0-byte propagation
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

Block the path in which `filer.sync` contaminates the cluster with 0-byte chunks in issue #9700.

# How are we solving the problem?


The existing `filer.sync` silently skips over malformed chunks or errors.
We prevent 0-byte chunks that do not match the source metadata from being propagated to the target cluster, and fail fast instead.

* First, compare the source metadata with the actual size of the received source chunk, and return an error to block the spread of corrupted data.
* After uploading the chunk that passed the source-side check, verify the uploaded size again, and fail fast if it does not match.

# How is the PR tested?

Added unit tests.

items.title: fix(filer/remote): keep re-cache work alive past caller cancellation (#9174)
items.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #9179 for the failure reported in discussion [#9174](https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/discussions/9174#discussioncomment-16670672): even with the Azure-side parallel block fix, re-caching a ~3 GB Azure blob through the S3 gateway still fails in a loop with `grpc: the client connection is closing` / `context deadline exceeded`, while disk usage on the volume server grows ~500 MB and is then reclaimed by vacuum before converging.

### Root cause

1. `cacheRemoteObjectWithDedup` (`weed/s3api/s3api_object_handlers.go:2996`) wraps the filer's `CacheRemoteObjectToLocalCluster` gRPC call in a 30 s bounded timeout.
2. For a 3 GB blob the filer's chunked download (~32 chunks × ~96 MB) does not finish inside 30 s.
3. When the 30 s fires, the S3 gateway's gRPC ctx cancellation propagates into `doCacheRemoteObjectToLocalCluster`. The first chunk whose `operation.Assign(ctx, …)` sees the canceled ctx sets `fetchAndWriteErr`, and the error path deletes every chunk written so far via `DeleteUncommittedChunks` (`filer_grpc_server_remote.go:281`).
4. boto3's first range GET surfaces as an ETag/InternalError at the 30 s mark; boto3 closes that connection and retries its sibling ranges. The sibling goroutines in the S3 gateway fall through to `cacheRemoteObjectForStreaming`, which uses `r.Context()` — already canceled by boto3's tear-down — so the follow-up gRPC call fails immediately with `Canceled: the client connection is closing`.
5. The retry starts the full download from scratch. It never finishes before the next client-side tear-down, so the loop never converges. The disk growth / vacuum cycle in the log is exactly this.

This pattern is invisible for small blobs (they finish inside 30 s), visible at 2 GB (borderline) and consistently broken at 3 GB+.

### Fix

Inside `CacheRemoteObjectToLocalCluster`, detach the caller ctx with `context.WithoutCancel` before entering the singleflight function. The download now runs to completion regardless of client cancellations, and the cached entry is persisted via `UpdateEntry` (already using `context.Background()`). Subsequent waiters — either singleflight followers, or a fresh retry landing after completion — observe the cached chunks and stream normally.

Same detach pattern is already used elsewhere in the filer/volume write paths (`filer_server_handlers_write.go:53`, `volume_server_handlers_write.go:51`, `filerstore_wrapper.go`, etc.) for exactly this reason: client disconnect must not undo server-side work that later requests will rely on.

Request-scoped values (trace IDs, etc.) are preserved via `WithoutCancel`.

### Not addressed here

- The reporter's secondary observation that there is no guard against unsync/uncache racing with an in-flight cache is a distinct bug — scoping that to its own change.
- No knob added for the S3 gateway's 30 s cap: with this fix, hitting the cap is benign (the fallback streaming path waits on `r.Context()` and joins the in-flight singleflight, or a fresh retry post-completion finds the cached entry).

## Test plan

- [x] `go build ./weed/server/... ./weed/s3api/... ./weed/filer/...`
- [x] `go vet ./weed/server/...` (only pre-existing complaints in unrelated files)
- [x] `go test -short ./weed/server/...`
- [ ] End-to-end validation on the #9174 repro: mount Azure remote, `remote.meta.sync`, GET a 3 GB blob via S3 after `unsync`, confirm the first GET succeeds (possibly after a client-side retry interval long enough for the background cache to finish) and the second GET hits local chunks.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Enhanced resilience of cache operations. Caching processes now continue in the background even when clients disconnect unexpectedly, ensuring cache completion.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

items.title: filer: stop an oversized metadata log flush from wedging the change feed
items.body:
Fixes #10422.

## What happens

One metadata event larger than the volume server's `fileSizeLimitMB` grows the log buffer past that limit, and the flush of that buffer can never be written. `logFlushFunc` retries with no exit, so the blob at the head of the flush queue blocks every later flush: the metadata change feed stalls until the filer is restarted, and the buffered events are lost.

## Reproduced

`weed server -volume.fileSizeLimitMB=16`, then one `CreateEntry` with 20 MB of inline `Content` (what `iceberg_maintenance` does with a compacted parquet file):

```
metadata log write failed /topics/.system/log/2026-07-24/18-12.07c3bb74: upload data
  http://127.0.0.1:8180/1,16ef8dca8a: file over the limited 16777216 bytes
```

73 attempts in three minutes, target file frozen, and a small file uploaded a minute later never reached the log. Each retry also burns a fresh volume assignment.

After the change the same event lands as `size=20972461 chunks=4 [727, 8388608, 8388608, 4194518]`, no failures, and the next minute's flush writes its own log file. `weed filer.meta.tail -timeAgo=1h` replays both events, so the record spanning a chunk boundary reads back fine.

## The three links

**`filer`** — split the flushed buffer into `BufferSize` pieces, on record boundaries where possible so each piece still decodes standalone and keeps the per-chunk cache path. Each piece retries separately so a partial success is not replayed. Log files are already read as a chunk stream with a whole-file fallback when a chunk does not decode standalone, so a record may cross a piece boundary.

**`log_buffer`** — an oversized entry grows the window array to `2*size+4`, and window arrays cycle through `SealBuffer` rather than being freed. One such entry left every later window carrying that size, with `currentSnapshotView` allocating a snapshot as wide as the array per window — the unbounded RSS growth in the report. Drop the array when `SealBuffer` hands it back; growth is on demand, so the next oversized entry reallocates.

**`iceberg`** — `saveFilerFile` had no size threshold, so compaction stored whole merged parquet files as `Entry.Content`. Manifests and metadata JSON stay inline; anything larger is uploaded to volume servers in chunks, assigned through the filer so the path's storage rules apply.

## Tests

`splitLogBuffer` piece sizes, byte-for-byte round trip, standalone decoding, and a truncated tail; the log buffer returning to `BufferSize` after an oversized entry (fails without the fix) while still flushing that entry; and `saveFilerFile` inline/chunked selection with chunk reassembly against a fake volume server.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Large Iceberg data files are now uploaded in chunks; smaller files are still stored inline.
* **Bug Fixes**
  * Metadata log uploads are now split into bounded pieces using record-aware boundaries, with limits adjusted when the server reports oversized writes.
  * Oversized log entries no longer permanently inflate internal flush buffers.
* **Tests**
  * Added unit coverage for chunked uploads (including failure cases), log-buffer splitting/reassembly, size-limit handling, and oversized-entry flush behavior.

items.title: perf(filer): parallelize StreamMutateEntry with path-keyed scheduler
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes the ~500 QPS ceiling reported in #9138. The server-side handler for `StreamMutateEntry` processed one mutation at a time per stream (one goroutine per stream), capping a mount's aggregate metadata throughput at `1 / filer_store_service_time` regardless of client concurrency. On a real filer with typical 1–3 ms commit latency and 12 concurrent rclone processes, this showed as ~500 QPS.

Replace the serial loop with a per-request goroutine admitted by a path-keyed scheduler, adapted directly from filer.sync's `MetadataProcessor` (`weed/command/filer_sync_jobs.go`). Cross-path mutations run in parallel; same-path mutations serialize in arrival order; recursive delete and directory rename act as subtree barriers; directory attribute bumps stay non-barrier so they don't serialize file writes under them.

## Benchmark

2 ms simulated filer-store service delay, 12 client workers (matching the 12-rclone reproducer in #9138):

| handler | distinct paths | same path | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| serial (baseline) | 440 QPS | 441 QPS | 1/serviceDelay |
| semaphore only | 4902 QPS | 4907 QPS | **unsafe** — reorders same-path ops |
| **scheduler (this PR)** | **4934 QPS** | **439 QPS** | correct ordering |

The semaphore-only number shows the upper bound of raw parallelism. The scheduler matches it on distinct paths (the realistic 12-rclone case, ~11× lift) and correctly falls back to serial when the workload touches one path. Peak concurrent mutations at the handler equals client worker count on the distinct-path workload and pins to 1 on the same-path workload, as intended.

## Design (mirrors `MetadataProcessor`)

- Four conflict indexes per stream: `activeFilePaths`, `activeBarrierDirPaths`, `activeNonBarrierDirPaths`, `descendantCount`
- Same `pathConflicts` rules: barrier at p blocks anything at p or under p; same-path file+file blocks; incoming barrier waits for descendants; non-barrier dir (attr bump) never blocks descendants
- `cond.Wait` admission loop bounded by `streamMutateConcurrency = 64` per stream
- No timestamp heap / watermark (mutations aren't event-ordered like `SubscribeMetadata`)

Classification of `StreamMutateEntryRequest`:
- `Create` / `Update` → kind from `Entry.IsDirectory` (dir updates are non-barrier since `UpdateEntry` doesn't rename)
- `Delete` → barrier if `IsRecursive`, else file (target type not carried on the request)
- `Rename` → barrier on both `src` and `dst` paths

## Correctness and safety

- `syncStream` wrapper serializes `stream.Send` across worker goroutines (gRPC `Send` isn't concurrent-safe).
- Handler `wg.Wait()`s in-flight workers before returning on recv EOF/error so no worker writes to a torn-down stream.
- First fatal Send error from any worker propagates as the handler's return value, tearing the stream down.
- Per-stream goroutine cap (`64`) bounds resource use from a single noisy mount.

## Test plan

- [x] `go test -race ./weed/server/` — all scheduler/stream tests pass with race detector
- [x] `TestMutatePathAncestors` — ancestor walk
- [x] `TestClassifyMutation` — each request variant (create file/dir, update file/dir, delete recursive/not, rename)
- [x] `TestPathConflictSamePathFile` / `…BarrierBlocksSamePath` / `…BarrierBlocksDescendants` / `…IncomingBarrierWaitsForDescendants` / `…NonBarrierDirAllowsDescendants` / `…IncomingBarrierWaitsForSamePathNonBarrier`
- [x] `TestAdmitDoneLifecycle` — blocked admit unblocks on Done
- [x] `TestAdmitParallelDistinctPaths` — no self-blocking across paths
- [x] `TestAdmitConcurrencyCap` — cap enforced
- [x] `TestAdmitRenameTwoPathConflict` — rename holds both paths
- [x] `TestAdmitPressureFromManyWaiters` — 100-waiter smoke test, no lost wake-ups
- [x] `TestSchedulerOrderedParallelism` — end-to-end through real gRPC stack on both same-path and distinct-path workloads
- [x] Existing `TestReproStreamSerializationCeiling`, `TestServerSerialVsConcurrentHandler`, `TestStreamSyncVsAsyncClient`, and rename tests still pass
- [ ] Validate against real deployment in #9138 reproducer (12 rclone processes, 4.21 mount)

## Notes

`DeleteRequest` has no `IsDirectory`, so non-recursive deletes classify as `kindMutateFile`. This is safe: non-recursive delete of a directory fails at the store level if non-empty, and same-path serialization still orders the delete correctly against concurrent updates.

Related: #9138, #8770 (introduced the stream handler).
